cards.title: Whose Fault Is It
cards.scenario: Lead volume is up 30 percent but booked jobs are flat. Your instinct says the appointment center is fumbling the calls. Their manager says your leads are tire-kickers. The owner wants the real cause diagnosed within one week. Where do you start?

A.text: Start with the calls, not the blame: pull 30 recorded calls this week and score them, and pull the lead sources for the same period. Data first, in both directions.

B.text: Start with your own leads: audit the sources, keywords, and targeting for quality slippage before pointing at anyone. Check your own house first.

C.text: Start with a joint meeting: both departments in one room, the numbers on the screen, one shared diagnosis before anyone leaves. Finger-pointing never solved anything.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why A wins: it starts with evidence instead of accusations, in both directions, so whichever department is right, the proof decides and the relationship survives. What good discussion sounds like: diagnosing without blaming, and what evidence you owe before you point. What the wrong answers cost: B audits only yourself; C holds a meeting without data.

cards.title: The One-Star Review
cards.scenario: A customer posted a one-star review saying your tech tracked mud through her living room and the office was rude on her follow-up call. Neighbors are already commenting. Your coordinator wants an immediate reply explaining your side. How do you handle it?

A.text: Reply within the hour: apologize, name your standard, invite her to call. Then call her yourself, fix the floors, and follow up until she confirms it is resolved.

B.text: Wait an hour so you reply calm, not defensive. Post a composed response: thank her, own the miss, give a direct line. Handle the substance privately.

C.text: Have the tech reply himself with his side of the story. Ask him to stay polite. Customers trust a working tech over a corporate statement.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: calm beats speed; the public reply is written for every future customer who reads it, while the real fix happens privately by phone. Discussion: speed versus composure, and who the public reply is really for. Costs: A (+150) is decent but rushed and risks sounding defensive; C (+150) puts the tech in the line of fire.

cards.title: How We Answer
cards.scenario: You mystery-shop your own phones and hear three different greetings, one CSR chewing gum, and one who sighs before saying hello. The appointment center manager says they are too busy for this and that greetings do not close jobs. You disagree.

A.text: Record the worst calls and play them at the next team meeting so everyone hears how they sound. Nothing changes behavior like hearing yourself sigh at a stranger.

B.text: Leave the appointment center alone. The manager knows her team and call volume is strong. A greeting script from marketing will only breed resentment.

C.text: Sit with the team, play two calls side by side, one warm and one flat, and ask which company they would hire. Let them write the greeting themselves.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why C wins: it lets the team set the standard they will be held to, then coaches the individuals privately with kindness; people deliver what they helped create. Discussion: scripts versus ownership, and public versus private correction. Costs: A (0) shames people publicly, which destroys the trust you need; B (+150) respects the manager's turf but abandons your own brand at the front door.

cards.title: Timing the Ask
cards.scenario: Your review count is flat. Techs say they ask when it feels right, which means almost never. The office wants an automated email three days later. A consultant says to ask at the door before leaving. Everyone disagrees. What system do you put in place?

A.text: The tech asks at the door, after the thank-you, while relief is fresh. The office sends one follow-up text the next morning with the link. Two touches: one human, one automatic.

B.text: Automate everything: one text after the job closes with the review link, then one reminder later. No tech involvement. Automation never has an off day.

C.text: Mail a handwritten thank-you card a week later with a QR code to the review page. It stands out and feels personal. A kept card outlasts a deleted text.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why A wins: it pairs the human moment (the tech, at the door, when gratitude is fresh) with one automatic reminder, covering both the willing and the forgetful with a simple repeatable routine. What good discussion sounds like: who owns the ask, and why one touch is never enough. What the wrong answers cost: B removes the human moment entirely; C is charming but slow.

cards.title: Whose Jerseys
cards.scenario: Two youth leagues ask you to sponsor them: the league in your best service area, and the league in a struggling neighborhood where your newest tech grew up and now coaches. The budget covers one jersey sponsorship. The owner wants the wealthy area.

A.text: Split the budget and sponsor both leagues at a lower tier. You get a presence in both neighborhoods and nobody feels rejected. Twice the jerseys, twice the visibility.

B.text: Sponsor the league your tech coaches, and tell the owner why: the tech who gives his evenings to those kids is your brand there. Put the logo on those jerseys and show up.

C.text: Sponsor neither and move the money into digital ads with trackable returns. Sponsorships are feel-good spending you cannot measure.

cards.host_note: Principle: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame. Why B wins: it backs the person who gives the company his evenings, visibly and without hedging, which is the kind of loyalty money cannot buy and competitors cannot copy. Discussion: exposure math versus loyalty math. Costs: A (+150) pleases no one fully but stays visible in both places; C (0) abandons the field and leaves the tech standing alone.

cards.title: Ten Thousand Emails
cards.scenario: A broker offers you 10,000 local homeowner email addresses for $300. Your own list is only 2,000 names. The owner says $300 for 10,000 prospects is a no-brainer. Your email tool warns that purchased lists trigger spam complaints and damage sender reputation. What do you do?

A.text: Refuse the purchase: those 10,000 people never asked to hear from you, and a purchased list buys spam complaints. Grow the list one permission at a time.

B.text: Buy the list and send your best offer this week. At $300 the risk is trivial, and one percent response is 100 new prospects. Deal with complaints if they come.

C.text: Buy the list but send only a soft introduction with no hard sell and a clear unsubscribe link. A gentle first touch respects recipients and still reaches 10,000 homeowners.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why A wins: it refuses the shortcut on the grounds that the first impression you buy with a purchased list is the wrong one, and commits to the slow permission-built list. What good discussion sounds like: what a list really represents, and what spam complaints cost beyond the inbox. What the wrong answers cost: B sprays strangers; C softens the spray.

cards.title: Pay to Delete
cards.scenario: A man who was never your customer posted a one-star review claiming your crew damaged his fence. Then he called and offered to delete it for a free AC tune-up. Your service manager says to just do it: one visit costs less than the business the review scares off.

A.text: Refuse the deal, kindly and firmly, and tell your team why. Paying one extortionist teaches the market your reviews are for sale. Report the review and reply with the plain facts.

B.text: Report the review as fraudulent and post a brief reply stating he was never a customer, with records to back it up. Keep generating genuine reviews to push his down.

C.text: Give him the tune-up. It costs one visit and the review disappears today. One tune-up is far cheaper than months of a false one-star review at the top of your profile.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Elongated Shadow. Why A wins: the decision is precedent, not math; what you pay once, you will pay forever, and the crew watches what the company rewards. Discussion: short-term cost versus long-term precedent, and what the team learns from the call. Costs: B (+150) refuses the shakedown but misses the leadership moment with the team; C ($0) pays the extortionist and teaches the whole market that your reviews are for sale.

cards.title: Too Many Emails
cards.scenario: Unsubscribes from your newsletter tripled after you moved from monthly to weekly sends. The content is solid: seasonal tips and reminders. The owner says email is free, so send even more. Your gut says you are burning the list. What do you do?

A.text: Ask the subscribers directly: one-question survey on how often they want to hear from you, and honor the answer. Segment the list so weekly tips go only to opt-ins.

B.text: Keep weekly but make every email shorter, punchier, more visual, so people stop leaving. The problem is boring content, not frequency. Brighter photos and tighter subjects fix it.

C.text: Drop straight back to monthly. The data is unambiguous: weekly tripled unsubscribes, so weekly is wrong. Tell the owner the test failed, show the numbers, and protect the list.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why A wins: it asks the actual humans on the list what they want and honors the answer, treating the inbox as borrowed trust rather than free inventory. What good discussion sounds like: what a list really is, and the cost of burning trust. What the wrong answers cost: B polishes the annoyance; C retreats without learning what subscribers want.

cards.title: Old Prices Online
cards.scenario: A customer waves a two-year-old blog post at your tech, demanding the $69 tune-up price it advertises. The real price is now $129. The post is still live and ranks well on Google. The tech caved on the spot and honored the $69. How do you fix this for good?

A.text: Honor the $69 for this customer and quietly delete the old post. The customer found your published price in good faith, and a doorstep argument costs more than $60.

B.text: Honor the $69, update the post to $129, and add a prices-subject-to-change line to every page. The disclaimer protects you next time, and the post keeps its strong ranking.

C.text: Honor the $69: that price was your published word and the customer trusted it. Then audit the site for stale prices and put one person in charge of keeping numbers current.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: it honors the published word at full cost, then builds a system with a named owner so stale numbers can never embarrass the company again. What good discussion sounds like: what your website promises on your behalf while you sleep. What the wrong answers cost: A patches the symptom; B lawyers the future.

cards.title: Asleep in the Truck
cards.scenario: A neighbor photographed your tech napping in his truck on his lunch break and posted it: this is what $200 an hour buys you. It is spreading fast through local community groups. The tech is mortified and offered to quit. The owner wants him fired today. What do you do?

A.text: Fire him today. The photo is everywhere, the brand damage is real, and examples matter. A public statement that he no longer works here shows the market you have standards.

B.text: Refuse the firing: tell the owner a man napping on lunch committed no crime, and throwing him to the mob teaches every tech the company will not stand behind them.

C.text: Suspend him without pay for a week and post that the behavior was addressed internally. The suspension shows the public you are serious without ending a career.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B wins: it refuses to sacrifice a person to the internet mob, answers the public with honest humanity, and coaches the tech privately on the part he can control. What good discussion sounds like: what you owe your people when the crowd turns. What the wrong answers cost: A destroys trust crew-wide; C performs discipline.

cards.title: Three Logos, One Fleet
cards.scenario: Your 22 trucks carry three different logo versions from three different eras. Full rewraps run about $3,000 per truck. The owner says customers do not hire you over a logo. Your newest tech says his truck looks like it belongs to a different company.

A.text: Rewrap on schedule, oldest trucks first, as a rolling budget line. Every truck is a billboard thousands see weekly, and mismatched trucks tell prospects you are sloppy.

B.text: Leave the trucks alone and move the wrap money into digital ads you can track to booked jobs. Nobody hires an HVAC company over a logo.

C.text: Run a customer contest to vote on which logo to keep, then rewrap to the winner over two years. The vote creates social content, and phasing spreads the cost.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why A wins: brand consistency is a basic done relentlessly, and the fleet is already the company's biggest ad buy; a rolling schedule makes it affordable without a fight. Discussion: whether branding is vanity or infrastructure, and how to sell a slow fix to an impatient owner. Costs: B (+150) defends trackable spend but abandons free impressions; C (+150) turns operations into theater.

cards.title: Who Owns the Account
cards.scenario: Your agency says their firm policy is that they own the Google Ads account, the campaigns, and all performance history. If you leave, you start over from zero. They built it over two years and insist this is industry standard. You are thinking of switching. What do you do?

A.text: Accept it and stay. Rebuilding two years of history costs months of performance, and their policy is genuinely common. Negotiate better reporting instead.

B.text: Leave and rebuild from zero, under an account you own outright from day one. Losing two years of history hurts, but staying hostage to a vendor is worse than a short-term hit.

C.text: Refuse to leave empty-handed: demand the full account transfer in writing, and ban vendor ownership of ad accounts in future contracts. Your money built that history.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Business Serves Its Owner. Why C wins: it asserts that the company's own assets belong to the company, bans the hostage clause going forward, and is willing to pay the rebuild cost rather than stay captured. What good discussion sounds like: what 'industry standard' is really selling you. What the wrong answers cost: A stays hostage; B pays ransom in rebuild.

cards.title: Only the Happy Ones
cards.scenario: Your review software can survey customers first and send the Google review link only to the happy ones. Your rating would climb fast. The owner loves the idea. A competitor was recently penalized by the platform for doing exactly this. What do you do?

A.text: Turn the filter on. The software is legal, everyone filters in some way, and a higher rating brings more calls. Unhappy customers can still find Google on their own.

B.text: Turn it on, but send unhappy customers a private feedback form so you still hear them. Public stars from the fans, private lessons from the critics: the best of both worlds.

C.text: Leave the filter off and ask every customer, happy or not. The unhappy ones teach you the most. A filtered rating is one you cannot trust.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: it gives every customer the same voice, trusts the team with the hard feedback, and earns a rating that means something; filtered stars are borrowed. What good discussion sounds like: what a rating is actually for, and who the filter really serves. What the wrong answers cost: A institutionalizes deception; B deceives politely.

cards.title: Buy Five Stars
cards.scenario: A vendor emails offering 50 five-star reviews for $500, quote, undetectable, from real-looking accounts. Your rating sits at 4.2 while your competitor holds 4.8. Your marketing assistant says everyone does it and the platforms never catch on. What do you do?

A.text: Delete the email and tell the team, exactly once: you do not buy reviews, ever, because the rating has to mean something when a real customer trusts it. Earn the 4.8 the slow way.

B.text: Buy a small test batch of 10 reviews and watch to see if anyone notices. Ten reviews will not trip any filter. If it works cleanly, consider more later.

C.text: Report the vendor to the platform and post about the offer. Publicly refusing turns the moment into a brand asset: customers love a company that says no to cheating.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: it kills the shortcut outright, says the rule out loud to the team once, and commits to the slow honest work; a bought rating is a lie you maintain forever. What good discussion sounds like: whether 'everyone does it' is ever a reason. What the wrong answers cost: B buys the lie retail; C turns refusal into theater.

cards.title: Where to Hang
cards.scenario: You have budget for 10,000 door hangers. Your gut says blanket the new subdivision going up across town. Your dispatcher says to hang them on past customers' streets, because those folks already trust you. The printer needs your targeting decision tomorrow.

A.text: Go all in on the new subdivision. Ten thousand hangers in one area create saturation, and new homeowners have not chosen an HVAC company yet.

B.text: Hang them on streets near your recent five-star reviews, and print the review on the hanger. A real review from their own street is the strongest headline a hanger can carry.

C.text: Target past customers' neighborhoods first, with a referral offer on the hanger. A warm street converts at multiples of a cold one.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Pre-Judge. Why C wins: it treats past customers as the highest-value audience instead of assuming print must mean new territory, and it layers a referral mechanic that multiplies the buy. Discussion: warm versus cold audiences, and what a door hanger can actually do. Costs: A (+150) pays full price for strangers; B (+150) is clever but untested.

cards.title: First Marketing Hire
cards.scenario: Budget is approved for a marketing coordinator. Two finalists: Priya, a sharp recent graduate with great instincts but no industry experience, and Dan, a 15-year print veteran who wants more money and seems set in his ways. The owner leans toward Dan. Who do you hire?

A.text: Hire Priya, and tell the owner plainly why: you are hiring for character and curiosity, not a resume built for yesterday's media. Set 90-day expectations and judge her on results.

B.text: Hire Priya but pay her Dan's higher asking salary to keep her from leaving. Overpaying for the right instincts is cheaper than turnover. Tell the owner the premium buys retention.

C.text: Hire Dan. Fifteen years of media relationships and hard-won judgment beat raw instinct, and the owner backs him. You can teach digital skills; you cannot teach relationships.

cards.host_note: Principle: Character Over Skill. Why A wins: it hires for character, curiosity, and fit with the company's future rather than renting a resume built for yesterday's media, with clear expectations and training to back the bet. What good discussion sounds like: what experience is actually worth, and how to disagree with the owner well. What the wrong answers cost: B buys a past; C tries to purchase loyalty.

cards.title: Who Works the Booth
cards.scenario: The town fair invited you to run a booth this Saturday: great exposure, but it means pulling two techs off paid jobs. The organizer says to just send whoever you can spare. Your service manager refuses to give up techs on a busy Saturday. What do you do?

A.text: Skip the fair. Pulling techs off revenue jobs for a maybe-payoff booth is bad math. The service manager is right; send brochures with a friendlier vendor instead.

B.text: Go, but staff the booth with office volunteers, not techs. The booth needs smiles and sign-up sheets, not tool belts. Offer a comp day and keep the service schedule intact.

C.text: Tell the organizer you will come only if you can do it right, with real techs. Work with the service manager on a slower Saturday or split shifts. Do it well or not at all.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why C wins: it refuses to do the event halfway, works with operations on timing instead of against them, and treats the town as an audience that notices effort. What good discussion sounds like: when to say no to exposure, and who pays for marketing's stage. What the wrong answers cost: A forfeits the town; B sends a hollow booth.

cards.title: Off-Duty Post
cards.scenario: A tech posted a heated political rant on his personal page Saturday night. Monday a customer emails: she saw it, he lists your company as his employer, and she is uncomfortable having him in her home. He calls it free speech and refuses to take it down.

A.text: Talk to him privately and with respect: acknowledge his right to his views, then show him the customer's email. Ask him to unlink the employer or go private.

B.text: Tell him to delete the post today or face a formal write-up. The customer decides who enters her home. A clear consequence sets the standard for the whole crew.

C.text: Quietly reassign him to jobs where no customer has complained and let the post stay. Routing around the discomfort solves the immediate problem.

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why A wins: it treats the tech as an adult, shows him the real consequence instead of issuing an edict, and gives him a choice that preserves both his dignity and the brand. Discussion: rights versus responsibilities, and coaching versus commanding. Costs: B (+150) breeds resentment with an edict; C ($0) hides the problem by routing around it and avoids the real conversation.

cards.title: The Directory Game
cards.scenario: A major home-services directory offers a premium profile for $800 a month with promised top placement. Your competitor pays and ranks above you. Your free listing there already brings a few calls. The rep says every serious company pays. What do you do?

A.text: Pay it. Your competitor sits above you, the rep is right that serious companies pay, and $800 is one good job a month. Visibility on the biggest directory is table stakes.

B.text: Negotiate to $400 and run a six-month test with a dedicated tracking number. If the tracked calls cover the cost, keep it; if not, cancel with data in hand.

C.text: Decline, and put the $800 a month into your own reviews and website. A directory you rent is an asset you will never own; every dollar deepens your dependence on their pricing.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why C wins: it refuses to rent an asset you can never own, and redirects the money into channels no vendor can repossess or raise the rent on. What good discussion sounds like: rented versus owned attention, and what dependence really costs. What the wrong answers cost: A pays the toll forever; B haggles over the cage.

cards.title: Sue the Reviewer
cards.scenario: A furious one-star review claims your tech stole jewelry from a customer's bedroom. Completely false: the tech never entered the bedroom, and she later found the jewelry herself. She refuses to take it down. The owner wants to sue for defamation. What do you do?

A.text: Sue her. The claim is theft, completely false, and a lawsuit shows the market you defend your people. The facts are on your side; even the threat of action often removes a review.

B.text: Talk the owner off the lawsuit: post a calm public reply with the plain facts and leave it there. Suing a customer, even a wrong one, makes you the bully in every retelling.

C.text: Report the review to the platform with your evidence and wait for their process. The platform may remove a provably false claim. Keep generating genuine reviews to push it down.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: it defends the tech with the public truth instead of a lawsuit, refusing to become the bully in every retelling of the story; the record, stated calmly, is the defense. What good discussion sounds like: when fighting for your people means restraint, not war. What the wrong answers cost: A wins the battle and loses the town; C waits on a platform.

cards.title: Junk Leads
cards.scenario: Your pay-per-lead vendor sent 40 leads this month; 30 were renters, wrong numbers, or outside your service area. You paid for all 40. The contract says every lead is billable and credits are at their discretion. Sales is wasting hours chasing dead ends.

A.text: Renegotiate so you pay only for leads that become booked appointments. Shifting the risk onto the vendor aligns incentives. Performance-based pricing ends the quality argument.

B.text: Cancel the vendor and tell the owner the real cost per good lead. Refuse to keep paying for fiction. Then define a billable lead in writing before you sign another contract.

C.text: Keep the vendor and have the appointment center pre-qualify every lead in a two-minute screen before sales touches it. A quick filter protects the sales team's time.

cards.host_note: Principle: Cash Is Life. Why B wins: it stops the bleeding immediately, tells the owner the true cost per real lead, and writes the definition of a billable lead before the next contract; leads are cash and you treat them that way. Discussion: when to fix a vendor versus fire one. Costs: A (+150) trusts the untrustworthy and hopes incentives fix a broken model; C (0) taxes your own team for the vendor's failure.

cards.title: Camera-Shy Tech
cards.scenario: Your best young tech, Marcus, is a natural on camera and customers love him, but he told you privately he hates being filmed and dreads the weekly shoots. The videos earn your best engagement by far. The intern says to keep pushing him because the numbers justify it.

A.text: Make video part of the job description and add it to reviews for every tech. The company needs content, and singling Marcus out was the real mistake. A universal policy is fairer.

B.text: Take Marcus off camera entirely and tell him his comfort matters more than the view count. Ask the crew who enjoys filming and build the series around volunteers.

C.text: Keep Marcus as the face but film him doing real work with no staged lines. You keep your best performer on screen while removing the part he hates most.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B wins: it refuses to trade a person's dignity for engagement metrics, and it solves the content problem sustainably with willing volunteers. Discussion: where the line sits between stretching people and using them. Costs: A (+150) turns a people problem into a policy; C ($0) keeps the pressure on Marcus wearing a nicer mask, solving nothing.

cards.title: His Name on the Truck
cards.scenario: A senior tech asks to put his first name and personal cell number on his company truck, saying customers ask for him by name. Brand guidelines say no personal names on fleet vehicles. He is a top performer and looks genuinely hurt by the no.

A.text: Hold the line on the brand guidelines. The trucks advertise the company, not individuals, and exceptions unravel standards fast. Thank him and keep the fleet uniform.

B.text: Compromise: add his first name to the truck but keep the company phone number. Customers get the personal connection and the company keeps control of the lead flow.

C.text: Sit down with him and ask what he is really after, then build it inside the brand: an ask-for-him bio line, his name on review requests, and an employee spotlight feature.

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why C wins: it hears what he is really asking for, which is recognition, and builds it inside the brand instead of breaking the standard or caving to it. Discussion: the difference between the request and the need behind it. Costs: A (0) dismisses a star to protect a rule; B (+150) is a halfway exception that satisfies no one.

cards.title: Whose Lead Is It
cards.scenario: A $14,000 system replacement closed this week. Your digital agency claims it as a Google Ads lead; the appointment center logged it as a repeat customer first reached by a door hanger. Both want credit, and the owner asks you who is right.

A.text: Credit the appointment center. The CSR did the real work converting the call, and the hanger put your name in that home first. Your team's work deserves the recognition.

B.text: Tell the owner the honest truth: your tracking cannot prove whose lead it was. Show both touchpoints, fix the tracking, and refuse to let either side claim what it cannot prove.

C.text: Split the credit 50/50 and move on. Both touched the customer, and the owner just wants a number. Splitting keeps the peace between the agency and your team.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why B wins: it refuses to award credit for what cannot be proven, shows the owner both touchpoints honestly, and fixes the system instead of picking a winner. Discussion: the difference between influence and sourcing, and what honest reporting costs. Costs: A (0) picks the internal team out of bias, not evidence; C (+150) splits the difference to keep the peace, which is still fiction.

cards.title: Flyers in the Truck
cards.scenario: You want every tech to leave a seasonal promo flyer at each job. The techs say it feels like begging and customers find it pushy. Your best tech flat-out refuses to carry them. The promo is a strong offer and the owner expects full participation. How do you get real buy-in?

A.text: Make it mandatory: every tech leaves the flyer at every job, tracked by unique codes, with a write-up for refusals. The owner expects full participation.

B.text: Ask the resisting techs what feels wrong, and listen: maybe the flyer is ugly or the timing bad. Redesign it with their input and pilot it with volunteers.

C.text: Offer a $25 bonus for every flyer that turns into a booked job, tracked by the code. Money motivates where mandates fail, and holdouts can opt out without punishment.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why B wins: it treats the techs' resistance as information instead of insubordination, and gives them authorship, which is the only motivation that survives the first awkward week. What good discussion sounds like: mandates versus ownership, and what resistance is telling you. What the wrong answers cost: A buys compliance and quiet sabotage; C rents enthusiasm.

cards.title: The Overspend
cards.scenario: Your agency spent $9,000 on search ads against your $6,000 monthly cap and never told you. They say the extra $3,000 brought excellent leads and they were just being proactive. The owner wants their head. The leads did look decent. What do you do?

A.text: Let it go this once, since the leads were genuinely good. Warn them firmly it cannot happen again, but do not make a scene. Punishing initiative teaches vendors to play it safe.

B.text: Make the agency absorb the full $3,000 overage, in writing, and put hard caps with automatic pause rules in the agreement. Good leads do not excuse spending what was never theirs.

C.text: Split the overage: you cover half, they absorb half, since the spend produced leads. Then put the cap rules in writing. Fairness keeps the relationship healthy.

cards.host_note: Principle: Delegate, Don't Abdicate. Why B wins: it draws the hard line that delegated spend stays inside delegated limits, with automatic enforcement so the lesson survives everyone's good intentions. What good discussion sounds like: the difference between initiative and authority. What the wrong answers cost: A teaches them the budget is decorative; C rewards the breach.

cards.title: Prove It or Kill It
cards.scenario: The owner wants to kill your digital ad spend because you cannot show which jobs came from it. Tracking is messy: calls get logged wrong, techs forget to ask how customers heard of you, and the agency just says to trust the process.

A.text: Tell the owner the truth first: the tracking failure is yours, not the channel's. Own the miss, fix the tracking, and report honest numbers monthly, good or bad.

B.text: Build a simple tracking sheet this week: unique numbers on every ad and a required source field on every ticket. Ask the owner to hold spend steady for 60 days.

C.text: Agree with the owner and cut digital by half now. If you cannot prove it works, do not defend it. Move the savings into mail and door hangers, where every response is countable.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why A wins: it names the real problem, your tracking and not the channel, before proposing anything, which is the only way the owner can trust the next number you show him. Discussion: owning a miss without groveling, and what honest reporting costs. Costs: B (+150) fixes the tool but skips the accountability; C (+150) destroys a channel over your own failure but at least admits the gap.

cards.title: Never a Customer
cards.scenario: A one-star review appears from someone whose name is nowhere in your system. It claims a tech was rude at her door. Your dispatcher is certain she was never a customer. To anyone reading it, though, the review looks completely real.

A.text: Reply publicly with warmth, not suspicion: apologize that she had this experience, say you cannot find her in your records, and invite her to call you directly.

B.text: Report it as a fake review and post a short reply stating she was never a customer. Never apologize for what never happened; a firm correction protects your team.

C.text: Offer her a free service call in the public reply. Generosity disarms critics, and if she accepts, you turn a critic into a customer.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why A wins: it leads with care for the person rather than suspicion about the review, which is the only reply that can win either way. Discussion: whether warmth looks weak, and who the reply is really for. Costs: B (+150) sounds defensive; C (0) tries to buy a stranger and rewards a possibly fake review.

cards.title: Two Sets of Numbers
cards.scenario: Your dashboard says marketing drove $400,000 this quarter. Accounting says $310,000. The gap: your agency counts every touch, including jobs that started as plain referrals. The owner spotted the difference and his trust is shaken. What do you do?

A.text: Defend the dashboard. Marketing touches influence jobs even when accounting credits them elsewhere. Walk the owner through the model so he understands what the numbers measure.

B.text: Blame the agency's reporting and make them rebuild everything from your CRM data. The inflated numbers came from their dashboard, not yours. Fix the vendor and move on.

C.text: Own it openly: tell the owner your numbers were inflated by loose attribution. Rebuild from closed, paid jobs only, and publish the method in plain words.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why C wins: it owns the inflation openly, rebuilds the report from closed paid jobs only, and publishes the method in plain words; trust returns through smaller true numbers. What good discussion sounds like: influence versus sourcing, and why the owner stopped believing the dashboard. What the wrong answers cost: A defends fiction; B blames the vendor for your own report.

cards.title: Whose Home Is It
cards.scenario: Your before-and-after photos earn the best engagement on your page. Then a customer calls, upset: her messy utility room is in front of 2,000 followers and she never agreed to photos. The tech says she smiled. The post is your top performer. What do you do?

A.text: Take the post down and apologize directly. Then make a written consent form the tech gets signed before every picture. Thirty seconds at the door prevents a month of headaches.

B.text: Keep the post up but blur anything identifying and strip her name. The photos show your work quality. Add a consent checkbox to the service agreement going forward.

C.text: Call her yourself, apologize without excuses, and take the post down while still on the phone. Then coach the tech: a home is personal, and a smile is not permission.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why C wins: it treats her home and her dignity as more important than the post's performance, and turns the incident into coaching the tech rather than punishing him. What good discussion sounds like: what consent actually looks like at the door. What the wrong answers cost: A is procedural without the real apology; B keeps up what she asked to remove.

cards.title: Fifty Percent Off
cards.scenario: The local paper offers a full-page ad at a steep discount if you run a 50-percent-off tune-up coupon in it. The owner loves the idea: cheap ad, huge response. Your service manager warns that deep-discount customers never convert to full price later. What do you do?

A.text: Run it. The ad space is cheap, the phones will ring hard, and volume covers the margin hit. Tell the techs to upsell every coupon job aggressively.

B.text: Kill the coupon and show the owner the math: 50 percent off trains the market to wait for the next coupon and fills the schedule with price shoppers. Discounts rent, never buy.

C.text: Run a smaller version: 20 percent off, capped at 100 coupons, first-time customers only. Caps and limits turn a gamble into a measured test.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Price Before Value. Why B wins: it runs the real math on what deep discounting trains the market to do, and refuses to rent customers at the cost of the brand. What good discussion sounds like: who a 50-percent-off customer really is, and what the second coupon costs. What the wrong answers cost: A fills the schedule with shoppers; C is a smaller version of the same trap.

cards.title: The Broken Form
cards.scenario: Your website's get-a-quote form has been broken for a full week, and nobody noticed until a customer emailed about it. The web vendor blames a plugin update. You are furious, and the owner wants your assurance this will never happen again.

A.text: Fire the vendor and bring the website under direct control with a freelancer who answers to you. A vendor who lets your lead form die for a week is not watching your business.

B.text: Ask the vendor for a written incident report and a monitoring proposal before deciding. Acting on anger risks a hasty switch. Decide with a clear head next week.

C.text: Fix it today, then set a weekly 60-second test: someone submits the form every Monday and confirms the lead arrives. Put it on a checklist with a name attached.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why C wins: it builds a named, weekly routine that catches the failure in days instead of weeks, and it keeps the vendor on a leash made of process rather than anger. Discussion: what you can never outsource, and the cheapest insurance in the building. Costs: A (+150) acts on fury and switches vendors mid-crisis; B ($0) studies the problem while the form stays broken, dithering dressed as diligence.

cards.title: Guaranteed Number One
cards.scenario: A slick agency rep promises the number one Google spot within 30 days for $2,500 a month, and adds that your current agency is incompetent. Your marketing lead is tempted because two competitors outrank you. The rep wants a decision by Friday.

A.text: Thank him and decline. State the policy: you do not buy dishonest shortcuts. Ask your current agency for a written plan with milestones.

B.text: Sign a three-month trial. If he delivers the top spot, the $7,500 pays for itself. Add a cancellation clause so you can walk away.

C.text: Switch only if he puts the guarantee in writing with a full refund. A written promise protects you. Keep your current agency on 30-day notice meanwhile.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why A wins: a vendor who opens by lying about guarantees and insulting competitors will run your money the same way; the policy protects the company from its own temptation. Discussion: whether the ends ever justify the vendor. Costs: B ($0) hands money to a dishonest vendor and rewards the exact behavior you punish in your own people; C (+150) is tempted by the guarantee but at least demands it in writing.

cards.title: Pay for Referrals
cards.scenario: You want to launch a customer referral program. The owner likes a $50 service credit to the referrer. Your top tech says customers would rather have $50 cash. Finance worries cash rewards will get abused by employees gaming the system.

A.text: Go with the $50 service credit. It keeps the money inside the company, brings the referrer back, and cannot be gamed for cash. Finance can track every credit cleanly.

B.text: Pay $50 in cash, fast: within a week of the referred job closing. Add simple rules: one reward per referred household, employee referrals excluded.

C.text: Skip the formal program and surprise referrers with thank-you gifts when dispatch notices them. Formal programs create paperwork; surprise gifts create delight.

cards.host_note: Principle: Pay for What You Want Repeated. Why B wins: it pays for the actual behavior you want, fast and in a form people value, with simple rules that prevent gaming; a program nobody uses is the most expensive kind. Discussion: cash versus credit psychology, and where gaming really comes from. Costs: A (+150) keeps money in-house but feels like a coupon; C ($0) is not a program at all, just hope dressed as goodwill.

cards.title: Her Full Address
cards.scenario: Your website features a glowing video testimonial, and beneath it you printed the customer's full name, street address, and the system she bought. She calls, furious: she never agreed to the address being published and feels unsafe. The page converts well. What do you do?

A.text: Take the street address down at once but keep the video and her first name. Removing the address solves her safety concern. Add a consent form going forward.

B.text: Offer her a free year of maintenance in exchange for keeping the testimonial. Fair compensation makes the exposure worth her while, and most customers accept a reasonable trade.

C.text: Take the testimonial down today and apologize directly. Then change the process: written consent, with the customer shown exactly what will be published before anything goes live.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why C wins: it puts her sense of safety ahead of a converting page, apologizes without hedging, and rebuilds the process around real consent shown in advance. What good discussion sounds like: what consent actually requires, and what a testimonial is worth. What the wrong answers cost: A keeps what she asked to remove; B tries to buy her fear.

cards.title: Their Ads Lie
cards.scenario: A competitor's radio ad says, quote, unlike some companies, we never use scare tactics. Everyone in town knows it means you after last year's controversy. Your sales manager wants a response ad naming them. Your agency says a counterpunch will get attention.

A.text: Ignore it and double your own positive ad schedule. Responding gives them free publicity and looks defensive. Stay positive and stay loud.

B.text: Refuse the counterpunch and put the energy into being visibly excellent: more genuine reviews, more community presence, techs worth praising by name. Win by deserving the business.

C.text: Run the counterpunch ad. Name them, deny the charge, and list your certifications. If you stay silent, listeners assume the accusation is true.

cards.host_note: Principle: Problems Are Tests. Why B wins: it treats the attack as a test of character rather than a media problem, and answers with the only thing that actually changes minds, which is deserved reputation. Discussion: when silence is strength versus when it is surrender. Costs: A (+150) stays positive but passive, without the excellence engine to back it; C (+150) starts a radio war you cannot win.

cards.title: Wrong Number Printed
cards.scenario: Twenty thousand mailers just landed in homes carrying your old phone number, which now belongs to a pizza shop. The printer admits the error, but the contract limits their liability to a reprint. The pizza shop owner is annoyed. Your owner is furious.

A.text: Act today: strike a deal with the pizza shop to forward your misdialed callers, and post a correction notice on your site. This week, negotiate the reprint.

B.text: Eat the loss and reprint immediately at your own cost. Speed matters more than blame; every day the wrong number circulates, you lose jobs you will never get back.

C.text: Sue the printer for the lost business. Their error cost you real leads, and a liability cap should not protect plain negligence. A strong legal response warns every future vendor.

cards.host_note: Principle: Handle It While It's Small. Why A wins: it recovers the leads first and argues about contracts second, because every day of missed calls costs more than the print bill; urgency ordered correctly. Discussion: what to fix in what order when everything is on fire. Costs: C ($0) performs anger with a lawsuit the contract already blocks, burning weeks while calls go to a pizza shop; B (+150) pays twice but at least gets correct mailers out fast.

cards.title: Cut the Budget
cards.scenario: The owner tells you to cut the marketing budget 20 percent this quarter. Your instinct is to trim a little from every channel so nothing dies. Your media buyer warns that spreading the cut everywhere will starve your winners along with your losers.

A.text: Cut every channel by 20 percent evenly. It is fair and fast, and every vendor shares the pain. No single channel collapses, and you can restore funding next quarter.

B.text: Pause the two newest channels entirely and protect the proven ones at full funding. New experiments are the riskiest spend, and the owner asked for a cut.

C.text: Gather the team, show the real cost-per-lead by channel, and cut the losers completely while protecting the winners. Tell the owner plainly which cuts hurt.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: it turns a cut into a performance decision driven by real numbers, and it protects the people producing results instead of punishing everyone equally. Discussion: which numbers to trust, and how to tell the owner bad news honestly. Costs: A ($0) starves the winners along with the losers, the exact failure the buyer warned about; B (+150) kills learning but at least protects proven channels.

cards.title: The Long Contract
cards.scenario: A radio rep offers a strong rate if you sign a 12-month contract, but you have never advertised on radio. Your gut says test first. She says the discount disappears Friday and her manager is pressuring her to close it.

A.text: Sign the 12-month deal. The discount is real money and radio is proven for home services. Locking the rate protects you, and a full year gives the campaign time to build.

B.text: Sign for 12 months but demand a 90-day out clause in writing. You get the discounted rate and the exit ramp. If the spots do not produce calls, you leave cleanly.

C.text: Tell her kindly you never sign year-long commitments on untested channels, and offer a three-month test with clear metrics. She has a quota and you have a budget.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why C wins: it replaces a pressure decision with a system, a short test with agreed metrics, and treats the rep as a person while holding a firm line on how you buy. Discussion: how you buy media as a policy, not a mood. Costs: A (+150) buys blind; B (+150) rents a discount with an escape hatch you will argue about.

cards.title: Billboard or Pixels
cards.scenario: A billboard company offers the best board in town, by the highway interchange, for $4,000 a month. Your digital campaigns cost $4,000 and produce 60 tracked leads. The owner loves seeing the name in lights. You can afford one. Which do you choose?

A.text: Take the billboard. That interchange is seen by 80,000 drivers a day, nearly every homeowner in the market. Being the famous name is what makes the phone ring in July.

B.text: Keep the digital spend and pass on the board. Show the owner the math: 60 tracked leads at your close rate is real revenue, while the billboard's return is a guess.

C.text: Take the billboard for three months, with a unique phone number on it to track every call. If it does not produce, walk away clean. A short test answers it with data.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: it answers a fame question with arithmetic, protects the proven producer, and offers the owner a measured test instead of a flat no. What good discussion sounds like: when visibility is worth buying blind, and how to say no to the owner usefully. What the wrong answers cost: A buys a guess; C rents an experiment at full price.

cards.title: The Cherry-Picked Callback List
cards.scenario: A callback list of 40 stale leads sits untouched while your CSRs cherry-pick the easy fresh inbound calls. The list is two months old. Your newest CSR admits she skips it because those people already said no, and the veterans agree with her.

A.text: Throw the list away. Two-month-old leads are dead and everyone knows it. Tell marketing to stop sending stale batches.

B.text: Work the list with the team for one morning. Open each call honestly about the gap in time. Split the list fairly, set a daily target, post revivals on the board.

C.text: Offer a spiff for every stale lead revived, paid weekly. Money moves behavior faster than speeches. The list gets worked with energy instead of resentment.

cards.host_note: Principle: Be a Learning Machine. Why B wins: the leader demonstrates the skill first, then makes the work fair, measurable, and visible. Discussion cues: leading from the phones; reopening stale conversations honestly. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) bribes instead of teaching; A (0) throws away paid-for leads.

cards.title: The Cancelled Maintenance Agreement
cards.scenario: A customer calls to cancel his maintenance agreement, frustrated after a tech was rude last month. Your CSR offers the standard retention script. The customer says nobody at your company cares.

A.text: Offer a free tune-up for the rude visit. A tangible make-good beats words, and the agreement stays active. Track whether the freebie actually saves the agreement past ninety days.

B.text: Process the cancellation quickly and move on. Some customers cannot be saved; the script already failed once. More time on a lost cause wastes everyone's afternoon.

C.text: Slow the call and listen fully to what the tech did. Apologize for the specific behavior, not a script line. Then ask what would make staying worthwhile.

cards.host_note: Principle: Problems Are Tests. Why C wins: it treats the complaint as a diagnosis opportunity, addresses the root cause with the tech, and lets the customer define the remedy. Discussion cues: listening before offering; closing the loop with the tech. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) throws a free tune-up at a trust problem; B ($0) quits on a saveable customer.

cards.title: The Script Error
cards.scenario: You discover the phone script promises a free second opinion that the company never approved. Three CSRs have quoted it this week. Two callers already booked expecting it free, and a third is on hold now.

A.text: Quietly fix the script and say nothing to anyone. The two booked callers will forget the word free by appointment day. Announcing the error just invites complaints you do not need.

B.text: Honor the promise for the callers who heard it and fix the script today. Tell the team exactly what happened. Our words on the phone are the company's word.

C.text: Honor it for the two booked callers and quietly tell CSRs to stop quoting it. The problem stays contained and nobody's confidence takes a hit.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: it honors the spoken promise at real cost and tells the team the truth, which is what makes future scripts trustworthy. Discussion cues: spoken promises as contracts; owning mistakes openly. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) hides the lesson; A (0) hopes callers forget.

cards.title: The Personal Cell Shortcut
cards.scenario: Your top CSR, Sam, gives customers his personal cell number for faster service. Customers now text him at all hours, he answers on weekends, and two other CSRs are copying him, with no posted hours.

A.text: Replace personal numbers with a monitored team text line with posted hours. Customers keep the speed they liked, and no one person becomes the single point of failure.

B.text: Do nothing until something goes wrong. Sam is an adult managing his own boundaries. Intervening now would punish initiative that is working.

C.text: Let it continue since customers love the access. Sam's booking numbers are up and the personal touch works. Do not fix what is not broken. Revisit quarterly to check for burnout.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Business Serves Its Owner. Why A wins: it replaces a fragile hero dependency with a system that outlasts any one person, without losing the speed customers liked. Discussion cues: heroes vs systems; giving customers access safely. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) lets burnout and liability grow; B (0) is the same gamble with a tripwire attached.

cards.title: The Competitor's Price List
cards.scenario: A caller offers to email you a competitor's full price list so you can beat every number. Your CSR is excited: with the list, the team could undercut every quote and win every price shopper.

A.text: Take the list and use it quietly. The caller volunteered it freely. Matching every number is smart business, and nobody will trace it back.

B.text: Decline the list but thank the caller warmly. Using a competitor's private pricing feels wrong. The team should win on value, not stolen numbers.

C.text: Decline the list and explain why in business terms. Stolen pricing collapses when the rival changes a number. Undercutters never learn to sell value.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why C wins: it declines on business grounds the team can respect (fragile pricing, atrophied selling skill) and redirects to the value conversation. Discussion cues: competing on value vs price; what shortcuts cost the team's skill. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) moralizes without teaching; A ($0) takes stolen data.

cards.title: The Discount to Save a Cancellation
cards.scenario: A long-time maintenance customer calls to cancel, saying money is tight. Your CSR, Elena, wants to offer 20 percent off on the spot to save the account. She has no authority to discount and asks you mid-call.

A.text: Tell Elena to offer the discount and sort out the paperwork later. Saving the account matters more than process. Back your people first and fix the system second.

B.text: Thank the customer for their years first. Ask what tight means; sometimes they need a skipped quarter, not a cheaper price. Set Elena's discount range afterward.

C.text: Have Elena hold firm with no discount and read the script exactly as written. Discounting trains customers to threaten cancellation every renewal.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why B wins: it diagnoses before prescribing and turns the moment into coaching, so Elena grows instead of just getting a yes. Discussion cues: questions before discounts; giving CSRs real authority ranges. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) rewards going around the system; C (150) reads a script at a human moment.

cards.title: The Lead Fight
cards.scenario: Two CSRs, Luis and Dana, both claim the same hot inbound lead. Luis answered first; Dana had been nurturing the caller last week. Voices are rising on the floor within earshot of other calls.

A.text: Split the commission between them and tell them to stop arguing. Fairness ends the fight fastest. Both walk away with something. Move on without another word.

B.text: Separate them from the floor immediately. Decide the lead by the written house rules, not who argues loudest. Clarify the rule this week; a public fight costs more than any job.

C.text: Give it to Luis since first touch wins, plain and simple. The rule is easy and everyone understands it. Dana will get the next hot lead. Write the rule into the playbook.

cards.host_note: Principle: Handle It While It's Small. Why B wins: it stops the public fight now, decides by rule not favoritism, and prevents the next fight. Discussion cues: house rules for lead ownership; what customers overhear. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) picks a winner and a loser; A ($0) teaches that arguing pays.

cards.title: The Out-of-Area Request
cards.scenario: A caller outside your service area wants a system replacement, a $14,000 job. Your CSRs are told to decline out-of-area work, but this caller found you through a strong referral source who sends steady work.

A.text: Book it. Fourteen thousand dollars is fourteen thousand dollars, and the techs can drive the extra miles. Turning away a referral insults the sender.

B.text: Decline politely and end the call. The service area exists for routing efficiency, and exceptions become the rule fast. A thank-you note protects the relationship.

C.text: Refer them to a trusted company in their area, then call your referral source to thank them personally. A stretched route risks a bad job and a lost referrer.

cards.host_note: Principle: Keep Customers for Life. Why C wins: it serves the caller, honors the referrer, and protects the company from a job it cannot do well. Discussion cues: when to break the service-area rule; referrals as relationships. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) wastes the referral warmth; A (0) chases revenue into a bad route.

cards.title: The Wrong Number Lead
cards.scenario: A high-intent lead from marketing arrives with a disconnected phone number. Your CSR, Tom, wants to mark it dead and move on. The address looks real and the request was for a full system replacement.

A.text: Mark it dead and move on to live leads. CSRs have enough real opportunities without chasing ghosts. Chasing disconnected numbers burns selling time.

B.text: Have Tom try once more tomorrow, then mark it dead. One extra attempt shows diligence without turning CSRs into detectives. The log shows marketing the lead got a fair shot.

C.text: Work the lead: verify the address, send a letter, try alternate contacts, log every attempt. A disconnected number is a puzzle, not permission to throw it away.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Pre-Judge. Why C wins: a full system replacement lead is worth real effort, and the standard it sets is that leads are precious. Discussion cues: what working a lead actually means; marketing handoff accountability. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) quits on a high-value lead; B (150) quits one attempt too early.

cards.title: The Falsified Call Log
cards.scenario: You discover CSR Anthony has been logging outbound calls he never made to hit his activity metric. His booking numbers are average. He says everyone pads a little and the metric is unrealistic.

A.text: Confront Anthony with the evidence and apply the stated consequence. Tell the team without naming him. Fake logs poison every number-driven decision the business makes.

B.text: Lower the activity metric so nobody needs to pad it. Unrealistic targets create dishonest logs. Reset the target with the CSRs in the room.

C.text: Adjust his numbers quietly and tell him to be more careful. The metric is the problem, not Anthony. Fix the target instead of punishing the person.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why A wins: it treats falsified data as the serious breach it is, applies the stated consequence, and teaches the team why honest numbers matter. Discussion cues: data integrity as a business issue; consequences without humiliation. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) rewards padding by lowering the bar; C ($0) covers up dishonesty.

cards.title: The Crying New Hire
cards.scenario: New CSR Sofia takes a brutal call, a customer screams at her for ten minutes, and she is crying at her desk between calls. The queue is building and her next call is already ringing.

A.text: Tell Sofia if she cannot handle the heat, the phones may not be for her. Put her back on immediately. Coddling creates fragile CSRs who quit anyway.

B.text: Pull Sofia off the queue for fifteen minutes. Debrief quietly: what the caller needed, what she did well, one thing to try next time. A minute after abuse is human, not weak.

C.text: Tell Sofia to shake it off and take the next call. Every CSR survives a first brutal call, and getting back on the phones is the fastest way through it.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B wins: it gives her recovery plus coaching, turning the worst call into her fastest lesson, and names the humanity as strength. Discussion cues: recovery time vs coddling; debriefing brutal calls. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) sends tears into the next call; A ($0) threatens a new hire for having feelings.

cards.title: The Caller Who Wants a Manager
cards.scenario: An upset caller demands a manager. You are in a hiring interview that cannot be interrupted. Your senior CSR, Rosa, has handled these calls well before but has no manager title and is nervous about the demand.

A.text: Brief Rosa in ninety seconds on the facts, what she can offer, and your full backing. She speaks with your authority today. Debrief her after.

B.text: Have Rosa promise a manager callback within the hour and take a message. The interview cannot be interrupted. Give Rosa a deadline she can quote, and make sure you hit it.

C.text: Step out of the interview for five minutes and take the call yourself. Nothing signals customers come first like a manager who drops everything.

cards.host_note: Principle: Delegate, Don't Abdicate. Why A wins: it deputizes Rosa with real authority and a debrief, growing a leader instead of abandoning or rescuing her. Discussion cues: ninety-second briefings; authority vs title. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) delays the remedy; C (150) teaches the team that everything stops for a demand.

cards.title: The Spanish-Speaking Caller
cards.scenario: A Spanish-speaking caller needs help and no bilingual CSR is on shift. Your CSR, Amy, is using a translation app and the call is going badly. The caller sounds frustrated and confused.

A.text: Take over and slow the call down, confirming understanding at each step. Book with a written Spanish confirmation. Then build a real plan for bilingual coverage.

B.text: Have Amy keep struggling through with the app and book the soonest slot. Effort counts and the appointment is what matters. The tech can sort out details on site.

C.text: Ask the caller to have an English-speaking family member call back. It is the fastest path to a clear booking. The family member translates better than any app.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why A wins: it serves the person in front of you now and fixes the coverage gap for next time. Discussion cues: language access as service; turning a bad call into a staffing plan. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) outsources the work to the caller's family; B ($0) books a confused customer.

cards.title: The Shift Swap Denied
cards.scenario: CSR Miguel asked to swap a Saturday shift to attend his daughter's recital. You denied it for coverage, and his energy has cratered. His call quality is slipping and teammates notice.

A.text: Remind Miguel the decision is final and his attitude needs to reset now. Every denial cannot become a slump. Professionalism means leaving it at the door.

B.text: Tell Miguel if his personal life affects his calls, maybe this is not the right job. Standards do not bend for recitals. Coverage comes first; document the conversation.

C.text: Revisit the denial before it hardens into resentment. Hunt for coverage yourself and ask the team directly. If it cannot be covered, show Miguel what you tried.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why C wins: it reopens the decision with real effort and honesty, showing Miguel he matters beyond his shift. Discussion cues: revisiting your own calls; partial solutions when full ones fail. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) demands a reset without earning it; B ($0) threatens a good employee over a recital.

cards.title: The Dispatcher Who Badmouths
cards.scenario: Your CSR overhears the dispatcher telling a tech that a customer is a nightmare and to get in and get out. The CSR looks shaken. The dispatcher is a 12-year veteran the techs idolize.

A.text: Tell the CSR she misheard or is overreacting. Twelve years earns the benefit of the doubt, and dispatch vents under pressure. Making an issue of it divides the office.

B.text: Ask what is driving his frustration privately; veterans do not vent for no reason. Listen first, then be clear his words shape every tech's attitude.

C.text: Talk to the dispatcher privately today and name what was overheard. Ask what is frustrating him first, then set a clear expectation and follow up.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why C wins: it hears the veteran out before judging, names the real impact, and sets a clear expectation with follow-up. Discussion cues: private directness with veterans; words as weather. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) listens well but never quite lands the expectation; A (0) dismisses a shaken employee.

cards.title: The Holiday Skeleton Crew
cards.scenario: The Saturday of a holiday weekend: two CSRs call in sick, phones ring nonstop, and the on-duty techs are booked solid through Monday. Wait times are climbing past ten minutes, and the queue keeps growing.

A.text: Be straight: honest wait times, real openings starting Tuesday, emergency line for true emergencies only. One honest weekend beats a packed board of broken promises.

B.text: Promise Monday slots you do not have, hoping cancellations open room. Optimism keeps callers from hanging up. The schedule usually finds a way to absorb a few extra jobs.

C.text: Offer same-day booking anyway and figure out staffing later. Telling callers the truth about the backlog sends them to competitors. A booked job can always be moved later.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why A wins: honest capacity, real bookings, and the emergency line kept for real emergencies. Discussion cues: what honesty costs on a brutal day; protecting the emergency line. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) sells slots that do not exist; B (0) is the same lie dressed up as optimism.

cards.title: Six Sick-Day Reschedules
cards.scenario: Your best tech calls in sick on the busiest Tuesday of the month. Six customers are confirmed for today. Two are elderly, one has a baby, and the rest are routine maintenance visits.

A.text: Triage the six by urgency before calling. No-heat and baby households get first offer today. Routine maintenance moves to the next open day.

B.text: Offer everyone the same choice: wait for the sick tech or take a sooner slot with another tech at a discount. Choice keeps people happy.

C.text: Call all six in board order and push each to the next available day. It is the fairest method. The routes stay clean without last-minute juggling.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why A wins: it triages by real urgency instead of treating all six as equal. Discussion cues: how to rank urgency fairly; owning bad news directly. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) treats a baby's no-heat like a routine tune-up; B (150) discounts what should be triaged.

cards.title: The Dominating Senior CSR
cards.scenario: Your senior CSR, Kevin, talks over teammates on shared calls, corrects them loudly, and takes the best inbound leads for himself. Two newer CSRs told you privately they dread shifts with him and are job hunting.

A.text: Move Kevin to outbound-only so his talent produces without poisoning the inbound queue. The newer CSRs get room to grow. Set a target so it is not a demotion.

B.text: Do nothing and let the floor sort itself out. Kevin books the most revenue by a wide margin. Top producers earn some latitude with their style.

C.text: Talk to Kevin privately with specifics and dates. How he treats teammates is part of his job. Set a clear expectation, check in weekly, and close the loop with the newer CSRs.

cards.host_note: Principle: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves. Why C wins: it addresses the behavior directly with specifics and a follow-up, and closes the loop with the people who spoke up. Discussion cues: private directness vs public hints; protecting people who raise issues. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) rearranges around the problem; B (0) sacrifices the team for one producer.

cards.title: The Phone Diagnosis Request
cards.scenario: A caller describes a banging noise and asks your CSR to diagnose it over the phone and quote the fix. The CSR is new and eager, wants to help, and is reaching for the price book while the caller waits.

A.text: Have the CSR walk the caller through a troubleshooting checklist of safe, simple homeowner steps. If it works, you saved a truck roll. Either way the CSR stayed useful.

B.text: Honor the caller's worry without guessing the cause. A real diagnosis needs eyes on the system. Book the visit as the fastest path to a certain answer.

C.text: Let the CSR give a best guess with a clear disclaimer that it is not official. Callers feel helped immediately. The booked visit will correct any wrong guess on site.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why B wins: it sets the expectation (never guess a diagnosis) while honoring the rep's good instinct and the caller's fear. Discussion cues: empathy that still books; coaching eager new hires. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) risks a wrong guess on the record; A (0) turns CSRs into phone techs.

cards.title: The Double-Booked Afternoon
cards.scenario: Dispatch double-booked two jobs in the same 2 to 4 p.m. window with one tech. Both customers confirmed. One is a warranty callback with no revenue, the other is a $900 repair. Dispatch wants you to pick which customer gets moved.

A.text: Call both customers and ask which one is willing to move. It is transparent and nobody feels singled out. The volunteer probably needed the flexibility anyway.

B.text: Keep the $900 repair and push the warranty callback to tomorrow. Revenue pays the bills and warranty work can wait a day. The tech's time goes where it earns the most.

C.text: Keep the warranty callback and move the $900 repair, with a firm tomorrow-morning window. Bumping a promise for revenue teaches customers our word has a price.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: it protects the promise already made even at a revenue cost, which is the sharper long-term call. Discussion cues: promise-keeping as a revenue strategy; preventing double-books. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) sells the company's word for $900; A (150) outsources the decision to customers.

cards.title: The Competitor on the Line
cards.scenario: A caller says a rival company quoted them half your diagnostic fee. Your newest CSR, Priya, is about to trash-talk the competitor to win the booking. You can hear her winding up as the caller waits on hold.

A.text: Take the call, thank the caller for the comparison, and reframe the fee: full check, written findings, a tech inside the window. Tell Priya tearing down rivals makes us look small.

B.text: Take the call and quietly match the competitor's fee to save the booking. Tell Priya winning matters more than the script. Keep it off the books so nobody expects the same freedom.

C.text: Let Priya finish, then coach her after. A little competitive fire keeps CSRs sharp, and mid-call coaching would shake her nerve. Debrief what worked and what crossed the line.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why A wins: it answers the real question (what am I buying?) instead of attacking the rival. Discussion cues: value reframing; when to step onto a call live. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) lets a bad habit form on a live call; B (150) teaches secret discounting.

cards.title: The Caller Who Is Cursing
cards.scenario: A customer whose appointment window was missed is shouting profanity at Dana, your calmest CSR. Dana's voice is shaking. The customer demands the job done today and a discount, and the board is already full.

A.text: Tell the customer the language stops or the call ends, then rebook at the next opening. Dana watches you set a hard boundary. The schedule stays intact and the standard is clear.

B.text: Take the call from Dana with a handoff that protects her. Thank her by name, let the customer vent, then own the missed window. Offer tomorrow's first slot and a firm arrival time.

C.text: Coach Dana live with written prompts so she learns to handle heat herself. Have her offer tomorrow's first slot. Stay on the line in case she needs rescue.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B wins: it protects the CSR publicly, owns the failure honestly, and gives a real remedy without inventing capacity. Discussion cues: handoff language that preserves dignity; when absorbing abuse stops being the job. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) leaves a shaken rep to drown; A (150) sets a boundary with no remedy attached.

cards.title: The Price Shopper
cards.scenario: A caller asks point-blank what you charge for a tune-up. Your policy is value before price, but callers increasingly hang up when CSRs deflect. Your newest CSR wants a straight answer she is allowed to give.

A.text: Keep deflecting and book the visit first; the policy exists for a reason. Price-first callers rarely convert, and giving the number feeds competitor comparisons. Hold the line.

B.text: Give an honest range, what it includes, and what changes it, then pivot to booking. Dodging the question sends the caller to the next listing.

C.text: Refuse to discuss numbers and give the price only in person. Mystery creates perceived value. Serious buyers will book blind if the brand is strong.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why B wins: it respects the caller's direct question with a real range, then earns the booking with specifics instead of evasion. Discussion cues: ranges vs exact quotes; when deflection backfires. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) bleeds callers to competitors; C (0) confuses secrecy with value.

cards.title: The Hold-Time Spike
cards.scenario: Abandoned calls spike between noon and 1 p.m. when two CSRs take lunch together. Hold times triple. The team says staggering lunches is unfair because everyone wants the noon hour.

A.text: Hire a part-time lunch-cover CSR for the noon hour. The cost is small next to lost bookings. Everyone keeps their preferred lunch.

B.text: Assign lunch by seniority, with the newest CSRs covering noon. Seniority has its privileges and the phones stay covered. Simple and enforceable.

C.text: Stagger the lunches and explain why. Every abandoned call is a customer who needed us and gave up. Rotate early and late slots weekly so the burden is shared.

cards.host_note: Principle: One Department: Customer Service. Why C wins: it puts the customer ahead of convenience, shares the burden fairly, and uses real numbers instead of authority. Discussion cues: fairness through rotation; making metrics visible. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) spends money to avoid a scheduling decision; B (0) builds a caste system.

cards.title: The Warranty Question
cards.scenario: A caller asks whether her repair is under warranty. Your CSR, Tom, does not know the policy and the warranty binder is missing from the office. The caller wants a yes or no before she books.

A.text: Tom verifies and calls back within the hour. Document the policy where the team can find it. A wrong guess costs free labor or a furious customer.

B.text: Have Tom say yes to get the booking and let the tech sort it out on site. A booked job is a booked job. The tech can explain the fine print in person.

C.text: Tell Tom to guess based on the system's age and keep the line moving. CSRs cannot research every question while the queue builds. Close enough is usually right on warranty calls.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why A wins: it refuses to guess on a question where wrong costs real money or real trust, and fixes the missing binder for everyone. Discussion cues: the cost of confident wrong answers; documenting what the team needs. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) books on a lie; C ($0) normalizes guessing.

cards.title: The Skipped Confirmation Calls
cards.scenario: Marcus leads the team in outbound bookings, but he stopped making next-day confirmation calls to save time. No-shows on his booked jobs jumped from 8 percent to 22 percent in three weeks. He calls confirmations busywork and says his numbers prove the approach works.

A.text: Keep his quota and give him a one-tap text template so confirmations take seconds. Partial confirmation beats none. Review the no-show data monthly and adjust if it climbs.

B.text: Show Marcus his no-show rate tied to the skipped confirmations. Reset his target so he can confirm every job and still hit it. A confirmed slot respects the customer's whole day.

C.text: Leave Marcus alone and let his numbers speak. No-shows are a dispatch problem, not his. Slowing your top producer costs more revenue than missed appointments.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why B wins: it treats the unglamorous step as the job and resets the target so the standard is achievable. Discussion cues: connecting skipped basics to real customer cost; targets that reward the full job. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) works around the behavior with a half-measure instead of fixing it; C (150) sacrifices the schedule to protect one producer's numbers.

cards.title: The Twice No-Show
cards.scenario: A customer has no-showed twice, each time tying up a two-hour window. She calls to book a third time, insisting this time is different, and she sounds sincere. Your policy is unclear on repeat no-shows.

A.text: Book her with a card-on-file deposit applied to the visit. Two missed windows cost real tech time. Frame the deposit as standard policy, not punishment.

B.text: Refuse the booking: the company cannot hold windows for repeat no-shows. The team will respect a manager who protects their time. The slot goes to a reliable customer.

C.text: Book her again with no changes. Turning away a willing customer costs revenue, and punishing past mistakes earns bad reviews that live online forever.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why A wins: it solves the repeat problem with a policy instead of hope or rejection. Discussion cues: deposits as mutual protection; policy vs punishment. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) repeats the loss; B (150) throws away a willing customer.

cards.title: The End-of-Month Overbook
cards.scenario: It is the last week of the month and the owner wants the board packed. Your lead CSR suggests booking jobs into days that are already full, borrowing from next month's capacity to hit the number.
