A.text: Say no openly. Borrowed days become next month's no-shows and angry customers. Do not spend next month's trust to buy this month's number. Take capacity data to the owner.

B.text: Do it quietly and have CSRs say the board looks open. The owner gets his number. Next month's problem is next month's problem. Keep it between you and the lead CSR.

C.text: Refuse and report the suggestion to the owner immediately. The lead CSR needs to know gaming the board is a firing-level offense. Draw the line hard and publicly.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Elongated Shadow. Why A wins: it refuses to fake capacity, explains the cost plainly, and carries the real issue (capacity) upward with data. Discussion cues: month-end pressure vs honest boards; managing up with numbers. Wrong-answer costs: C (150) turns a coaching moment into a threat; B ($0) lies to customers and the owner at once.

cards.title: The Review Threat
cards.scenario: A customer threatens a one-star review unless you move his appointment up two days. The board is genuinely full. Your CSR is panicking and wants you to bump someone else to make it stop.

A.text: Bump the least urgent job quietly and move him up two days. One moved customer who never knows is cheaper than a one-star review. The review would live online forever.

B.text: Call his bluff and dare him to post the review. Bullies back down when confronted. The team will love the backbone. Coach the CSR afterward on holding the line calmly.

C.text: The schedule is full. No bumping another customer to quiet a threat. Offer the earliest real opening with a firm window; caving once teaches every caller threats work.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: it refuses to trade another customer's promise for quiet, and names the precedent caving would set. Discussion cues: review threats as a policy question; calming a panicking CSR. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) sacrifices a stranger for peace; B (0) picks a fight instead of holding a line.

cards.title: The Squeeze Play
cards.scenario: Dispatch asks you to squeeze an extra job onto a board that is already full, promising the techs can handle it. Your CSRs would have to call three confirmed customers and push their windows later to make room.

A.text: Hold the board. The three confirmed customers got our word first, so offer the new caller tomorrow's first slot. Moving confirmed customers teaches the team our word is flexible.

B.text: Do it and call the three moved customers yourself. Revenue today beats comfort today. They will understand when you explain a family has no heat.

C.text: Refuse the squeeze but offer the new caller tomorrow's first slot with a small discount. Nobody's promise breaks. The discount costs less than the trust you would spend.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: it protects promises already made even though the extra job is tempting, and names the lesson the team would learn otherwise. Discussion cues: short-term revenue vs promise-keeping; how to say no to dispatch. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) still breaks confirmed promises; C (150) trains callers to expect payment for waiting.

cards.title: The Pattern at One Address
cards.scenario: Your CSR notices the same address has called four times in two months for no-heat issues, each booked as a separate dispatch. The techs keep patching it. Nobody has flagged the pattern.

A.text: Keep booking as usual. Each call is revenue and the techs are handling it. Diagnosing equipment is not the appointment center's job.

B.text: Send the pattern to the service manager with the call history. Book the next visit as a senior-tech diagnostic, not another patch. Her catch may prevent a midwinter failure.

C.text: Tell the CSR to stop overthinking and just book the calls. Pattern-spotting is above her pay grade. The system works as designed. Extra analysis slows the phones down for everyone.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: it turns frontline observation into action, escalates with data, and upgrades the visit type instead of repeating the failure. Discussion cues: CSRs as pattern-spotters; escalating across departments. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) repeats the failure for revenue; C ($0) punishes the thinking that prevents callbacks.

cards.title: The Robotic Script Reader
cards.scenario: New hire Jamal reads the greeting script word for word in a flat monotone. His booking rate is half the team average. He told another CSR he feels silly saying the words, is thinking about quitting, and his trainer is out of ideas.

A.text: Tell Jamal the script is mandatory and his numbers have thirty days to improve. Standards are standards. Put the expectation in writing so it is clear.

B.text: Sit with Jamal on live calls and help him find his own voice inside the script. Same promises in his own phrasing. The script is the skeleton, he is the person.

C.text: Pair Jamal with your top CSR to shadow for a week and mirror her exactly. Imitation is the fastest teacher. Hearing it done with energy shows him it can be done.

cards.host_note: Principle: Train or Remove. Why B wins: it coaches instead of threatening or surrendering, keeping the standard while building the person toward it. Discussion cues: script as skeleton vs cage; coaching cadence for strugglers. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) manages by ultimatum; C (150) copies a copy without addressing his actual block.

cards.title: The Scripts Feel Fake
cards.scenario: At the morning huddle, three CSRs say the scripts feel fake and customers can tell. Booking rates are fine, but the team sounds flat, one CSR dreads the greeting, and two others nodded along.

A.text: Let them drop the scripts for a week and compare booking rates to the prior month. Data settles the argument better than opinions. If rates hold, the scripts were the problem.

B.text: Tell them feelings do not matter and the script stays exactly as written. Booking rates are fine, which proves the script works. Professionals do the job as designed.

C.text: Ask which lines feel false and rewrite them together, keeping every promise intact. The script is a tool, not a cage. Reward the honesty so it keeps coming.

cards.host_note: Principle: Safe to Speak. Why C wins: it treats the complaint as useful data, improves the tool with the people who use it, and rewards the honesty. Discussion cues: co-writing scripts; promises vs phrasing. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) gambles a week of bookings; B ($0) crushes the feedback loop.

cards.title: The Personal Calls at the Desk
cards.scenario: Hold times are rising and you notice CSR Jenna taking personal calls at her desk between inbound calls. When confronted, she says she only takes them when the queue is empty, but the queue has not been empty all week.

A.text: Ignore it since Jenna's booking numbers are still decent. High producers earn flexibility with the small stuff. Policing personal calls feels petty and small.

B.text: Ban phones at desks for everyone effective immediately. One person's habit becomes the team's excuse. A blanket rule is easier to enforce. Apply it to managers too.

C.text: Show Jenna the numbers behind her queue-empty claim. Personal calls happen on breaks. Every hold minute is a waiting customer. Recheck the metrics with her weekly.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: it confronts with evidence rather than blanket rules or avoidance, and follows up on the metric. Discussion cues: data in difficult conversations; expectations with check-ins. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) punishes the whole team for one person; A ($0) excuses it for decent numbers.

cards.title: The Waived Dispatch Fee
cards.scenario: An angry customer demands the $89 dispatch fee be waived after a reschedule. Your CSR has no authority to waive fees and the caller is escalating. The fee policy is clear and firm.

A.text: Waive this one fee and document why: our reschedule, a calm explanation, a manager's approval. An $89 stand on our own mistake risks a customer worth thousands.

B.text: Hold the fee with no exceptions and let the caller cancel if he wants. Policies only work when they never bend. The CSR learns to hold the line under pressure.

C.text: Tell the CSR to waive fees whenever a caller gets loud. Loud callers post reviews, and the fee is small. Keeping the phones quiet is worth more than $89.

cards.host_note: Principle: You Deserve Your Results. Why A wins: it makes a judgment call with a documented rule, balancing the customer's lifetime value against a policy worth keeping. Discussion cues: exception rules vs no exceptions; documenting judgment calls. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) loses a good customer over $89; C ($0) trains the team to fold at the first raised voice.

cards.title: The Blame Game After the Audit
cards.scenario: A call audit reveals CSRs routinely skip the required safety question about gas appliances. When asked, the team blames the script: it sounds awkward, customers get confused. The skipped question is a compliance requirement.

A.text: Write up every CSR who skipped it, without exceptions. The rule was clear and the audit proves noncompliance. Consequences will fix the behavior faster than coaching.

B.text: Own it as a leadership miss: the team flagged the awkward line and you never fixed it. Rewrite it with the team so it sounds human, retrain everyone, and re-audit in two weeks.

C.text: Blame the auditors and dispute the findings as a gotcha exercise. The question confuses customers. Stand between your people and the auditors.

cards.host_note: Principle: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame. Why B wins: the leader takes the blame for the ignored feedback, fixes the wording with the team, and holds the compliance line with a re-audit. Discussion cues: owning leadership misses; making compliance sound human. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) punishes people for a leadership failure; C ($0) shoots the messenger.

cards.title: The VIP Referral
cards.scenario: A dealer who sends you steady work calls: his mother needs same-day service and expects the royal treatment. The board is full, and bumping a stranger for a VIP will be noticed by your CSRs.

A.text: Be honest: the board is full today, but his mother gets tomorrow's first slot, a senior tech, and your follow-up call. Tell the team what you did and why.

B.text: Bump a routine maintenance job and fit her in today. The dealer's referrals are worth thousands every year. One moved customer will never know why.

C.text: Squeeze her in without telling the team how it happened. The dealer stays happy and the board absorbs one more. What the CSRs do not know cannot hurt morale.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: it honors the referrer with real priority without secretly breaking a stranger's promise. Discussion cues: transparent VIP treatment; what the team learns from watching. Wrong-answer costs: B (150) trades a stranger's promise for peace; C ($0) runs a hidden exception that rots trust.

cards.title: The After-Hours Emergency
cards.scenario: At 9:40 p.m. a caller reports a gas smell and asks for a tech tonight. Your on-call tech is not answering his phone. The caller's voice is rising with panic, and she has small children in the house.

A.text: Keep trying the on-call tech while keeping the caller on the line. Assure them help is coming and stay calm for them. Do not leave a panicked caller alone on hold.

B.text: Tell the caller to shut off the gas and wait until morning, since you cannot dispatch a tech you cannot reach. Document the call and follow up at dawn.

C.text: Tell the caller to leave the house now and call 911 or the gas utility first. A gas smell is beyond our scope. Keep working the phones and call back with a status.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why C wins: it puts the human's safety ahead of the dispatch problem and gives clear next steps instead of false comfort. Discussion cues: knowing the limits of your scope; what to say when you cannot deliver. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) promises what you cannot deliver; B (150) gambles a family's safety on usually minor.

cards.title: The Do-Not-Call List
cards.scenario: Your outbound campaign list includes past customers, but twelve of them previously asked not to be called. Your top CSR says those twelve are probably over it by now and wants to dial anyway. The list would boost his numbers.

A.text: Call but open with a warm, brief apology. It respects the request while giving the campaign its best shot. Most people will not mind one polite check-in.

B.text: Dial them anyway; past customers are fair game and requests go stale. If anyone complains, apologize and move on. The bookings are worth the small risk.

C.text: Pull the twelve names off before dialing. A no-call request is a promise; breaking it trades the company's reputation for one campaign. Scrub the list and document it.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: it treats an opt-out as a promise and fixes the list systemically. Discussion cues: reputation vs one campaign; documenting customer requests. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) apologizes while doing the thing; B ($0) dials into complaints and possible violations.

cards.title: The Late-Shift Teammate
cards.scenario: CSR Nicole is late three shifts in a row, and morning hold times are suffering. She is a single mom whose childcare fell through. She is embarrassed, has not asked for help, and is a strong performer otherwise.

A.text: Write her up according to policy without exceptions. The policy is clear and the team sees favoritism if you bend it. Consistency keeps the team trusting the rules.

B.text: Ask Nicole privately what changed and what would fix it. Offer a shifted start or a temporary swap while she finds care. Document it and hold her to it with kindness.

C.text: Ignore it and hope the childcare resolves itself in a couple of weeks. Confronting a struggling single mom feels cruel. Most personal crises pass on their own.

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why B wins: it solves the actual problem with dignity, documents the arrangement, and keeps accountability intact. Discussion cues: temporary accommodations vs permanent exceptions; kindness with documentation. Wrong-answer costs: A (150) punishes a solvable problem; C (0) hopes it away.

cards.title: The Promised Install Date
cards.scenario: To close a hesitant buyer, your advisor promises installation this Friday. The production schedule is already full through next Wednesday. The customer rearranged her work week around Friday.

A.text: Own it: Friday was promised without checking the board; the real opening is next week. Apologize, confirm with production. Rule: check the schedule before promising dates.

B.text: Call and move the install to next Thursday; the schedule filled faster than expected. Apologize, offer a small credit, and have production confirm the new date in writing.

C.text: Bump another job to fit this one in Friday. The advisor made a promise, and the company keeps its word even at another customer's expense. The new sale matters more.

cards.host_note: Principle: Handle It While It's Small. Why it wins: owning the error fast, with a confirmed new date and a process fix, stops one bad promise from becoming a habit. What good discussion sounds like: players distinguish between keeping a promise (good) and stealing from another customer to do it, and land on the schedule check as the real fix. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) apologizes but never fixes the root cause; C ($0) robs Peter to pay Paul.

cards.title: The Extra Find
cards.scenario: During a paid repair visit, your tech finds a cracked heat exchanger plus a worn blower motor and a filter housing that is not sealed. The repair the customer approved is already done. The dispatcher asks if the tech should present the rest now.

A.text: Present all three findings with photos and prices, and push to finish everything today while the truck is stocked. One trip beats two, and the problems are visible now.

B.text: Quote the full replacement now, since a cracked exchanger usually means the furnace is near end of life. Offer the motor and housing repairs only if he declines the new system.

C.text: Show the cracked exchanger first: photos and the safety risk in plain words. Present the motor and housing separately and say what can wait. Let them choose with no pressure.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why it wins: separating the safety issue from the optional work, with honest timelines, lets the customer decide without feeling ambushed. What good discussion sounds like: players wrestle with the line between thorough and pushy, and notice the safety finding earns the right to mention the rest. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) feels like an ambush and kills trust; B (150) leaps to replacement before the customer is ready.

cards.title: The Tire Kicker Marathon
cards.scenario: Your advisor just spent three hours with a homeowner who asked fifty questions, took notes, and will definitely call three competitors. The advisor is frustrated and behind schedule.

A.text: Praise the thoroughness. Detailed shoppers become the most loyal customers. Three hours now buys a buyer who never price-shops again. Generosity with time is the brand.

B.text: Qualify early and kindly: in fifteen minutes learn timeline, decision makers, and cost of waiting. Research trip? Give an overview, leave the proposal, and reclaim the afternoon.

C.text: Change nothing and let the advisor manage his own calendar. One long appointment is an outlier, not a trend. Trust him to read the room and protect his own time.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Pre-Judge. Why it wins: early, kind qualification protects the advisor's day without prejudging the shopper, who still gets real help. What good discussion sounds like: players distinguish between judging a person (never) and qualifying a situation (always), and see the fifteen-minute check does both. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) romanticizes a blown schedule; C (0) treats one bad afternoon as no signal at all.

cards.title: The Review Scheme
cards.scenario: Your online rating slipped to 3.9. A marketing friend offers a service that posts glowing reviews from accounts that were never customers. Nobody would know, and the phones would ring again.

A.text: Refuse outright and earn it back. Read every complaint, fix the patterns, and build follow-up earning genuine reviews. Fake reviews are fraud; a liar in public lies in the home.

B.text: Buy the reviews. A 3.9 is quietly killing the close rate, the fakes will bury among real ones, and every competitor does this. Revenue first; the phones ring again within weeks.

C.text: Buy a small batch to cross 4.0, then stop and earn real ones. A limited run limits the risk and buys the team breathing room to fix the real issues. A bridge, not a lifestyle.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Elongated Shadow. Why it wins: the company's public face is the owner's shadow, and fake reviews make the shadow a lie customers eventually catch. What good discussion sounds like: players admit the 3.9 hurts and the offer tempts, then reckon with what discovery would do to every real review earned since. What the wrong answers cost: B ($0) commits fraud for a metric; C (150) commits a smaller fraud and calls it a bridge.

cards.title: The Sticker Shock
cards.scenario: The Hendersons need a full system. When your advisor presents $14,800, Mrs. Henderson goes quiet and says they cannot afford it. Your advisor believes a smaller repair could buy them two or three years.

A.text: Trim the margin and drop the extended labor warranty to sharpen the price now. A smaller number keeps the deal alive today, and beats a repair that only delays the inevitable.

B.text: Pivot to financing and reframe the price as a monthly payment. Most sticker shock is cash flow, not the total. Once the monthly figure fits, the objection usually fades.

C.text: Ask their budget, then lay the honest repair beside the replacement with real costs and expected life. Let them choose, and stand behind whichever path they pick.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why it wins: laying the honest repair next to the replacement, with real numbers, respects the family's actual budget instead of selling past it. What good discussion sounds like: players admit how tempting the instant discount is, then see the repair option often returns as a replacement customer who trusts you. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) trains discount reflexes; B (150) dodges the real budget conversation.

cards.title: The Poached Lead
cards.scenario: An advisor notices a hot lead assigned to a struggling teammate and works it on the side, closing the deal and keeping the full commission. The teammate found out and the sales floor is splitting into camps.

A.text: Give the commission to the assigned advisor and discipline the poacher plainly. Leads are company property; taking a teammate's lead is theft, not hustle. Protect the system.

B.text: Let the closer keep the commission; he did the work and the company got the revenue. Reassign the teammate to easier leads. Assignments are guidelines, not guarantees.

C.text: Praise the hustle publicly. Hunger is what the scoreboard rewards; the team learns opportunities belong to whoever moves first. Make him the example and watch the floor hunt.

cards.host_note: Principle: You Are Not the Doer. Why it wins: this is really about the manager's system: leads belong to the company and the assignment process, and protecting it protects every advisor including the poacher. What good discussion sounds like: players admit B feels like celebrating a winner, then see the floor-wide tax when nobody trusts assignments anymore. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) rewards the grab and demotes the victim; C ($0) canonizes theft as hustle.

cards.title: The Skipped Calculation
cards.scenario: Your top closer has a full day of appointments and asks to skip the load calculation on a straightforward ranch home, sizing from the existing unit like the old days. He promises the numbers will be fine.

A.text: Let him skip it this once. He is your best producer, the house is simple, and matching the old size has worked for years. His judgment has earned some latitude on a packed day.

B.text: Require the full calculation on every job, no exceptions, and help him rework the day to fit it. It separates a proposal from a guess, and protects you when systems underperform.

C.text: Skip the calculation but disclose that sizing follows the existing equipment. The disclosure covers the company and the closer keeps his pace. Transparency, without the paperwork.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why it wins: the unglamorous calculation is the basic done brilliantly, and exempting the star tells everyone the standard is optional. What good discussion sounds like: players notice the shortcut never gets blamed until the callback, and connect the install crew's pain to the sales table's hurry. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) creates a two-tier standard; C (150) discloses a guess instead of doing the work.

cards.title: The Stalling Customer
cards.scenario: The Parkers loved the presentation but keep saying they need more time to decide. The proposal expires Friday. Your advisor wants to extend the price another 30 days to stay friendly.

A.text: Ask what the extra time is for, then solve that specific thing. If it is money, rework the options or financing. Keep Friday real, and book the follow-up call before you hang up.

B.text: Extend the price hold 30 days and check in weekly. Friendliness keeps you in the running; pressure pushes them to a competitor. Respect today becomes referrals tomorrow.

C.text: Text them Friday with a one-day-only discount to force the decision. A sharp incentive breaks stalls, and even at a lower margin the job keeps the crew busy next week.

cards.host_note: Principle: Follow Up Forever. Why it wins: naming the specific stall and solving it beats both endless friendliness and manufactured pressure. What good discussion sounds like: players realize 'more time' is never the real objection, and practice asking what the time is for without sounding pushy. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) funds indefinite stalling with your price hold; C (0) spends margin to buy a decision a question could have earned.

cards.title: The Silent After the Install
cards.scenario: Crews finish installs and disappear. No follow-up call, no review request, no referral ask. Your best marketing, happy customers, is going quiet, and the shrinking review count proves it.

A.text: Have the crew ask for the review before leaving the driveway. Satisfaction peaks at completion, and the tech's direct ask beats any later email. It takes ten seconds.

B.text: Leave customers alone after the install. Nobody likes being pestered, and a quiet customer is a satisfied customer. The truly delighted review on their own.

C.text: Make follow-up a process, not a personality. Two days after install the office calls, sends happy customers the review link, and asks for two names. Track it like a job step.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why it wins: a tracked office process produces reviews and referrals every week, while hoping the crew remembers produces them sometimes. What good discussion sounds like: players see the satisfaction check doubles as an early warning system for unhappy customers, which is worth as much as the reviews. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) depends on the crew's mood at 5pm; B (0) confuses silence with satisfaction.

cards.title: The Discount Commission
cards.scenario: Your pay plan pays advisors on total revenue, so they discount freely to close deals. Average margin per job has slid six points in a year. The advisors insist the market demands it.

A.text: Pay on gross margin, not revenue, with accelerators for holding price. Show each advisor what their discounts cost them last quarter. When paychecks reward margin, discounts die.

B.text: Cap discounts at five percent without manager approval. The ceiling stops the worst bleeding, and the approval step makes them think twice before giving money away.

C.text: Raise list prices ten percent so discounts land where margins used to be. Advisors keep their closing tool, customers feel they won, and the math repairs itself quietly.

cards.host_note: Principle: Pay for What You Want Repeated. Why it wins: compensation on margin aligns the advisor's wallet with the company's, and the personal math makes the lesson stick. What good discussion sounds like: players see the six-point slide was designed by the old plan, not the market. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) treats the symptom with a ceiling people will game; C (0) inflates prices to fund the same bad habit.

cards.title: The Blame Circle
cards.scenario: At the Monday sales meeting, the team spends twenty minutes blaming the appointment center, the pricing, and the weather for last week's lost deals. Nobody mentions their own presentations.

A.text: Let them vent; the week was rough. Morale matters more than one unproductive meeting, and the team refocuses when the schedule fills. A heard team sells harder all week.

B.text: Redirect without shaming: put one lost deal on the board and ask what the advisor controlled at each step. Go first with one of your own so the team sees honesty is safe.

C.text: Shut the blame down hard: excuses do not close deals. The meeting covers this week's pipeline only; dwelling on last week loses the floor. Discipline resets the room fast.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why it wins: examining one real deal, with the manager going first, replaces the blame ritual with a learning ritual. What good discussion sounds like: players admit the weather has never once been the real reason, and feel the difference between being shamed (C) and being led (B). What the wrong answers cost: A ($0) funds the complaint habit with meeting time; C (150) rules by fear and drives the blame underground.

cards.title: Think About It
cards.scenario: Every advisor hears it daily: I need to think about it. Most say okay and leave the home. The follow-up pile grows week after week, and the thinking rarely turns into a signed proposal.

A.text: Counter on the spot with your best concession to collapse the thinking time. A decision today is worth a small discount, and a stated objection beats two weeks of guessing.

B.text: Move on fast and fill the pipeline with fresh appointments. Think-about-it buyers close at miserable rates; advisor hours are better spent with new buyers than chasing maybes.

C.text: Treat think about it as the start, not the end. Ask warmly what they want to think through and address it before leaving. Set a callback time; named steps get decisions.

cards.host_note: Principle: Follow Up Forever. Why it wins: isolating the real question and booking a named next step converts thinking into deciding. What good discussion sounds like: players practice the warm version of 'what exactly' and discover most stalls are one solvable worry, not indecision. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) bribes a decision the customer has not made; B (0) throws away buyers the company already paid to meet.

cards.title: The Discount Reflex
cards.scenario: Your advisor follows up on a week-old unsold estimate and the homeowner hesitates. His instinct is to offer 10 percent off on the spot to save the deal, before he has asked what is actually holding her back.

A.text: Reopen around the problem, not the price. Ask what changed, revisit the photos, and answer the hesitation. Discount only if money is the true barrier, never as the opening move.

B.text: Offer the 10 percent now. The estimate is cooling, and a fast discount shows you want the work. A closed deal at a thin margin beats a perfect price that never signs.

C.text: Restate the proposal and price hold by email, then move to fresh leads. Chasing old estimates burns selling hours. Ready customers call back on their own.

cards.host_note: Principle: Follow Up Forever. Why it wins: re-diagnosing the hesitation before touching price keeps the discount as a tool instead of a reflex. What good discussion sounds like: players catch themselves reaching for the discount first, then see how often the real barrier was never money. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) teaches every customer to stall; C (150) abandons warm buyers the company already paid to acquire.

cards.title: Is It Really Necessary
cards.scenario: A homeowner looks at the proposal and asks point blank whether the new system is truly necessary or whether your advisor is just selling. The old unit still runs, though it is 19 years old and uses phased-out refrigerant.

A.text: Tell him it is absolutely necessary and the old unit could fail any day. At 19 years the breakdown is a matter of time. Customers want confidence from their advisor, not a maybe.

B.text: Agree it might last another year and suggest he wait, proving you are not pushy. The honesty impresses him, and when it fails he calls you first. Play the long game.

C.text: Answer with evidence, not a verdict: the phase-out timeline, repair history, efficiency gap, cost of a mid-summer failure. Then say it could run another season; the call is his.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why it wins: laying out the facts and refusing to issue the verdict respects the customer's intelligence and removes the feeling of being sold. What good discussion sounds like: players realize the question is a trust test, not a technical one, and that evidence answers it better than confidence. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) uses fear as a closer; B (150) performs honesty by surrendering a sale he may genuinely need.

cards.title: The Proposal Typo
cards.scenario: Your advisor is about to email a signed proposal when she notices the price is $1,900 higher than the quote worksheet. The customer already agreed verbally to the lower number on the worksheet during the visit.

A.text: Send the higher number and hope she never compares it with the worksheet. Most homeowners miss line-item differences, and the worksheet was only a working document.

B.text: Call her first, explain the error plainly, and honor the worksheet number she agreed to. Fix the proposal to match and alert your manager. One costly correction beats lost trust.

C.text: Send the higher number with a note about updated material costs. Customers accept that prices move, and the note explains the increase without reopening the negotiation.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why it wins: honoring the number she agreed to turns a costly error into the story she tells her neighbors. What good discussion sounds like: players weigh the $1,900 against the lifetime value of a customer who trusts you completely, and the math flips. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) bets she will not notice, which is contempt disguised as strategy; C (150) launders the error as a market change.

cards.title: The Angry Homeowner
cards.scenario: A homeowner yells at your advisor over a rescheduled install, using language nobody should hear at work. The advisor holds it together in the moment, then sits in his truck shaking.

A.text: He probably provoked it; review his calls for attitude problems. Customers rarely explode for no reason. Find what he did wrong and correct it. Accountability starts at home.

B.text: It comes with the territory; shake it off. Every advisor meets one of these, and a thick skin is part of the job. The next appointment needs him present.

C.text: Check on him as a person first, not a producer. Let him talk it through, then take the next customer call yourself. Debrief: what set him off, and what can the team change?

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why it wins: caring for the person first, then debriefing the trigger, keeps a good advisor in the seat and improves the process. What good discussion sounds like: players feel how different C feels from the truck, and admit the 'shake it off' speech is how companies lose good people quietly. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) abandons him to process it alone; A ($0) blames the victim of verbal abuse, which teaches the team management will not stand with them.

cards.title: The Inflated Resume
cards.scenario: You learn your newest advisor has been telling customers he spent ten years as a service tech. He was a helper for one summer. Customers trust him more because of the story, and his close rate is the team's best.

A.text: Confront him: the invented background ends today. Real training so his confidence is earned, not performed. Tell the team plainly why lying to customers ends careers here.

B.text: Keep him selling, stop the story, and file a written warning. His numbers are real and the team needs the production. Correct the claim quietly and keep the revenue flowing.

C.text: Say nothing while the numbers hold. Customers are happy and a little resume polish harmed nobody. Pulling your best closer over a backstory punishes success.

cards.host_note: Principle: Character Over Skill. Why it wins: a closer who lies about who he is will lie about what the customer needs; training the skill honestly is the only keep. What good discussion sounds like: players feel the revenue temptation honestly, then ask what happens when a customer discovers the lie and tells the internet. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) files a warning while keeping the liar in living rooms; C ($0) institutionalizes fraud as long as it converts.

cards.title: The Wrong Fit Job
cards.scenario: A homeowner wants your company to relocate his ductwork through a finished attic, a job your crews rarely do and your advisor cannot price with confidence. He is ready to sign today and the commission is large.

A.text: Take the job. Revenue is revenue, and the crew will figure out the attic work once opened up. Price it with a healthy cushion and let production sort the details on install day.

B.text: Sign him at a premium covering a subcontractor for the attic work. He gets one point of contact, you keep the relationship, and the sub absorbs the risk you cannot price.

C.text: Tell him plainly this is outside your crews' weekly work; he deserves a contractor who does it daily. Refer him to one you trust, and invite him back for the system replacement.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Pre-Judge. Why it wins: this one is about judging the job honestly rather than the customer; declining work you cannot do well protects the customer and your name. What good discussion sounds like: players admit how hard it is to walk past a ready signature, then name the callbacks and reviews that follow jobs sold on hope. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) sells confidence you do not have; B (150) rents competence you cannot supervise.

cards.title: The Slipping Close Rate
cards.scenario: Marco's close rate has dropped from 38 percent to 24 percent over two months. He blames the leads. Your gut says something changed in his presentations, but you still have no proof yet.

A.text: Move Marco to your best lead source for a month. If the leads were the problem, his numbers bounce back. If not, you have the answer without a confrontation.

B.text: Pull the numbers: close rate by lead source, average ticket, where deals stall. Ride two appointments to find where momentum dies. Coach that step and recheck in two weeks.

C.text: Give it another month. Close rates move in cycles, and Marco was a top performer not long ago. Intervening early can rattle a good rep; patience with proven people usually pays.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why it wins: diagnosing with segmented data and live observation finds the real leak instead of litigating opinions about lead quality. What good discussion sounds like: players admit how often they manage by gut, then see that two ride-alongs reveal what two months of debate never did. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) wastes a month of premium leads on an experiment; C (0) calls neglect patience while the slide compounds.

cards.title: The Bounced Check
cards.scenario: A customer's final payment check bounces. The advisor who sold the job wants to call the customer and demand payment immediately, hinting he will tell the neighbors if she does not pay up.

A.text: Let the advisor handle it; pressure works. A bounced check is theft of services, and the threat of embarrassment gets checks rewritten fast. Fire in the belly beats any clerk.

B.text: The office calls once, politely, for a replacement payment. One courteous call resolves most of these; bounced checks are usually bank errors or timing. Assume the best first.

C.text: Remove the advisor; the office collects with dignity. Call calmly, assume a mistake first, offer ways to make it right. Threats in her neighborhood cost far more than one invoice.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why it wins: removing the hot-headed advisor and collecting with dignity protects the company's name in the neighborhood where it earns its living. What good discussion sounds like: players picture the threat landing on a real street and realize the invoice is the smallest thing at stake. What the wrong answers cost: A ($0) weaponizes shame for cash; B (150) is polite but leaves the advisor's threat unaddressed.

cards.title: The Financing Afterthought
cards.scenario: Your advisors present financing only when the customer flinches at the price. Applications get rushed at the kitchen table, approvals stall, and too many deals die waiting on the bank.

A.text: Make financing part of every presentation, a normal way people buy, not a rescue move. Show the monthly figure beside the total, and coach advisors whose sheets lack one.

B.text: Push the financing application to right after the inspection. Pre-approval before the price lands removes the awkward pause, and the monthly payment does the heavy lifting.

C.text: Drop financing and focus on cash or check buyers. Finance deals carry fees and delays, and a cash pipeline closes faster with less paperwork. Simplicity beats what financing saves.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why it wins: normalizing financing in every presentation, and measuring that it happens, fixes the process instead of depending on heroic saves at the table. What good discussion sounds like: players see that financing-as-rescue stigmatizes it, while financing-as-normal removes the flinch entirely. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) still treats financing as a setup move; C (0) surrenders a huge buyer segment to avoid paperwork.

cards.title: The Staged Photo
cards.scenario: An advisor photographs a small rust spot on a heat exchanger with a flashlight angle that makes it look like a major crack. The photo helps close a $16,000 replacement the customer might otherwise have declined.

A.text: Praise the creativity privately and share the technique. Dramatic photos close deals and the unit was old; customers cannot judge technical conditions themselves. Teach the angle.

B.text: Call it deception that stole her choice. Make the advisor face her with the truth. Set the standard: photos tell the truth; anyone who stages evidence is finished selling here.

C.text: Refund the gap between replacement and repair, and retrain on honest documentation. The customer keeps the system, the company corrects the money, and he learns the line.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why it wins: staged evidence is fraud against a customer who cannot verify it, and only a public, costly standard restores the team's credibility. What good discussion sounds like: players sit with how easily 'the unit was old anyway' excuses the lie, and see that excuse is exactly how cultures rot. What the wrong answers cost: C (150) treats deception as a pricing error; A ($0) turns fraud into team training.

cards.title: The Lost Handoff
cards.scenario: Sales promises the customer a Tuesday install and a specific thermostat. Production arrives Thursday with the wrong thermostat and no notes. The customer is furious, and each department blames the other.

A.text: One handoff form both sign: models, thermostat, dates, access notes, anything promised. No install scheduled until it is complete. Review misses weekly, both sides in the room.

B.text: Fine the advisor whose handoff caused the complaint. Money gets attention, and one painful deduction makes every advisor double-check notes. Consequences beat memos.

C.text: Stop promising specific dates and models; let production set expectations after the sale. Fewer promises, fewer broken ones, though softer commitments. The shouting stops.

cards.host_note: Principle: One Department: Customer Service. Why it wins: a single signed handoff makes both departments serve the same customer instead of serving their side of the argument. What good discussion sounds like: players recognize every interdepartmental fight they have ever seen, and admit the paper form beats the memory of a busy advisor. What the wrong answers cost: C (0) gags the sales team instead of fixing the transfer; B (150) punishes one person for a system failure.

cards.title: The Phone Quote Request
cards.scenario: Dana calls your office and asks what it costs to replace her air conditioner. She wants a number before she agrees to a visit. Your newest comfort advisor is ready to give her one to keep the lead alive.

A.text: Give a broad phone range, basic to high-efficiency, and stress the real figure comes after the inspection. The range wins the appointment without locking you in.

B.text: Email three equipment tiers so she can shop on her own time, and tell her to call back when she picks one. She asked for numbers first; meet her on her terms.

C.text: Never quote a job you have not seen. A blind number is a guess, and guesses become broken promises. Book the visit, then price it only after she has seen the inspection findings.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Price Before Value. Why it wins: quoting blind teaches the customer to buy on price alone and guarantees you are wrong in one direction or the other. What good discussion sounds like: players debate whether a range is harmless, then realize the range becomes the anchor the whole visit fights against. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) keeps the lead warm but trains price shopping; B (150) surrenders the visit, which is where value is actually built.

cards.title: The Burned Out Closer
cards.scenario: Your best advisor, eight years in, tells you the daily rejection is getting to him. His numbers are still fine, but the fire is gone and he is quietly thinking about quitting for good.

A.text: Offer a raise. Money is the simplest retention tool, his production justifies it, and a bigger paycheck rekindles motivation. Eight years of mastery costs far more to replace.

B.text: Ask what part of the work still matters, and listen. Often it is the sameness, not the rejection. Mentoring rookies can relight him; reshape the role around the spark.

C.text: Help him plan his exit. A burned-out closer poisons younger advisors, and an honest goodbye beats a slow fade. A graceful exit preserves the relationship and the culture.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why it wins: reconnecting him to a purpose inside the work addresses the actual disease rather than the symptom. What good discussion sounds like: players realize nobody quits over rejection alone; they quit when the work stops meaning anything, and a bigger check cannot fix that. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) buys time at a higher price without fixing anything; C ($0) gives up on eight years of mastery.

cards.title: The Confused Homeowner
cards.scenario: Mrs. Alvarez, 78, nods along to everything your advisor says but cannot repeat back any of the options. Her son, on speakerphone, keeps pushing her toward the premium system. The advisor senses she does not understand.

A.text: Slow down and speak to Mrs. Alvarez; her home, her signature. Explain each option plainly and have her repeat it back. If she cannot, stop and reschedule with the son present.

B.text: Proceed with the son's choice; he is the decision maker and the premium system is the best equipment. Get the signature, schedule the install, and note he directed the decision.

C.text: Reschedule when the son can attend in person. Phone participants cannot read the room, and this decision deserves everyone at one table. A short delay beats a painful cancellation.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why it wins: the teach-back check protects the actual homeowner, and stopping a sale you could have closed is the proof the company serves people first. What good discussion sounds like: players feel the tension between the son's authority and the mother's signature, and land on the person signing as the person who must understand. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) takes an order from someone who is not the customer; C (150) delays without first trying to serve her directly.

cards.title: The Competitor Trash Talk
cards.scenario: A rival company is telling customers your installs leak and your techs are trainees. Your advisors want permission to hit back with what they have heard about the rival's callbacks.

A.text: Let advisors answer in kind with the rival's callback stories. Disarmament lets the lies stand. A sharp counterpunch ends the rumor fast and shows the team you have their backs.

B.text: Forbid the counterattack; arm the team with proof. Photos, permits, certifications, and review counts beat rumors. When the claim comes up, answer with evidence and move on.

C.text: Ignore it completely. Responding gives the rumor oxygen, and most customers see through gossip on their own. The high road costs nothing and keeps the team selling, not feuding.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Experience Is Half the Product. Why it wins: answering rumors with documentation keeps the customer's experience of you professional while the rival looks small. What good discussion sounds like: players feel the pull of revenge, then admit customers remember who stayed classy. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) turns your advisors into gossip carriers; C (0) lets a lie sit unanswered in the customer's mind.

cards.title: The Struggling New Hire
cards.scenario: Priya is three weeks into the advisor role. Her product knowledge is strong, but her close rate is zero after eleven appointments. She is starting to dread pulling into the driveway.

A.text: Move her to smaller repair tickets. Small wins steady her nerves, and a few closes in a row earn her way back to full presentations. Confidence is built in stages.

B.text: Eleven straight losses means selling may not be for her; start interviewing a replacement. The team cannot carry a zero forever. A fast, honest exit beats months of dread.

C.text: Ride along on two visits to watch and listen. Find the one gap, usually inspection to presentation, and drill it with role play. Coach ninety days before any talk of fit.

cards.host_note: Principle: Train or Remove. Why it wins: diagnose the specific gap, drill it, and give real coaching time before judging fit; removal comes after training, not instead of it. What good discussion sounds like: players admit how rare the ride-along is, and how often 'not a fit' really means 'never coached.' What the wrong answers cost: A (150) hides her from the skill she needs; B ($0) quits on a three-week employee.

cards.title: The Single Option Trap
cards.scenario: Your advisors present one system, one price, take it or leave it. Close rates are flat and average tickets are drifting down. Customers keep saying they want to think about it first.

A.text: Add a low-priced repair option to every proposal as something to say no to. The contrast makes the replacement look reasonable, and even small approvals add revenue otherwise lost.

B.text: Offer good, better, best, with the middle as the smart value most homes need. Present all three side by side. The question becomes which fits, not whether to buy.

C.text: Keep the single-option presentation and ride out the flat close rate. Changing the format mid-year would confuse the team, and consistency has value while conditions improve.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why it wins: three honest options move the decision from whether to which, which is where close rates actually live. What good discussion sounds like: players notice the middle option does the real work, and that 'which one fits' feels like help while 'take it or leave it' feels like pressure. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) uses a decoy that insults the customer's intelligence; C (0) defends the format that caused the flat rate.

cards.title: The Cash Discount Ask
cards.scenario: A homeowner offers to pay cash today if your advisor knocks 15 percent off the system price. The advisor is tempted: the money is real, the close would be instant, and nobody would know.

A.text: Hold the price and refuse the cash discount plainly. The price reflects equipment, crew, permits, warranty, none of which changes with how he pays. Offer standard options.

B.text: Take the cash at 15 percent off. Money today beats margin tomorrow, the job fills the schedule, and one quiet discount stays off the books. A bird in the hand.

C.text: Counter at five percent off for payment in full today. It captures the urgency and protects most of the margin, and he gets a win for the neighbors. Meeting halfway keeps the deal.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why it wins: the price is the price because the costs behind it are real, and a cash discount is just margin donated to whoever asks loudest. What good discussion sounds like: players admit the temptation is the instant close, then see that every exception becomes the new rule by Friday. What the wrong answers cost: B ($0) teaches the team that off-book discounts are policy; C (150) negotiates against yourself for a payment method that costs you nothing extra.

cards.title: The End Run
cards.scenario: Your sales manager denies an advisor's request for an extra discount on a big job. The advisor goes directly to you, the owner, hoping you will overrule the manager and approve it.

A.text: Approve the discount this once; the job is large and the margin works. The advisor showed initiative, and the manager will understand big jobs need owner flexibility.

B.text: Send the advisor back to the sales manager; do not rule on it yourself. Tell the manager privately you backed his call and learn his reasoning. An overruled manager loses his team.

C.text: Approve the discount and tell the advisor to skip the manager next time. Faster decisions close more deals. Cut the bottleneck out; let closers run straight to yes.

cards.host_note: Principle: Delegate, Don't Abdicate. Why it wins: backing the manager's call while learning his reasoning develops the leader instead of bypassing him. What good discussion sounds like: players admit the discount is tempting and fast, then count what an overruled manager costs over the next year of decisions nobody brings to him. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) teaches every advisor to appeal over the manager's head; C ($0) formally demolishes the chain of command for one deal.

cards.title: Cheaper Down the Street
cards.scenario: A homeowner shows your advisor a competitor quote that is $2,200 lower for what looks like the same equipment. She asks why she should pay more. Your advisor knows the competitor skips permits and uses smaller crews.

A.text: Warn her the cheaper bid likely means skipped permits and rushed labor, and she will pay the difference later in repairs. Customers need the blunt truth about low bidders.

B.text: Match the price and protect the margin with your fastest crew and trimmed commissioning. Winning matters most; volume covers the thin margin, and she will see the quality.

C.text: Compare both proposals side by side without attacking anyone. Show the permit, load calculation, crew size, and warranty, and what each one protects. Then let her decide.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why it wins: a calm side-by-side on scope lets the customer see what the $2,200 buys instead of hearing an attack on the competitor. What good discussion sounds like: players notice A feels honest but actually trashes the rival, while C informs without insulting. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) makes you the mudslinger; B (150) guts your own quality to win on price.

cards.title: The Driveway Upsell
cards.scenario: Your advisor is taught to offer indoor air quality add-ons at every visit. Lately she pushes them hard, and two customers complained the visit felt like a timeshare pitch. Her attach rate is up; trust is down.

A.text: Coach her to earn the add-on talk. The offer follows a real finding, dust or allergies, backed by test results. A recommendation rooted in findings beats a pitch at every door.

B.text: Keep pushing; two complaints are just venting. Air quality carries the best margins, and backing off costs thousands a year. The numbers justify the pressure.

C.text: Pull her off add-ons for a month. Straight sales rebuild trust, the complaints stop, and she can reintroduce the products later with a lighter touch. Distance restores perspective.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why it wins: coaching her to connect the offer to a real finding leaves her bigger and more skilled, while protecting customers from pressure. What good discussion sounds like: players notice B treats the advisor like a vending machine and the customer like a wallet, while A develops both. What the wrong answers cost: B ($0) burns trust for margin; C (150) benches a producer instead of coaching her.

cards.title: The Blame the Leads Habit
cards.scenario: Two advisors keep saying the appointment center sends weak leads. The center says the advisors do not work them. Unsold estimates are piling up and nobody owns the follow-up anymore.

A.text: Side with the advisors and demand better-qualified leads. Tighter qualification means fewer wasted trips and higher morale. Quality in, quality out.

B.text: End the debate with shared numbers. Track every lead from booking to outcome in one visible report by advisor and source. Review it weekly together. Same facts end finger-pointing.

C.text: Let it play out. Departments grumble and both sides have a point. Stepping in makes you the referee in every future dispute. Pick your battles; grumbling usually fades on its own.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why it wins: one shared report replaces two competing stories with facts, and the weekly review keeps it honest. What good discussion sounds like: players recognize this exact fight from their own companies and admit the data usually indicts follow-up, not lead quality. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) picks a winner in a fight where both sides are half right; C (0) renames avoidance as wisdom while the estimate pile grows.

cards.title: The Sales-Caused Callback
cards.scenario: An advisor promised a customer the new system would cut her electric bill in half. It dropped 15 percent. She is furious and demanding a refund. The advisor says production must have installed it wrong.

A.text: Send production back to recommission the system. It might squeeze out more savings, shows you take her seriously, and buys time for tempers to cool. Action calms anger.

B.text: Back the advisor publicly and blame the install. Pressure production to find something, anything, to fix. Unity in front of the customer matters most.

C.text: Stand with the facts and the customer. Show the advisor privately where he overpromised. Face the customer, acknowledge it, make it right. Never blame production.

cards.host_note: Principle: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame. Why it wins: the manager absorbs the failure publicly, corrects the advisor privately, and fixes the claim standard going forward. What good discussion sounds like: players feel how easy B is in the moment, then see it sacrifices the install crew's trust to protect one bad promise. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) treats a sales lie as a technical problem; B ($0) frames an innocent crew to save face.

cards.title: The Verbal Promise
cards.scenario: At the kitchen table, your advisor verbally promises the customer that the crew will haul away the old bushes by the condenser. It never makes the proposal. Install day arrives and the bushes are still there.

A.text: Clear the bushes today, even if someone goes back out. Coach the advisor: verbal promises outside the proposal are dangerous. If promised at the table, write it down.

B.text: Have the crew clear the bushes on the spot as goodwill. Twenty minutes, and the customer remembers the extra effort. The advisor learns to watch his promises.

C.text: Landscaping was never in scope, so the company owes nothing. Offer to clear the bushes for a fee. The contract is the contract; blurring it invites free extras forever.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why it wins: fixing the bushes today plus retraining the promise habit serves both the customer and the advisor's future. What good discussion sounds like: players see the advisor meant well, which is exactly why the system has to catch it: good intentions without paperwork still break trust. What the wrong answers cost: B (150) fixes the symptom and skips the coaching; C ($0) hides behind the contract after the company's own words created the expectation.

cards.title: The Referral That Needs Nothing
cards.scenario: A past customer refers his neighbor, Mr. Okafor. Your advisor runs the full inspection and finds a three-year-old system running clean, with a simple clogged condensate line. The advisor could easily sell a maintenance plan and a duct cleaning.

A.text: Sell the plan and the duct cleaning. Both are legitimate, the plan locks in the relationship, and the photos justify the cleaning. A referral visit should still produce revenue.

B.text: Clear the line free as goodwill, then enroll him in the maintenance plan. The free fix builds trust and the plan creates recurring revenue. Everybody wins on this visit.

C.text: Clear the line, show the clean readings, and say plainly he needs nothing today. Thank him for the referral trust. Leave your card with no pitch; this kind of honesty travels fast.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why it wins: telling a referred neighbor he needs nothing protects the referrer's name, which is worth more than any single ticket. What good discussion sounds like: players feel the pain of a zero-revenue visit, then realize the referral stream is the actual asset being protected. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) monetizes trust the referrer lent you; B (150) spends the goodwill with a plan pitch right after the free fix.

cards.title: The Slow Season Stall
cards.scenario: October arrives and new appointments thin out. Your advisors sit idle between calls while a file of 400 unsold estimates from the past year gathers dust in the office, still untouched.

A.text: Cut advisors to part time until spring. Payroll is the biggest cost, and a full team through a slow season burns cash needed later. Cash saved now funds the spring hiring push.

B.text: Work the unsold estimate file: segment by age and job size, rewrite the script around what changed, and set daily targets with results posted. It is prepaid pipeline.

C.text: Do nothing special. Slow seasons are normal and the team recharges for spring. Forcing activity in a dead market trains customers to expect deals and burns out advisors.

cards.host_note: Principle: Cash Is Life. Why it wins: the unsold estimate file is prepaid pipeline, and a segmented, measured follow-up plan turns idle payroll into revenue. What good discussion sounds like: players do the math on 400 estimates at even a 10 percent close rate and realize the slow season was never actually slow. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) sheds trained closers you will rehire at a premium in spring; C (0) confuses a seasonal dip with a vacation.

cards.title: The Complaint Nobody Logged
cards.scenario: A customer calls the office to say your advisor was rude and dismissive in her home. The office manager, not wanting drama, deletes the message and tells no one. You hear about it from the customer herself a week later.

A.text: Call the customer yourself, hear the full story, and hear the advisor's side. Tell the office manager: deleting a complaint is never her call. Every complaint gets logged.

B.text: Say it is hard to verify after a week and offer a service credit to close it out. Warn the office manager to forward complaints next time. A quick credit keeps the phones quiet.

C.text: Log the complaint, note the deletion in the manager's file, and move on. The process fix matters more than one visit. The advisor gets the benefit of the doubt; systems over drama.

cards.host_note: Principle: Safe to Speak. Why it wins: hearing the customer, hearing the advisor's side, and making complaint-burying unacceptable keeps truth flowing. What good discussion sounds like: players see the office manager meant to keep the peace, and realize peace kept by deletion is a delayed explosion. What the wrong answers cost: B ($0) pays hush money and teaches customers that complaining loudly works; C (150) files paperwork while the customer still feels unheard.

cards.title: The Rebate Shortcut
cards.scenario: A customer asks your advisor to date the install paperwork a week earlier so the job qualifies for a utility rebate that just expired. It is a small lie, nobody checks, and the customer promises a five-star review.

A.text: Adjust the date. The rebate is real money, nobody will audit one residential job, and the goodwill plus the review outweigh a paperwork technicality. Keep him happy and move on.

B.text: Refuse clearly and kindly: no false dates on company documents, ever. Offer to help with current rebates and write the utility for an exception. Honest paperwork beats one review.

C.text: Give a company credit equal to the lost rebate as a goodwill gesture from the job margin. He gets the money he expected, the paperwork stays honest, and nobody bends the truth.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why it wins: a false date on a company document is fraud, however small, and the letter to the utility keeps you an advocate without lying. What good discussion sounds like: players test whether C is really different from A, and realize generosity still spends margin to avoid an honest conversation. What the wrong answers cost: A (150) puts the company's name on a false record; C (150) spends margin to dodge a two-minute honest talk.

cards.title: The Supplier Price Hike
cards.scenario: Your main supplier raises prices fifteen percent across the board, effective immediately. Your quoted jobs for the next month were priced on the old costs. The increase wipes out the margin on six scheduled installs if you absorb it.

A.text: Absorb the increase quietly and say nothing to customers or crew. Honor every quoted price exactly and eat the lost margin.

B.text: Switch to a cheaper supplier for next month's jobs to recover the margin. Tell customers nothing changes.

C.text: Honor every signed quote at the old price; your word on paper is your word. Re-price future quotes on the new costs today.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Price Before Value. Why C wins: signed quotes are honored, future pricing reflects real costs, and the supplier gets renegotiated instead of silently dictating margins. What good discussion sounds like: how to value-engineer a quoted job honestly, and what volume commitments are actually worth. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): the cheaper supplier gambles six installs on untested equipment; A ($0): absorbing silently bleeds margin with no plan to stop it.

cards.title: The Snowstorm Callout
cards.scenario: A snowstorm hits overnight and half your crew cannot reach the shop. Phones ring with no-heat calls, including several elderly customers. Roads are bad but passable, and the techs who made it in are willing to work.

A.text: Triage by risk: elderly and medical no-heat calls first. Offer double-time to the techs who made it in.

B.text: Run a skeleton crew on no-heat calls only today. Tell every other caller you will reach them tomorrow.

C.text: Close the shop and put an emergency message on the phones referring callers elsewhere. Tell the crew to stay home today.

cards.host_note: Principle: Keep Customers for Life. Why A wins: it sorts by human risk, rewards the crew that showed up, borrows trusted capacity, and tells every caller the truth. What good discussion sounds like: which partner shops you actually trust, and how to triage without playing favorites. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): the skeleton crew abandons every routine caller to silence; C ($0): closing the doors leaves customers with no heat and a long memory.

cards.title: The Rainy Week Backlog
cards.scenario: Rain is forecast for six straight days. Outdoor work is piling up: three condenser changeouts, two line-set runs, a trench for a new service. Indoor crews are light. Customers with dead systems are calling daily, and the schedule is slipping.

A.text: Work through the rain with pop-up canopies over the work areas. Keep the original schedule and tell customers you push through.

B.text: Pull indoor jobs forward; push changeouts to the first dry day. Call each outdoor customer tonight with a firm date.

C.text: Keep the schedule as booked and let crews decide day by day. Tell customers you are monitoring the weather.

cards.host_note: Principle: Created Twice. Why B wins: the week gets planned before it happens, indoor work fills the rain days, and outdoor customers get honest dates instead of daily maybes. What good discussion sounds like: how far ahead to re-sequence, and what to tell a customer with a dead system who cannot wait for dry weather. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): working through the rain risks quality and safety for the schedule; C (+0): letting crews decide day by day leaves every customer waking up wondering if today is the day.

cards.title: The Tech Who Wants More
cards.scenario: Jordan, your best young tech, wants to train new hires and eventually run a crew. He is great with customers but has never led anyone. Your current lead tech is protective of his role and has told Jordan to stay in his lane.

A.text: Promote Jordan to lead tech of a second crew immediately, splitting the work. Give him the title and the raise now.

B.text: Thank Jordan for his ambition and say you will keep it in mind going forward. Change nothing for now.

C.text: Make Jordan a training buddy for new hires, with a pay bump tied to their retention and callbacks. Define his responsibilities clearly.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why C wins: it gives Jordan's ambition something real to attach to, a defined role, measurable outcomes, and a path, while turning the lead tech from gatekeeper into builder. What good discussion sounds like: what a training buddy should actually be measured on, and how to tell a protective lead tech his job includes building his replacement. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the immediate promotion hands leadership to someone who has never led; B (+0): the empty promise parks ambition until it quits.

cards.title: The Vanishing Tools
cards.scenario: Small tools keep disappearing: multimeters, manifolds, tubing cutters. Each tech blames the shared shop stock, and you spent $2,000 this quarter replacing tools bought last year. The crew is starting to hoard tools in personal vans.

A.text: Run a locked tool crib with a daily sign-out sheet. Techs check tools out each morning and back in each night.

B.text: Give every tech a personal kit with a signed sheet, and audit vans weekly. Replacements come from each tech's own tool budget.

C.text: Send a memo that repeated tool losses will be deducted from paychecks. Change nothing else about tool handling.

cards.host_note: Principle: Pay for What You Want Repeated. Why B wins: it makes ownership personal and visible, with a budget consequence tied to the behavior and a weekly check that keeps it honest. What good discussion sounds like: whether techs should pay for lost tools, and how big a personal tool budget should be. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the tool crib builds a daily bureaucracy that wastes crew time; C (+0): the memo threatens without changing anything.

cards.title: The Unsigned Inspection
cards.scenario: A longtime customer asks you to sign the final inspection card for a panel upgrade your crew finished while you were on vacation. You did not see the finished work. He needs the signed card tomorrow for his home sale closing, and says everything passed already.

A.text: Sign the card. Your crew does good work, the customer says it passed, and his closing depends on it.

B.text: Sign the card but note the inspection was done by your crew in your absence. The customer gets his closing document today.

C.text: Refuse to sign, plainly and kindly. Your signature means you verified the work; offer to inspect it yourself tomorrow.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Elongated Shadow. Why C wins: your signature is your shadow; it means you verified the work, so you refuse kindly, inspect it yourself, and own the delay. What good discussion sounds like: how to tell a longtime customer no without damaging the relationship, and what your sign-off process should require. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): signing with a footnote signs a lie with an asterisk; A ($0): signing blind trades your name for a closing date.

cards.title: The Tablet Holdout
cards.scenario: Ray has twenty years in the trade and a loyal customer following. He refuses the new digital job checklist on the tablet, calling it a toy. His paperwork returns on paper and the office re-enters everything. Younger techs are asking why they must use it if Ray does not.

A.text: Ask Ray privately what frustrates him about the tablet. Pair him with a younger tech to learn it on real jobs.

B.text: Issue a written policy: every tech uses the tablet starting Monday, with warnings for refusal. No one is above the standard.

C.text: Move Ray to repeat customers where the office preloads job details. His paper forms stay easy to process.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why A wins: it sets one clear standard for everyone while respecting Ray's experience, and converts the holdout into an owner of the system. What good discussion sounds like: how to hold a veteran accountable without humiliating him, and whether exceptions for top performers ever stay contained. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): the mandate with warnings gets compliance through threats and loses his goodwill; C (+150): the special track builds a two-tier system the young techs will rightly resent.

cards.title: The Rude Tech Complaint
cards.scenario: A customer calls, furious: your tech Chris was dismissive and rude when she asked questions about her repair options. Chris says she asked the same question a third time and he was behind schedule. She wants an apology and says she will never use your company again.

A.text: Apologize to the customer and offer a discount on the repair. Tell Chris to watch his tone in a quick chat.

B.text: Listen fully without defending Chris, and apologize sincerely. Coach Chris privately on resetting mid-call, then follow up with her.

C.text: Back Chris fully: explain he was under schedule pressure and his technical work was correct. Offer a different tech for future visits.

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why B wins: the customer is heard fully before anyone defends the tech, the apology is real, and Chris gets coaching on the actual moment instead of a hallway scolding. What good discussion sounds like: how to coach tone without making a tech walk on eggshells, and what a mid-call reset sounds like. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the hallway chat and discount close the complaint but teach Chris nothing; C (+0): backing Chris fully tells the customer her feelings were wrong.

cards.title: The Flooded Laundry Room
cards.scenario: Luis, a second-year trainee on his first solo service call, cross-threaded a washing machine supply valve and flooded a laundry room. The customer is upset, the water is stopped, and the damage is minor. Luis waits in the truck, convinced he is about to be fired.

A.text: Return with Luis and own the mistake together, making it right at company cost. Debrief at the shop on what he missed.

B.text: Send Luis home and have a senior tech finish the call. Tell him tomorrow whether he still has a job.

C.text: Finish the repair yourself and quietly cover the damage. Tell Luis it happens to everyone and skip the debrief.

cards.host_note: Principle: Train or Remove. Why A wins: it treats the mistake as a training event, not a character verdict, and Luis owns it with support, learns the skill gap, and keeps developing under a clear guardrail. What good discussion sounds like: the difference between accountability and fear, and what check-in rules actually prevent repeat mistakes. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): sending him home to wait teaches him that mistakes end careers; C (+150): skipping the debrief means the lesson never lands.

cards.title: The Tech's Side Jobs
cards.scenario: You learn Dan, a good tech, has been doing side jobs on weekends using the company van and your customer list. Two of those customers called your office asking about warranty on Dan's side work. He says he needs the money and everyone does it.

A.text: Tell Dan to keep his side jobs quiet and stop using the company van, but otherwise leave him alone for now.

B.text: Get the full picture from Dan on whose van and materials he used. Draw the line: no company resources for side work.

C.text: Put Dan on a final written warning banning side work with company resources, with termination next. Handle the warranty calls yourself.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why B wins: the line is absolute and specific, the warranty mess comes home to be fixed, and Dan's financial pressure gets addressed as a human problem with a real path. What good discussion sounds like: where the line on side work should sit, and how to talk money with a tech without it becoming a shakedown. What the wrong answers cost: C (+150): the final warning documents the boundary but ignores why he crossed it; A ($0): blessing quiet side work trades your customers for his weekends.

cards.title: The Scratched Floor
cards.scenario: After a two-day boiler install, the customer refuses to pay the final $3,000, pointing to a scratch in his hardwood floor where the old unit was dragged out. Your crew swears they used drop cloths. The scratch is real, and a floor guy quoted $400 to fix it.

A.text: Hold firm on full payment, calling the scratch wear and tear. Send the invoice to collections after thirty days.

B.text: Waive the final $3,000 to keep the peace and move on. He gets a free finish, the crew avoids a fight, and the review risk disappears.

C.text: Fix the scratch this week at your cost, then collect final payment in full. Add floor protection to your checklist.

cards.host_note: Principle: Wow! Is the Standard. Why C wins: it fixes the actual damage fast, collects what is owed with a signed walkthrough, and turns the incident into a checklist improvement. What good discussion sounds like: when to eat a cost versus when to hold the line, and what the completion walkthrough should cover. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): holding firm fights over $400 while risking $3,000 and a review; B ($0): waiving the final payment gives away three thousand dollars to avoid a conversation.

cards.title: The Hidden Knob and Tube
cards.scenario: During a panel upgrade, your electrician finds old knob-and-tube wiring feeding two bedrooms. The customer says to ignore it, finish the panel, and tell no one. He will pay cash for the panel today. The wiring is a known fire risk.

A.text: Stop work and document the wiring. You cannot leave a known fire risk; quote making it safe before the panel goes on.

B.text: Refuse to continue until he agrees to a full rewire. You cannot energize a new panel on dangerous wiring.

C.text: Finish the panel, then quote the knob-and-tube replacement for next month. Mention the fire risk briefly to him.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: it refuses to energize a known fire risk, documents everything, gives the customer a real path forward, and puts the disclosure in writing. What good discussion sounds like: whether the written acknowledgment is enough protection, and how to have the conversation without accusing the customer. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): the ultimatum likely sends him to a cheaper contractor; C (+0): the quote-next-month option treats a fire risk as a sales opportunity.

cards.title: The Saturday Grumble
