cards.scenario: Your crew is grumbling about Saturday rotations: the same three techs seem to draw every busy Saturday, and one says his kid's games are always on Saturdays. Morale is dipping and two techs have mentioned looking at other shops.

A.text: Make Saturdays mandatory for everyone on a strict rotation with no swaps and no exceptions. Publish the full quarter so all can plan.

B.text: Rebuild the rotation with the crew: equal turns, a clear swap policy, and no forced back-to-back Saturdays. Honor hard conflicts.

C.text: Tell the crew Saturdays are part of the trade; the rotation stays. Remind them the busy season ends soon.

cards.host_note: Principle: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves. Why B wins: the crew builds the rotation, so the crew defends it, with real conflicts honored, clear rules, and the leader holding the line. What good discussion sounds like: which conflicts are truly hard, and how strict the no-back-to-back rule should be. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the mandatory rotation imposes fairness without buy-in; C (+0): leaving it as-is tells good techs their lives do not matter until fall.

cards.title: The Gas Leak Discovery
cards.scenario: During a water heater swap, your tech finds an active gas leak at the old shutoff valve; you can hear it hissing. The customer says the house has smelled like gas for weeks and asks if you can just tighten the fitting and finish the install. It is 4 p.m. on a Friday.

A.text: Shut gas off at the meter, tag the valve, and reschedule for Monday. Tell the customer to call the utility if worried.

B.text: Tighten the fitting and finish the heater. Tell the customer to call the gas company if the smell returns.

C.text: Stop work. Evacuate the house, shut gas off at the meter, and call the utility emergency line from outside.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why C wins: it sees the situation exactly, an active gas leak, and acts on what it is, not on what the schedule wishes it were. What good discussion sounds like: what your techs should do in the first sixty seconds of finding a leak, and how to explain the delay to an unhappy customer. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): shutting off and leaving her to call the utility alone abandons a scared customer; B ($0): tightening the fitting and finishing gambles a house on a Friday shortcut.

cards.title: The Failed Vent Run
cards.scenario: The city inspector failed a furnace install: the vent run has too many elbows and the slope is wrong. The job passed rough-in six months ago under a different inspector. The homeowner is embarrassed and asking whether your company does shoddy work.

A.text: Tell the homeowner this is inspector opinion and the install is safe. Suggest requesting a different inspector for the re-check.

B.text: Call the homeowner today and own the correction, scheduling rework at your cost. Fix the slope and update the checklist.

C.text: Offer a maintenance discount as goodwill. Leave the vent run in place and add the detail to training.

cards.host_note: Principle: Problems Are Tests. Why B wins: it treats the failed inspection as a chance to get better, fixes the work at company cost, owns it to the customer, and updates the checklist so the lesson is permanent. What good discussion sounds like: when to fight an inspector's call versus when to fix it, and how to tell a customer their install needs rework without losing them. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): blaming inspector opinion spends nothing and fixes nothing; C (+0): the goodwill discount papers over a defect that is still in the wall.

cards.title: The Feuding Techs
cards.scenario: Two of your best techs, Andre and Sam, are feuding over the on-call rotation. Andre says Sam trades away every holiday weekend. Sam says Andre cherry-picks the easy calls. It has spilled into the shop, and the other techs are taking sides.

A.text: Bring Andre and Sam in together with the actual rotation data. Have them redesign the rules together for your approval.

B.text: Take over the rotation and publish a fixed schedule with no trades. Tell both techs the feud ends now.

C.text: Split coverage so Andre and Sam never overlap: alternate weekends, no trades. Tell each the other wanted this.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why A wins: it replaces two competing stories with shared data, then gives both techs ownership of the fix. What good discussion sounds like: how to surface rotation data without it feeling like surveillance, and what fair trade limits look like. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): the fixed schedule kills the flexibility the crew values; C (+150): separating them resolves nothing and makes resentment permanent.

cards.title: The Slipping Senior Tech
cards.scenario: Paul, your senior tech of eight years, has had three callbacks in a month. His work used to be flawless. He is quiet in the shop, skipping the morning huddle, and a helper mentioned his wife is dealing with a serious illness. His review is in two weeks.

A.text: Put Paul on a formal improvement plan with callback targets and a thirty-day timeline. The standard is the standard.

B.text: Move Paul to easier maintenance calls until his numbers recover. Give his complex jobs to the other senior tech.

C.text: Ask Paul privately how he is and what support looks like now. Adjust his schedule and restate the quality bar kindly.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why C wins: it treats the symptom as information, asks before judging, adjusts the load, and still names the standard. What good discussion sounds like: how to ask about a personal crisis without prying, and where support ends and accountability begins. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the immediate PIP punishes a man in crisis; B (+150): the easier calls hide the problem in maintenance work.

cards.title: The Licensing Board Complaint
cards.scenario: A customer filed a complaint against your company with the state licensing board over a failed rough-in inspection. The complaint exaggerates, but the failed inspection is real. Your office manager suggests calling the inspector, who is a friend, to make it go away quietly.

A.text: Cooperate with the board: respond in writing, fix the rough-in past code, and document with photos. Own it with the customer.

B.text: Fix the rough-in now and ask the customer to withdraw the complaint. Offer a free year of maintenance.

C.text: Call the inspector, who owes you a favor from way back. A quiet word from him makes the complaint disappear.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: it answers the board with facts, over-corrects the work, owns the failure to the customer, and kills the favor-trading suggestion outright. What good discussion sounds like: how to respond to an exaggerated complaint without sounding defensive, and how to tell your own office manager no. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): buying the withdrawal with free maintenance dodges the formal answer; C ($0): calling the inspector friend trades a favor to bury a real failure.

cards.title: The Filthy Van
cards.scenario: A customer complains your tech's van looked like a dumpster: fast-food bags on the dash, parts rolling around, mud on the seats. Eddie is skilled and popular, but this is the third complaint about his van this year.

A.text: Dock Eddie's bonus and put a formal warning in his file. The next complaint costs him his van privileges.

B.text: Issue a company-wide van cleanliness policy with weekly photo check-ins for every tech. Eddie is not singled out.

C.text: Talk to Eddie privately about what the customer saw. Set a Friday van-reset standard, and walk it with him yourself.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Experience Is Half the Product. Why C wins: the van is part of what the customer buys, and the fix builds the habit with Eddie instead of punishing him or hiding him, private, specific, and supported. What good discussion sounds like: whether a van standard should be written down, and how to coach a popular tech without embarrassing him. What the wrong answers cost: A ($0): the bonus-dock fines a good tech over a habit; B (+150): the company-wide photo policy builds bureaucracy for everyone because of one van.

cards.title: The Delayed Parts Run
cards.scenario: The warehouse is out of 40-gallon gas water heaters. A scheduled replacement is set for tomorrow morning and the customer took the day off work. The supplier has the unit an hour away, but will-call pickup takes ninety minutes. Your lead tech already has two service calls.

A.text: Send your helper on a paid parts run while the lead keeps his calls. Slot the install for the afternoon.

B.text: Send the lead tech to the supplier first, then the install late morning. Push his two service calls to the afternoon.

C.text: Have the lead pick up the unit on his way in tomorrow. Shift his first service call to another tech.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why A wins: it uses the cheapest available labor for the low-skill task, keeps every skilled tech on revenue work, and honors the customer's day off with a confirmed window. What good discussion sounds like: the real cost of pulling a lead tech off billable work for a parts run, and how to build a parts-runner system before the next stockout. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): sending the lead burns his billable morning on driving; C (+150): shuffling the first call onto other techs moves the problem instead of solving it.

cards.title: The CO Alarm Call
cards.scenario: A customer calls at 7 a.m.: the carbon monoxide alarm went off last night in the home where your crew installed a furnace last winter. The family is scared. The fire department cleared the house but found no source. She wants answers today.

A.text: Walk her through alarm troubleshooting on the phone: reset steps, placement, battery age. Dispatch a tech promptly if it trips again.

B.text: The fire department found nothing, so the furnace is fine. Offer a tech next week if she is still worried.

C.text: Send your senior tech to her home today, first call. Inspect what your crew touched and fix anything of yours free.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why C wins: a scared family gets same-day answers, everything your crew touched gets inspected, and anything of yours gets fixed free with plain-words reporting. What good discussion sounds like: what to say on the first call before the tech arrives, and how to report findings that clear you without sounding defensive. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): phone triage troubleshoots a potential CO event from a desk; B ($0): blaming the alarm leaves a family afraid in their home for a week.

cards.title: The Rushed Weld
cards.scenario: Devon, your fastest installer, finished a furnace swap in four hours. The homeowner is happy and the unit runs fine. But his photos show rough, uneven brazed joints, the kind that fail in three winters. No callback has come in yet.

A.text: Have a senior tech pressure-test every joint today. Re-braze suspects at company cost and supervise Devon until he passes.

B.text: Log the photos in Devon's file and schedule a recheck next month. Tell him you noticed and expect better.

C.text: Leave the install alone unless the customer calls. File the photos and raise joint quality generally at the next crew meeting.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why A wins: it fixes the actual defect at company cost, protects the customer in writing, and coaches the installer privately with a clear standard and supervised reps. What good discussion sounds like: whether speed should ever outrank joint quality, and how to coach a fast tech without crushing him. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): the recheck-next-month option gambles that rough joints hold; C (+150): doing nothing until a callback bets the winter on hope.

cards.title: The Dead Truck
cards.scenario: A tech's truck dies at 10 a.m. with a full day of calls ahead and a van loaded with parts for three jobs. The tow takes two hours, the shop is forty minutes away, and customers expect arrivals inside their windows.

A.text: Rent a truck nearby and have the tech transfer his own parts and finish the day solo. Call all customers with a one-hour delay.

B.text: Send the helper with the spare van to transfer parts curbside. Reassign his third call and notify every customer.

C.text: Cancel his remaining calls and reschedule for tomorrow with an honest explanation. The tech handles the tow.

cards.host_note: Principle: Delegate, Don't Abdicate. Why B wins: it deputizes the helper and the nearby tech with clear tasks instead of watching one truck sink the whole day, and every customer gets a real window. What good discussion sounds like: what your curbside-transfer plan should be before the next breakdown, and whether you actually have a usable spare van. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the rental-truck option pays rental money to keep a solo hero running; C (+0): cancelling surrenders a full day of revenue to one dead truck.

cards.title: The Side-Job Shortcut
cards.scenario: A homeowner asks you to replace his condenser off the books: cash, no permit, no inspection, twenty percent off your normal price. He says his neighbor did the same and it was fine. Easy money on a Saturday, and nobody at the shop would ever know.

A.text: Decline clearly and quote the real price with the permit included. Explain unpermitted work voids the warranty and leaves him unprotected.

B.text: Take the job at your normal standard but pull no permit. Do the work Saturday morning before scheduled calls.

C.text: Refer the homeowner to a tech on your crew who does side work. Tell him you cannot do it off the books.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: it refuses cleanly, explains the real stakes to the customer, warranty and liability, and offers the legitimate path. What good discussion sounds like: whether a permit is really worth losing a Saturday of cash, and what happens the first time an unpermitted job fails. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): taking the cash job puts your license in a Saturday secret; C (+150): referring it to your tech puts the risk on his hands and your name nearby.

cards.title: The Drinking Suspicion
cards.scenario: Two techs tell you privately they smelled alcohol on Miguel's breath on a morning job. Miguel is a strong tech going through a divorce. No customer has complained, and you have not seen it yourself. Company policy is zero tolerance.

A.text: Suspend Miguel pending investigation. Policy is policy, and the crew must see it enforced today. He returns when it is resolved.

B.text: Keep Miguel on interior jobs away from customers, and have the techs watch him quietly. His work is still good.

C.text: Talk to Miguel privately about the report. Require a fitness check, offer support, and keep him off driving until resolved.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why C wins: it refuses to punish on hearsay, verifies through the proper fitness check, holds the zero-tolerance line, and treats Miguel as a person in crisis. What good discussion sounds like: what a fitness-for-duty check actually involves, and how to reassign driving duties without it feeling like punishment. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): suspending him punishes a man on unconfirmed reports; B ($0): hiding him on interior jobs buries a potential safety risk out of sight.

cards.title: The Overloaded Friday
cards.scenario: It is Thursday night and Friday is overbooked: six jobs, four techs, two full-day installs. The dispatcher wants to squeeze everything in. You know a jammed Friday means rushed work, late arrivals, and callbacks on Monday.

A.text: Reschedule the lowest-urgency call to Saturday with the customer's agreement. Offer Saturday at time-and-a-half to one volunteer.

B.text: Keep all six jobs and ask for a big Friday push. Promise Monday morning off and stagger the start times.

C.text: Move the two installs to Monday and keep the four Friday service calls. Call the install customers tonight with a sincere apology.

cards.host_note: Principle: Handle It While It's Small. Why A wins: it fixes the overload Thursday night instead of paying for it in Monday callbacks, protects the high-value installs, and serves every customer within a day with honest windows. What good discussion sounds like: the true cost of a jammed Friday, and how to say no to the dispatcher's squeeze without losing revenue. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): the all-out Friday bets the week's quality on crew heroics; C (+150): moving the installs to Monday delays big-ticket revenue three days.

cards.title: The Neighbor's Gas Line
cards.scenario: A good customer asks you to certify the gas line his neighbor installed himself over the weekend. He says it looks fine and just needs a professional's sign-off for the insurance company. He offers $200 cash for five minutes of your time.

A.text: Decline the sign-off but offer a full paid inspection with a written report. He gets a legitimate path forward.

B.text: Refuse outright: your signature on another's gas work makes you responsible. Offer a proper inspection at your rate, or nothing.

C.text: Stop by and give the line a visual once-over, saying it looks fine without signing anything. Take the $200 as a consultation fee.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: it names the liability plainly, refuses the shortcut, and offers the only legitimate path. What good discussion sounds like: how to say no to a good customer without losing him, and what a real gas inspection actually requires. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the paid inspection is decent but still dances around the ask; C ($0): the visual once-over gives an unqualified blessing for cash.

cards.title: The Lead Tech Quits
cards.scenario: Your lead tech, Marcus, quits with two weeks' notice in the middle of cooling season. He is taking three years of customer relationships with him. The crew is rattled, and two techs are asking who is in charge now.

A.text: Counter-offer Marcus with a raise to keep him through the season. Deal with the underlying issues in the fall.

B.text: Post the opening on every job board tonight and hire the strongest resume within the week. Get the new lead in a van by Monday.

C.text: Give Marcus an honest exit interview and listen. Name your strongest tech interim lead with ninety days to earn it.

cards.host_note: Principle: Be a Learning Machine. Why C wins: the exit interview turns a loss into intelligence, the interim promotion gives the crew a real leader with a fair trial, and the team sees the plan. What good discussion sounds like: what to ask in an exit interview when someone is already gone, and how to pick an interim lead without splitting the crew. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the counter-offer bribes a departing tech to stay resentful; B ($0): the panic hire puts a stranger in the leadership seat by Monday.

cards.title: The Cash Discount Ask
cards.scenario: At the end of a $14,000 system replacement, the customer offers to pay the full amount in cash today if you knock ten percent off and skip the paperwork. He trusts your work and needs no receipt. Your crew stands by the truck waiting for the word.

A.text: Thank him, decline the discount, and run the payment normally. Explain the warranty and your books need real paperwork.

B.text: Take the cash, give him the ten percent, and hand-write a receipt. Skip office paperwork and pay the crew from the cash.

C.text: Accept the cash at full price with no discount. Write a proper receipt from the job folder on the spot.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why A wins: no exceptions to the standard, even for cash in hand, because the paperwork is the warranty, the permit record, and the company's integrity. What good discussion sounds like: what the crew learns watching you decide, and whether any discount is worth an undocumented $14,000 job. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): the handwritten receipt trades the paper trail for a quick discount; C (+150): the middle path keeps paper but caves on process.

cards.title: The Chaotic Warehouse
cards.scenario: Your warehouse is a mess: unlabeled bins, parts on the floor, techs spending thirty minutes every morning hunting for what they need. Two jobs started late this week because the right breaker was buried somewhere. The lead says he is too busy receiving to organize.

A.text: Order new shelving and bin labels for a full-crew Saturday morning warehouse reorganization. Everyone builds the new layout together.

B.text: Map the warehouse by job type and label every bin with part numbers. Set the rule: nothing hits the floor, ever.

C.text: Tell the warehouse lead that organization is now his top priority. Give him two weeks, with a review at the end.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: it builds the warehouse as a measurable system, labeled bins, reorder points, a daily check, with the leader auditing until the habit holds. What good discussion sounds like: what thirty minutes times six techs really costs per week, and how to audit without hovering. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the Saturday blitz gets one clean Monday that drifts by Friday; C (+0): the mandate orders results without changing the job design.

cards.title: The Reused Flex Duct
cards.scenario: Your installer suggests reusing the existing flex duct on a system changeout to save the customer $900. The duct is fifteen years old, dusty, and undersized for the new unit, but it looks intact. The customer is price-sensitive and would love the savings.

A.text: Reuse the duct but add a booster fan and extra sealing to compensate. The customer keeps most of the savings.

B.text: Let the customer decide: present reuse as a budget option with a signed waiver. His energy bills absorb the real cost.

C.text: Replace the duct. Old undersized duct chokes airflow, weakens the warranty, and eats the savings in energy bills.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why C wins: it helps the customer with honest math instead of selling him a discount that costs him more later. What good discussion sounds like: how to show a price-sensitive customer the two-year cost without sounding like an upsell, and when a waiver actually protects you. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the booster-fan workaround engineers around a problem that should be replaced; B ($0): the waiver blesses a bad install and lets his energy bills pay for it.

cards.title: The Three-Week Backlog
cards.scenario: Summer demand has your install backlog at three weeks. Customers are getting quotes from competitors who can start Monday. Your crews are at full capacity, and the dispatcher is fielding angry calls about wait times.

A.text: Subcontract the overflow to a trusted crew at a thin margin. Have your lead vet their first two jobs.

B.text: Open evening and Saturday slots at a premium price. Bring on two seasonal installers and give timelines in writing.

C.text: Quote every new customer a ten-day start date to stop losing bids, and push the crews to find the time somehow, starting now.

cards.host_note: Principle: Cash Is Life. Why B wins: it treats demand as pricing information, adds real seasonal capacity, and gives every customer an honest written choice. What good discussion sounds like: how high the premium can go before it backfires, and how to hire seasonal installers you actually trust. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): subcontracting rents someone else's quality at a thin margin; C ($0): quoting ten days lies to win bids, and the dates keep slipping.

cards.title: The Melted Panel
cards.scenario: Zoe, a trainee, landed the wrong wire size on a panel upgrade and the lug overheated, melting part of the panel. The rework costs $1,800 and delays the job two days. Zoe is twenty, in tears, offering to pay for the damage from her paycheck.

A.text: The company absorbs the cost; trainees never pay for supervised mistakes. Require a lead's sign-off for a month.

B.text: Accept Zoe's offer to repay through payroll deductions. Keep her on panel work so she learns directly.

C.text: Deduct the $1,800 from Zoe's pay and tell the whole crew as a warning. She needs to feel the cost of carelessness.

cards.host_note: Principle: Train or Remove. Why A wins: the mistake happened under your supervision, so the company owns the cost and builds the skill, with retraining, a sign-off guardrail, and an honest call to the customer. What good discussion sounds like: what the sign-off rule should cover, and how to debrief a crying trainee so she learns instead of shutting down. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): payroll deductions bill a supervision failure to the smallest paycheck; C ($0): the public deduction teaches every trainee what loyalty costs in this shop.

cards.title: The Sloppy Subcontractor
cards.scenario: Your ductwork subcontractor's latest job is sloppy: sagging runs, gaps at the boots, one disconnected return. The homeowner's drywall goes up next week. The sub blames your schedule pressure and wants full payment now, threatening to walk off your remaining jobs.

A.text: Agree partial payment and a punch list: he fixes the worst runs, your crew handles the rest. Confirm by email.

B.text: Reject the work in writing with photos. The sub redoes deficient runs at his cost before drywall; you hold payment.

C.text: Accept the work as-is and have your crew seal the gaps with mastic on the next visit. The system will function fine once sealed.

cards.host_note: Principle: Wow! Is the Standard. Why B wins: merely acceptable ductwork behind drywall is a future failure with your name on it, so the rejection is written, the rework is his, and the specs go in the contract. What good discussion sounds like: how to hold a needed sub accountable without losing him, and what belongs in the subcontractor specs. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the split payment negotiates the standard downward; C (+0): sealing over defects hides them behind drywall and hope.

cards.title: The Lifting Injury
cards.scenario: Your tech strains his back lifting a condenser with a helper who left early. He can barely stand. He begs you not to report it, saying he will rest over the weekend and be fine Monday. He worries about his record and the company's rates.

A.text: Get him medical attention now and file the comp report today. Fix the cause: no condenser moves without the full crew.

B.text: Drive him to urgent care yourself and pay the visit out of pocket. Give him Monday off paid, off the books.

C.text: Agree to keep it quiet as he asked. Pay the clinic visit in cash and tell him to be more careful next time.

cards.host_note: Principle: Safe to Speak. Why A wins: the injury gets real medical care and a proper report, the tech learns hiding it helps no one, and the root cause becomes a written rule. What good discussion sounds like: how to convince a scared tech that reporting protects him, and what the condenser-move rule should actually say. What the wrong answers cost: B (+150): paying urgent care out of pocket keeps the injury off the record that protects you; C ($0): keeping it quiet for cash trades the books for a secret.

cards.title: The Dirty Jobsite Photo
cards.scenario: A customer posted a photo online of her yard after your crew's panel upgrade: boot prints across the lawn, wire scraps in the bushes, a cigarette butt on the porch. The post is getting comments. Your lead tech swears the yard was clean when they left.

A.text: Reply with your crew's facts: the yard was clean at departure. The debris must have come from elsewhere.

B.text: Own it publicly: apologize on the post, send two techs back to clean the yard today, and state what changes now.

C.text: Call the customer privately, apologize, and offer a partial refund. Note the complaint in the lead tech's file.

cards.host_note: Principle: One Department: Customer Service. Why B wins: every department owns the customer's experience, so Production owns the yard it leaves behind, with public accountability plus a real system change. What good discussion sounds like: whether to ever argue with a customer's photo, and what a departure checklist should actually contain. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): replying with the crew's version argues with photographic evidence in public; C (+150): the private refund buys silence without fixing the cause.

cards.title: The Wrong Unit Arrives
cards.scenario: The supplier delivered a three-ton condenser for tomorrow's changeout, but the load calculation calls for three and a half tons. The crane is booked for 8 a.m. and the customer took the day off. The supplier says the correct unit can be there by noon for an expedite fee.

A.text: Install the three-ton unit anyway and adjust the airflow to compensate. The customer keeps his day off.

B.text: Cancel the crane, eat the fee, and reschedule for next week. Apologize to the customer with a discount.

C.text: Demand the supplier cover the expedite fee since the error was theirs. Confirm the correct unit in writing by noon today.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why C wins: it names the situation exactly, the supplier's error, and assigns the cost to the party that caused it, while keeping the customer's day productive and honest. What good discussion sounds like: how hard to push a supplier you depend on, and when to tell the customer about a problem they would never have noticed. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): installing the three-ton anyway trades a day for the wrong equipment; B (+150): cancelling the crane wastes the booking and the customer's day off.

cards.title: The Padded Hours
cards.scenario: You discover Victor, a solid mid-level tech, has been adding thirty minutes to his time sheets on flat-rate jobs for two months. The jobs pay the same either way; the padding only inflates his hourly bonus. He has a family and has never had a callback issue.

A.text: Reduce Victor's bonus this quarter to offset the padding, and tell him privately you noticed the pattern.

B.text: Confront Victor privately with the dates and require repayment of the inflated amounts. Put the expectation in writing with clear consequences.

C.text: Watch his time sheets closely for the next month without saying anything. If the pattern stops, call it a rough patch.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Elongated Shadow. Why B wins: the business is the leader's shadow, and padded time sheets are the shadow too, direct, private, specific, with repayment and a written standard. What good discussion sounds like: whether to fire over thirty minutes, and how to confront without destroying a good tech. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): quietly docking pay never names the standard; C (+0): watching and waiting lets the padding continue another month.

cards.title: The Heat Wave Surge
cards.scenario: A heat wave hits and no-cool calls triple overnight. Your schedule is full for four days, the phones are ringing off the hook, and two techs are showing signs of burnout. The dispatcher is booking three weeks out and customers are angry.

A.text: Book everyone first-come, first-served and ask for twelve-hour days until the wave breaks. Promise a daily bonus.

B.text: Hire two temp techs for the surge from a staffing agency. Keep your regular crew on normal hours; temps take the simple calls.

C.text: Triage every call by risk: elderly, infants, and medical needs first. Run staggered shifts so techs rotate rest days.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why C wins: it sorts by human need instead of call order, protects the crew with real rest, and gives every caller an honest window. What good discussion sounds like: who counts as vulnerable, how to tell a paying customer they wait behind someone else's grandmother, and what staggered shifts actually cost. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the twelve-hour sprint burns out the crew for a week of revenue; B (+150): the temp crew gambles quality on unvetted hands.

cards.title: The Slow New Hire
cards.scenario: Nadia is three months into her first tech role and still takes twice as long as the standard on service calls. Customers have commented on the wait, and one asked for a different tech next time. Her attitude is excellent and she studies the manuals every night.

A.text: Give Nadia a straight talk: reach standard times within thirty days or you will let her go. Check her numbers weekly yourself.

B.text: Build Nadia a ninety-day coaching plan: weekly ride-alongs, the ten most common calls first, and check-ins on her times.

C.text: Leave Nadia on her current schedule and hope experience kicks in. Reassign complaining customers to another tech.

cards.host_note: Principle: Character Over Skill. Why B wins: Nadia already has the character, so you invest in the skill with a structured plan, real reps, and honest communication to customers. What good discussion sounds like: how long is fair to carry a slow learner, and what the ten most common calls list should contain. What the wrong answers cost: A (+150): the thirty-day ultimatum threatens a good attitude out the door; C (+0): hoping time alone fixes it leaves a skill gap untaught.

cards.title: The Fudged Job Cost
cards.scenario: A production supervisor asks accounting to shift $3,000 of labor hours from his crew's losing job to a profitable one, so his job-cost report looks better at the leadership meeting. He says everyone does it, it does not change total payroll, and he asks off the record.

A.text: Move the hours this once as a favor, and tell him it is the last time. But it corrupts the data every future pricing decision will rest on, and he will ask again.

B.text: Refuse, but soften it with a footnote explaining the job's unusual site conditions. It keeps the books honest, but footnotes quietly become the new way of hiding bad numbers.

C.text: Refuse clearly: job-cost reports are the company's eyes, and if the numbers lie, every pricing decision made from them is blind. Help him present the real story of the tough job.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why C wins: it protects the integrity of the data everything else depends on, while giving the supervisor a better way to look good: owning the real story. Discuss: why 'it doesn't change total payroll' misses the point, and how leaders present bad numbers well. Wrong answers: A poisons future decisions for one favor (150); B creates a footnote loophole (150).

cards.title: Installs Are Losing Money
cards.scenario: The new job-costing report shows the install department lost money on 6 of the last 10 jobs. Flat-rate pricing has not changed in two years, but costs have risen. Sales blames production for being slow; production blames sales for underpricing.

A.text: Bring both managers into one meeting with the real data on which job types lose money. Frame the two levers honestly and ask each to own one with a 90-day target.

B.text: Adjust the overhead allocation so install numbers look closer to break-even. But it hides the real problem in a formula change, and the company keeps losing money it cannot see.

C.text: Side with production and tell sales their pricing is the problem. It may even be true, but delivering the verdict as accounting's judgment turns a business problem into a turf war.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why A wins: it uses the data as a shared diagnostic, assigns each side a lever it controls, and converts blame into targets. Discuss: accounting as truth-teller vs. judge, and how to run a numbers meeting that ends in commitments. Wrong answers: B hides the loss in a formula (150); C picks a side and starts a turf war (150).

cards.title: The Supplier's Mistake
cards.scenario: A supplier's invoice arrives $900 lower than their written quote on a large equipment order. The equipment is installed and working. The supplier is a small local distributor with a new billing clerk. Nobody there has noticed the error.

A.text: Pay the invoiced amount and say nothing. The invoice is their document, but it builds a habit of profiting from others' mistakes.

B.text: Pay $450 above the invoice as a quiet goodwill gesture, without explaining why. The supplier will be confused, and the books will carry $450 nobody can reconcile.

C.text: Call the supplier, point out the $900 gap, and pay the correct quoted amount. Keeping it would take money from people the company depends on.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: the error belongs to a small partner the company depends on; correcting it protects the relationship and future pricing. Discuss: how you treat vendors when they err, and what 'partnership' costs. Wrong answers: A profits from a new clerk's mistake (150); B creates a mystery payment that confuses everyone (0).

cards.title: The Agency Pitch
cards.scenario: A collections agency pitches the company: hand over all past-due accounts and they collect for a 30% fee, no effort required. AR aging shows $85,000 over 60 days, and the AR clerk is overwhelmed. The sales manager loves the idea.

A.text: Decline, and fix the real problem first: the AR clerk is drowning in a broken process, not a broken work ethic. Streamline invoicing and set a follow-up routine she can run.

B.text: Threaten customers that accounts are 'going to the agency' without hiring one. The bluff might work once, but customers who call it learn the company makes empty threats.

C.text: Sign a 90-day trial on a small batch of accounts. A trial limits the risk, but 30% of anything they collect is a steep price for skipping the process fixes.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why A wins: it diagnoses the true cause (process, not people), equips the clerk to collect early, and keeps customer relationships in-house. Discuss: the real cost of a 30% fee vs. fixing follow-up, and who owns the customer during collections. Wrong answers: B pays 30% to avoid fixing the system (150); C bluffs and gets caught, draining trust ($0).

cards.title: The Budget Wish List
cards.scenario: Three department heads each submitted budget requests 20% above last year: new trucks, more staff, upgraded software. Total revenue is flat. The owner told accounting to 'make the numbers work.' Two managers implied their teams will quit without full funding.

A.text: Give each department a 7% bump so everyone gets something. But it funds nothing fully, starves the highest-return request, and quietly bakes a deficit into the year.

B.text: Build the budget from the real numbers: flat revenue means flat total spending. Rank every request by expected return and fund from the top until the money runs out.

C.text: Approve the loudest department's full request and deny the other two. It rewards lobbying instead of merit, and teaches managers that threatening wins budgets.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: it replaces lobbying with ranked returns and makes the trade-offs visible, so the budget is a business decision, not a political one. Discuss: how to rank requests by return, and presenting 'no' with data instead of authority. Wrong answers: A funds nothing fully and bakes in a deficit (150); C rewards threats over performance (150).

cards.title: The Questionable Expenses
cards.scenario: Tom, the top sales rep, submits $420 in client dinners that look personal: a Saturday steakhouse, no client names listed. Policy requires names and a business purpose. His manager says to approve it quietly because Tom is 'worth ten of these.'

A.text: Approve the report and say nothing. But every other rep sees what gets approved, and the policy becomes a suggestion the moment it meets a top performer.

B.text: Approve this one, then email the whole company a reminder of the policy without naming Tom. Tom learns his report passed, so the email is noise to the one person it was for.

C.text: Talk to Tom privately and ask him to add the missing details or remove the personal charges. Assume sloppiness before dishonesty, and hold every rep to one standard.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why C wins: it holds the standard without exception, assumes good intent first, and keeps the correction private and dignified. Discuss: whether stars get different rules, and private correction vs. public policy. Wrong answers: A kills the policy for every rep watching (150); B signals to everyone except the person who needs it (0).

cards.title: Book It Now
cards.scenario: Sales just signed a $90,000 commercial contract, with work starting next month. The sales manager asks accounting to book the revenue this month so his team hits its quarterly bonus. He argues the deal is certain and 'revenue is revenue.'

A.text: Refuse, and book the revenue only as the work is completed. Bonuses reward results, not signatures. If the bonus plan punishes honest timing, fix the bonus plan, not the books.

B.text: Book it all now, since the contract is signed and the customer is solid. But the books then claim unearned money, and every future 'certain deal' will expect the same.

C.text: Book half now and half when the work is done, as a compromise. But revenue is either earned or not: half-earned is not a real category.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why A wins: revenue recognition follows earned reality, not bonus calendars, and it names the real fix (the bonus structure) instead of corrupting the books. Discuss: what 'earned' means, and how bonus plans can accidentally incentivize misstatement. Wrong answers: B sets a precedent for every 'certain deal' (150); C invents 'half-earned' as a category ($0).

cards.title: Three Months Behind
cards.scenario: The bank reconciliation is three months behind. The bookkeeper says she will 'catch up when things calm down,' but things never calm down. Last month a $1,700 duplicate vendor payment slipped through unnoticed for weeks. The owner trusts the balance on the screen.

A.text: Hire the bookkeeper an assistant to clear the backlog. But reconciliation fell behind because it is treated as filler work, and filler work still gets skipped when busy.

B.text: Reconcile only the current month going forward and let the old months go. But 'mostly matched' is how a $1,700 duplicate hid for weeks, and the old errors are still in the numbers.

C.text: Block time this week to reconcile all three months and find every outstanding item. Then make reconciliation a non-negotiable weekly 30-minute routine.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why C wins: it clears the backlog fully, then installs a small weekly rhythm that prevents recurrence; discipline beats heroic catch-ups. Discuss: why reconciliations slip (treated as filler), and what a 'non-negotiable routine' requires from leadership. Wrong answers: A adds hands to a habit problem (150); B abandons the old errors to compound in the dark ($0).

cards.title: Cash or Financing
cards.scenario: New dispatch software costs $36,000. The vendor offers 0% financing over 12 months or a 10% discount for paying cash up front. The operating account is healthy, but three slow months are coming. The owner hates tying up cash.

A.text: Take the cash discount: 10% of $36,000 is $3,600 saved, a guaranteed return no safe investment can match. Run the cash forecast to confirm the cushion holds, then pay.

B.text: Take the 0% financing to keep all $36,000 in the account. But it leaves a guaranteed $3,600 on the table to guard against a shortfall the forecast says will not happen.

C.text: Delay the purchase until after the slow months, when cash is flush. But the old software keeps costing hours every week, and waiting is the most expensive option.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why A wins: a certain 10% discount beats any safe alternative, and the forecast (not feelings) confirms the cushion survives the slow months. Discuss: guaranteed returns vs. cash comfort, and what a forecast is actually for. Wrong answers: B leaves $3,600 behind for comfort (150); C pays in lost hours while waiting (0).

cards.title: Credit Hold Mid-Season
cards.scenario: The largest equipment supplier puts the account on credit hold over a $28,000 past-due balance, right at the start of busy season. Trucks are scheduled and customers are booked. The supplier wants the full balance before releasing new orders. Cash is tight but not empty.

A.text: Pay the full $28,000 immediately and empty the cushion completely. The hold lifts today, but the company enters busy season with no safety net.

B.text: Keep ordering through a junior buyer's personal account, bypassing the hold quietly. The jobs stay on schedule, but when the supplier discovers it, the relationship is over.

C.text: Call the supplier today: acknowledge the balance, pay a meaningful portion immediately, and propose a written payment schedule tied to the season's cash flow.

cards.host_note: Principle: Handle It While It's Small. Why C wins: direct contact with money and a written plan turns a hold into a negotiation; suppliers want paying customers, not standoffs. Discuss: why holds are attention-seeking, and what 'meaningful portion' plus a schedule achieves. Wrong answers: A empties the safety net at the worst moment (150); B dodges dishonestly and kills the relationship ($0).

cards.title: The Secret Credit Card
cards.scenario: The company credit card is maxed at $50,000 and supplier bills are piling up. A department manager asks accounting to open a new business card in the company's name without telling the owner, 'to smooth things over until revenue picks up.'

A.text: Open the card as asked and keep it off the main books until revenue picks up. But this is hidden borrowing, and when it surfaces, the issue is trust, not cash flow.

B.text: Refuse, and take the real problem to the owner immediately: the card is maxed and bills are piling up. Bring options, from supplier payment plans to a temporary spending freeze.

C.text: Open the card but set a low limit and monitor every charge personally. But it still creates company debt behind the owner's back.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why B wins: it refuses hidden borrowing and brings the full picture to the owner with real options; cash crises are solvable, secret ones are fatal. Discuss: the difference between a cash problem and a trust problem, and what 'the owner would approve' really means. Wrong answers: A hides debt behind personal monitoring (150); C turns a cash crisis into fraud ($0).

cards.title: The Drowning AR Clerk
cards.scenario: Priya, the AR clerk, works late three nights a week and still falls behind on invoicing. Two completed jobs were never billed, found only when a tech mentioned it. She is capable and conscientious, but volume has doubled since she was hired and the process never changed.

A.text: Hire a part-time assistant to help Priya catch up. But it layers cost onto a broken process, and soon there will be two people drowning instead of one.

B.text: Set Priya a strict daily invoicing quota and check her output each morning. But it treats a good employee like the problem, and quotas burn out conscientious people fastest.

C.text: Talk to Priya first: ask where the hours actually go, then fix the process before adding people. Batch the repeated steps and build templates for common job types.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why C wins: it treats unbilled jobs as a process failure, learns from the person closest to the work, and fixes the system before adding headcount. Discuss: process-first diagnosis, and what to ask before hiring. Wrong answers: A doubles the drowning at extra cost (150); B punishes the conscientious with quotas (150).

cards.title: The Dead Receivable
cards.scenario: A $4,200 receivable from a restaurant build-out has sat unpaid for 14 months. The restaurant closed, the owner filed personal bankruptcy, and the attorney says collection would cost more than the balance. The controller wants to keep it on the books 'so AR doesn't look worse.'

A.text: Write it off this quarter but tell no one outside accounting. The books get clean, but burying the write-off wastes the lesson, and hidden adjustments are how bigger ones start.

B.text: Make one final collection attempt, then write it off and report AR honestly. Keeping a dead balance to protect this quarter's looks picks appearance over reality.

C.text: Hold the receivable through year end and write it off quietly next year. But it keeps a known-dead balance in the numbers everyone manages by for months.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why B wins: it closes the loop honestly (final attempt, then write-off), reports AR as it is, and preserves the lesson about the original credit decision. Discuss: appearance vs. reality in AR, and what write-offs should trigger (a credit-policy review). Wrong answers: A keeps fiction in the numbers for months (150); C buries the lesson along with the balance ($0).

cards.title: The Unreachable Refund
cards.scenario: A $350 refund is owed to a customer who moved with no forwarding address. The check was returned twice, the phone is disconnected, and the email bounced. Eight months have passed. The controller suggests writing it off to income since 'nobody is coming for it.'

A.text: Use the state's unclaimed property process: hold the funds and file the required report. Money owed to a customer stays owed to the customer, no matter how hard they are to reach.

B.text: Write it off to income as the controller suggested. But 'nobody is coming for it' is a guess, and converting his money into income is quietly keeping what is not yours.

C.text: Leave it in the liability account and revisit it 'someday.' But the account will accumulate mystery balances until no one remembers who any of them belong to.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: the obligation does not expire with difficulty; the unclaimed-property process is the lawful, low-cost way to honor it. Discuss: when a debt to a customer ever stops being owed, and what 'immaterial' really justifies. Wrong answers: B converts his money to income on a guess (150); C grows mystery balances (0).

cards.title: The Holiday Advance
cards.scenario: Rosa, a dispatcher of five years, asks accounting for a $1,000 advance on her next paycheck to cover a family emergency before the holidays. Policy forbids pay advances, a rule made after advances became routine and messy years ago. She is reliable and embarrassed to ask.

A.text: Grant the $1,000 quietly and tell no one else. But secret exceptions are exactly how the old mess started, and the next person denied will rightly call it unfair.

B.text: Grant a one-time documented advance with clear written terms: amount, repayment from the next check, and a note that this reflects her record, not a new policy.

C.text: Lend her the money personally from your own pocket. It avoids touching policy, but it mixes personal charity with a company obligation and sets up an awkward dynamic.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why B wins: it helps a loyal employee in a real emergency while protecting the company with written terms and a policy review, not a secret. Discuss: exceptions with terms vs. exceptions in secret, and when old policies deserve re-examination. Wrong answers: A repeats the old mess in secret (150); C mixes personal money with company obligations (0).

cards.title: Payroll Week Cash Crunch
cards.scenario: It is Tuesday. Payroll of $48,000 hits Friday, and the operating account holds $31,000. Two big commercial invoices totaling $60,000 are due sometime this week, but neither customer confirmed a date. The $100,000 credit line is unused. The owner is unreachable until Thursday.

A.text: Wait until Thursday and ask the owner what to do, while pressing both customers for Friday payment. It respects the chain of command, but payroll rides on customer timing.

B.text: Pay only the field technicians Friday and delay the office staff. It keeps the visible team happy, but it splits the company into two classes and guarantees lasting resentment.

C.text: Draw $20,000 from the credit line this morning so Friday is safe no matter what. Check in with both customers calmly, without pressure, and repay the draw when the invoices land.

cards.host_note: Principle: Cash Is Life. Why C wins: payroll is sacred; a cheap, short draw removes all timing risk, and the interest is trivial next to certainty. Discuss: which obligations are never gambled with, and the real cost of a short draw vs. a missed payroll. Wrong answers: A risks payroll on customer timing (150); B creates a two-tier company (150).

cards.title: The Struggling Bookkeeper
cards.scenario: Dana, the junior bookkeeper hired four months ago, keeps miscoding invoices and missing the weekly payables run. The senior accountant redoes her work every Friday and is growing frustrated. Dana is earnest and improving slowly, but vendor relationships are starting to strain.

A.text: Give Dana a written warning with a 30-day improvement plan and clear error targets. But fear rarely builds the careful habits that good bookkeeping requires.

B.text: Sit with Dana and map exactly where the errors happen. Build her a checklist for the payables run and pair her with the senior accountant for two supervised cycles.

C.text: Let her go and hire a more experienced bookkeeper at a higher salary. It costs months of recruiting, and it teaches the team that mistakes here are fatal, not fixable.

cards.host_note: Principle: Train or Remove. Why B wins: it diagnoses the failure point and fixes it with process plus coaching before concluding she cannot do the job. Discuss: the difference between a people problem and a process problem, and what 'train' actually costs in hours per week. Wrong answers: A manages by fear instead of building habits (150); C pays recruiting costs to avoid a few hours of coaching (150).

cards.title: The 20-Day Close
cards.scenario: Month-end close takes 20 days. By the time the owner sees the numbers they are ancient history, and every decision is made on gut feel. The team blames field paperwork, unreconciled accounts, and a close checklist that lives in one person's head.

A.text: Rebuild the close as a system: a written 5-day checklist with owners and deadlines, field paperwork due by the 2nd, reconciliations done weekly. Never let the work pile up.

B.text: Accept the 20-day close as normal and stop promising faster numbers. But it surrenders the purpose of reporting: timely numbers drive decisions, and late numbers drive none.

C.text: Buy close-management software and expect it to fix the timeline. But software cannot create a process: automating a 20-day mess produces a faster 20-day mess.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why A wins: it fixes the underlying rhythm (weekly reconciliations, deadlines, a written checklist) instead of adding labor or software to a broken process. Discuss: what actually causes slow closes, and working harder vs. working on rhythm. Wrong answers: B gives up on timely numbers (150); C automates the mess (0).

cards.title: The Unfair Late Fee
cards.scenario: Mrs. Kowalski, 72, calls in tears. A $45 late fee was added because her check arrived two days late; she mailed it on time. She has paid every bill for nine years and feels punished for something that was not her fault. Policy says late fees are automatic.

A.text: Keep the fee but explain the policy kindly and at length. Understanding the logic is not accepting it, and she still feels punished for what the mail did.

B.text: Transfer her to a supervisor so accounting does not have to decide. But it makes a 72-year-old loyal customer wait on hold to beg for $45, which ends relationships.

C.text: Waive the fee, apologize sincerely, and note her nine-year record. Then suggest auto-pay so mail delays never touch her again.

cards.host_note: Principle: One Department: Customer Service. Why C wins: accounting is customer service too; a nine-year record earns discretion, and auto-pay prevents recurrence. Discuss: when policy should bend, and what 'non-negotiable' really costs. Wrong answers: A explains without helping (150); B makes her wait on hold to beg (0).

cards.title: Backdate the Invoices
cards.scenario: The owner is $12,000 short of his annual bonus target, which is tied to this year's revenue. He asks accounting to date $12,000 of January invoices as December, 'just this once.' The work was done in December; only the invoicing slipped. He says no one will know.

A.text: Backdate the invoices, and pull a few February jobs into January too. Once dates flex, every quarter's numbers become negotiable, and the financial history becomes fiction.

B.text: Refuse, and record the invoices in January when they were created. Statements must reflect what happened when it happened, especially when someone's pay depends on the answer.

C.text: Date the invoices in December as asked, since the work was truly done in December. But the request is about hitting a bonus number, not accuracy, which is what makes it dangerous.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why B wins: it holds the line on when things happened, names why it matters most (pay tied to the numbers), and refuses the 'just this once' logic directly. Discuss: how to refuse the owner's request without disrespect, and why bonus-linked numbers need the most protection. Wrong answers: A moves numbers for pay (150); C turns one favor into a system of fiction ($0).

cards.title: Padding Her Hours
cards.scenario: Accounting discovers that Karen, an office employee of eight years, has added about two hours a week to her timesheet for three months: roughly $1,400 total. Her work is excellent. She recently mentioned money troubles after her husband's injury.

A.text: Terminate her immediately and quietly, per the written policy. But eight years of excellent work and a family crisis suggest a good person making a bad choice.

B.text: Fire her on the spot and announce the reason at the next all-hands meeting. But it humiliates an eight-year employee in crisis and teaches the team to hide mistakes.

C.text: Talk to her privately: show her the records and ask her to explain. Require repayment on a schedule she can meet and set clear expectations in writing, plus help finding resources.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why C wins: it confronts the facts directly, sets written expectations with a real consequence, requires repayment, and still treats her as a person worth keeping. Discuss: firmness plus fairness, and when policy should bend toward a path back. Wrong answers: A loses eight years over $1,400 (150); B destroys trust publicly and teaches hiding ($0).

cards.title: The Short Paycheck
cards.scenario: An installer, Marcus, was underpaid by $180 because his overtime was entered under the wrong pay code. He texted his supervisor Friday night and was told accounting would 'look at it Monday.' Marcus lives paycheck to paycheck and is angry. It is Monday morning.

A.text: Add the $180 to his next regular paycheck with a short note. It is the least extra work, but it asks Marcus to float the company's mistake for two full weeks.

B.text: Fix it today: cut a manual check or same-day deposit, call Marcus to apologize, and audit the pay-code process. When the company is wrong about pay, speed is the apology.

C.text: Pay the $180 today, but require Marcus to sign a form saying it is final. It guards against a double claim, but leading with paperwork when you owe money signals distrust.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: the company caused the error, so the company absorbs the hassle, and the process gets fixed; speed is the apology. Discuss: what 'making it right' costs in effort vs. money, and why pay errors get same-day treatment. Wrong answers: A makes him float the company's mistake (150); C leads with distrust instead of the fix (150).

cards.title: The Early-Pay Discount
cards.scenario: A key supplier offers 2% off for payment within 10 days instead of the usual 30. The company owes this supplier about $40,000 a month. Cash is comfortable but not flush, and the line of credit charges 9% annual interest.

A.text: Take the discount and systematize it. Two percent for paying 20 days early annualizes near 36%, far above the 9% credit line. Pay on day 8, every month.

B.text: Decline and keep the standard 30-day terms for maximum cash flexibility. But it leaves real money on the table every month for comfort rather than math.

C.text: Take the discount only in months when cash feels strong. But 'feels strong' is not a system, and the savings will quietly shrink as busy months get skipped.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why A wins: the math is decisive (2% for 20 days annualizes near 36%), so this is arithmetic, not opinion; systematize it. Discuss: annualizing short-term discounts, and 'comfortable cash' feelings vs. a forecast. Wrong answers: B pays for comfort instead of doing the math (150); C runs savings on mood, not a rule (150).

cards.title: The Burning-Out Manager
cards.scenario: Lisa, the accounting manager, works 60-hour weeks doing reconciliations, payroll backup, and everyone's month-end close. She skips lunch, snapped at two coworkers, and her doctor warned her about her blood pressure. Two junior staff sit underused while she redoes their work.

A.text: Hire another senior accountant to share Lisa's load. It adds capacity fast, but Lisa will redo the new hire's work too, and soon there will be two exhausted people.

B.text: Tell Lisa leadership is demanding, and if she cannot handle it she should say so. It treats burnout as a performance issue, and the company learns how bad it was when she quits.

C.text: Redistribute the work: give the juniors clear ownership of reconciliations with checklists, and train a payroll backup. Require Lisa to take lunch and leave on time.

cards.host_note: Principle: You Are Not the Doer. Why C wins: it fixes the delegation failure structurally (owned tasks, checklists, a backup person) and coaches Lisa that her real job is building the department, not being its hero. Discuss: why heroes make departments fragile, and what 'leave on time' takes from leadership. Wrong answers: A duplicates the problem at a higher salary (150); B punishes the warning and guarantees silence until she quits ($0).

cards.title: The 1099 Suggestion
cards.scenario: The tax preparer suggests reclassifying the W-2 installation techs as 1099 contractors to save $40,000 a year in payroll taxes. The techs work set schedules, drive company trucks, and wear company uniforms. He says 'everyone in the trades does it.'

A.text: Refuse. Classification follows the facts of the work: set schedules, company trucks, and uniforms mean employees, not contractors.

B.text: Ask the preparer to put the recommendation in writing, then have the attorney review it. It adds a second opinion, though the facts of the work already answer the question.

C.text: Reclassify all technicians as 1099 contractors and have them sign agreements. But set schedules, company trucks, and uniforms still describe employees.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: classification follows the facts of the work, not the savings; it protects the company legally and the techs practically, and it ends the relationship with an advisor who suggested breaking the law. Discuss: the actual control test for contractors, and what to do when a professional advises wrongdoing. Wrong answers: B entertains a proposal the facts already answer (150); C buys back taxes, penalties, and interest ($0).

cards.title: The Invoicing Turf War
cards.scenario: Jen and Marco both claim ownership of customer invoicing. Some customers are billed twice, others not at all. Both are good employees who feel disrespected, and the tension is spreading through the office.

A.text: Tell both to sort it out or you will replace them with one person. It ends the talk fast, but it shames two good employees for confusion that unclear direction created.

B.text: Name one clear owner and write the backup process down. Let both help design the handoff. Most turf wars are really clarity wars: nobody told them plainly who owns what.

C.text: Split invoicing by alphabet: A-M to Jen, N-Z to Marco. It ends the argument, but it doubles handoffs and leaves customers unsure who to call.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why B wins: one named owner, a written backup process, and both employees given a voice in the handoff; it treats the fight as a clarity problem, not a people problem. Discuss: clarity wars vs. turf wars, and how to assign ownership without creating losers. Wrong answers: A doubles handoffs and customer confusion (150); C shames good people and sends the loser job hunting ($0).

cards.title: The Garnishment Order
cards.scenario: A wage garnishment order arrives for Luis, a well-liked installer going through a divorce. It is legal and must be processed, cutting his take-home pay noticeably. He does not know yet, and in this small office news travels fast.

A.text: Tell Luis privately before the next payroll: explain what the order requires and what changes in his check. Make clear the details stay between accounting and him.

B.text: Ask his supervisor to break the news, since they are closer. But it hands confidential payroll details to someone who should never hold them.

C.text: Mention the garnishment to the office manager 'so she can be supportive.' Kind intention, but his private financial business will be office talk within a week.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why A wins: private advance notice with clear facts, plus a firm confidentiality boundary; the legal duty is met and his dignity is intact. Discuss: who truly needs to know about a payroll action, and how discretion builds trust across the company. Wrong answers: B misuses the supervisor as messenger (150); C turns kindness into office gossip ($0).

cards.title: The $600 Overpayment
cards.scenario: During reconciliation, accounting finds that Mr. Chen overpaid his final invoice by $600 four months ago. He never noticed and never called. No one but accounting knows. The month is tight, and $600 would help cover a small shortfall.

A.text: Leave the $600 as a credit on his account against future work. But it was never his choice to leave it there, and a credit he does not know about quietly keeps what is not yours.

B.text: Call Mr. Chen, tell him about the overpayment, and mail the refund check this week. It is his money, and a tight month does not change that.

C.text: Donate the $600 to a local charity in the company's name. It does something good, but it spends someone else's money on the company's generosity, which is not generosity.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: the money is his regardless of the company's month; proactive refunds build durable trust. Discuss: whose money it is when no one is watching, and the long-run value of an unexpected refund. Wrong answers: A keeps it quietly under a customer-service label (150); C spends his money on the company's image (150).

cards.title: Cash Piling Up
cards.scenario: The operating account holds $280,000, far above what the company needs, and it earns nothing. The owner likes the big balance; it feels safe. Meanwhile a $60,000 equipment loan at 8% is being paid on schedule, and prices keep rising.

A.text: Leave the cash where it is. The big balance feels safe, but paying 8% on a loan while cash earns nothing buys that feeling with real money.

B.text: Invest the surplus in the stock market for higher returns. But operating cash is not investment capital: a dip before payroll turns an investment into a crisis.

C.text: Keep a 60-day cushion, sweep the rest into an interest-bearing account, and pay off the 8% loan. Then set a monthly sweep rule so the pile never builds again.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: it sequences by return (kill the 8% loan first), keeps a real cushion, and systematizes the sweep so the pile never rebuilds. Discuss: the price of cash that only 'feels safe,' and guaranteed returns vs. market risk for operating funds. Wrong answers: A pays real money for the feeling of safety (150); B gambles payroll timing on the market (0).

cards.title: The Review Threat
cards.scenario: A customer owes a legitimate $1,100 balance on a completed job. He emails accounting: waive the balance or he will post one-star reviews everywhere and 'tell everyone how you scam people.' The work was done well. The owner worries about the 4.8-star rating.

A.text: Offer a 25% courtesy discount to make the problem go away. But it rewards the threat with $275, and he learns that pushing harder next time gets even more.

B.text: Hold the line politely: confirm the balance is valid, offer a reasonable payment plan, and document everything in writing. Do not mention the reviews at all.

C.text: Waive the balance, then have the team post fake positive reviews to bury the negatives. The books lose $1,100 and the review profile becomes fiction.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: it refuses extortion without escalating, keeps the door open with a payment plan, and defends the rating with facts instead of payoffs. Discuss: the long-run price of rewarding threats, and how to answer bad reviews with calm facts. Wrong answers: A funds the next threat with a discount (150); C manufactures a fake reputation ($0).

cards.title: Pricing Without Numbers
cards.scenario: The owner wants to raise the flat-rate price book 8% across the board because 'everything costs more.' Sales supports it; production fears losing bids. Nobody has looked at actual job costs by job type in over a year. Accounting is asked to bless the increase.

A.text: Bless the 8% as asked. But instinct is not costing: some job types may need 15% and others may already be overpriced, and a flat increase fixes the wrong jobs.

B.text: Delay the increase until a full pricing study is done next quarter. But the company bleeds margin for three more months waiting for perfect data.

C.text: Pull the real job-cost data by job type first, then show which prices are underwater and by how much. Recommend targeted increases where margin is thin.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: targeted increases from real job-type costs beat both flat instinct and delay; accounting's value is the analysis. Discuss: flat vs. targeted increases, and 'good enough data today' vs. perfect data next quarter. Wrong answers: A misprices in both directions on instinct (150); B bleeds margin waiting for perfect data (0).

cards.title: Net-60 for BigCo
cards.scenario: A large commercial client, BigCo, wants net-60 terms on a $120,000 annual contract, take it or leave it. Sales is thrilled. But 60-day terms would tie up roughly $20,000 of the company's cash at all times, and BigCo's procurement is famous for paying late.

A.text: Accept the net-60 terms to win the contract. But the company becomes BigCo's interest-free bank, and every late payment becomes a payroll risk it never agreed to.

B.text: Counter with net-30 plus a 2% discount for payment within 10 days, and run a credit check before signing. The discount gives their payables team a reason to pay fast.

C.text: Walk away entirely and focus on smaller clients with better terms. But it surrenders $120,000 of real revenue over terms that could have been negotiated.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: it quantifies the cash cost, negotiates terms that change behavior (early-pay discount), and verifies credit before committing. Discuss: revenue vs. cash flow, and negotiating terms instead of accepting ultimatums. Wrong answers: A banks the client for free (150); C lets fear decide instead of math (0).

cards.title: The Disputed Invoice
cards.scenario: Mrs. Alvarez calls, upset. Her water heater invoice is $2,400, but she says the technician quoted $1,950 in her kitchen. His handwritten ticket is hard to read, and the office has no signed estimate on file. She is a repeat customer, ready to leave a bad review.

A.text: Pull the work order and confirm with the tech what he quoted. If he quoted $1,950, bill her $1,950 and absorb the $450 gap. Then retrain him on signed estimates.

B.text: Offer to split the difference at $2,175 as a goodwill gesture. But it teaches the customer that prices are negotiable and leaves the broken quoting process as it was.

C.text: Stand firm on the full $2,400 since the work is complete. But it risks a repeat customer over the company's own mistake, and her review will cost more than $450.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: the company made the quoting error, so the company absorbs it; the fix is systemic (signed estimates), not just a refund. Discuss: who bears the cost of an internal mistake, and how signed estimates prevent the next one. Wrong answers: B trains customers to haggle (150); C trades a relationship for $450 (150).

cards.title: Payroll Comes Up Short
cards.scenario: Thursday night, accounting finds the payroll file went in with wrong hours: the company is $9,000 short for Friday payroll. The owner is at a conference, the credit line needs his signature, and the team expects checks at 8 a.m.

A.text: Delay payroll to Monday, telling the team the bank had a processing delay. It buys the weekend, but it lies to everyone about money they earned.

B.text: Tell the team the truth first thing in the morning: the file had an error and the money lands by noon. Reach the owner, get the draw signed, and have every check out by noon.

C.text: Quietly move $9,000 from a customer's large prepayment into payroll. Checks clear, but this spends a customer's money without permission to cover the company's mistake.

cards.host_note: Principle: Safe to Speak. Why B wins: immediate honest communication plus a concrete fix time; payroll trust survives a half-day delay it does not survive a cover-up. Discuss: what to say when the company is at fault, and why specifics ('by noon') beat vague reassurance. Wrong answers: A lies about the bank to buy a weekend (150); C misuses customer funds to hide the error ($0).

cards.title: The Hidden Bills
cards.scenario: The new controller opens a desk drawer and finds unpaid vendor bills totaling $22,000, some 120 days old. The previous bookkeeper hid them to make cash flow look better before she left. Two vendors stopped shipments. The owner does not know.

A.text: Tell the owner everything today: what was hidden, how much, and for how long, with a plan to pay the vendors. Then fix the process with dual controls on payables.

B.text: Pay the bills quietly this week and tell no one. But the owner keeps deciding on reports that were fiction for months, and the process hole stays open for the next person.

C.text: Pay the most urgent bills now and disclose the rest gradually. But staged honesty is still managed honesty, and every delay is another week of decisions made on wrong numbers.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why A wins: full immediate disclosure plus a process fix; the owner cannot lead on numbers he cannot trust. Discuss: why 'quietly fixing it' feels tempting, and what dual controls actually prevent. Wrong answers: B leaves the process hole open ($0); C manages the truth on a schedule (150).

cards.title: She Wants to Learn Costing
cards.scenario: Alina, the junior accountant, asked to learn job costing, the most valuable skill in the department. The senior accountant says there is no time to teach: month-end, payroll, and payables fill every hour. Alina is sharp and motivated, but without a path she will leave.

A.text: Tell Alina to learn job costing on her own time, and the company will reimburse the fees. But it signals that her growth is her private hobby, not the company's investment.

B.text: Give her the costing files to review whenever she has downtime, with no guidance. There is no downtime, so this is a polite no, and unguided files teach bad habits.

C.text: Carve out two hours a week: Alina shadows one real job-cost review, then owns a small piece of the next one with feedback. Shift one routine task off her plate to make room.

cards.host_note: Principle: Be a Learning Machine. Why C wins: it makes training real with scheduled hours, shadowing, and owned work, funded by rebalancing load; it also builds department capacity. Discuss: what 'no time to train' really costs, and how teaching builds the bench. Wrong answers: A outsources her growth (150); B is a polite no that teaches bad habits (0).

cards.title: Ninety Days Past Due
cards.scenario: The Hendersons, customers for six years, owe $3,800 and are 90 days past due. Mr. Henderson called, admitted his hours were cut, and offered $200 a month. Policy says accounts over 90 days go to a collection agency.

A.text: Set a written payment plan: $200 a month, auto-drafted, with no late fees while payments stay current. Thank him for calling instead of hiding.

B.text: Send the account to collections as the routine requires. But the agency's cut leaves less than a payment plan would, and a six-year relationship ends over one hard year.

C.text: Accept $200 a month verbally, with no formal agreement in place. Without written terms the payments will drift, and accounting will chase this balance next year.

cards.host_note: Principle: Keep Customers for Life. Why A wins: it keeps a six-year customer, recovers the full balance, and written auto-draft terms make the plan durable; kindness plus structure. Discuss: when policy should bend, and why written terms protect both sides. Wrong answers: B trades lifetime value for an agency fee (150); C is kindness with no structure, so it drifts (150).

cards.title: The Vendor's Offer
cards.scenario: A materials vendor takes the purchasing manager to lunch and offers him a personal $200 gift card 'for every $10,000 order you steer our way.' The manager mentions it to accounting casually, laughing, and says he has not decided. The vendor's prices are already competitive.

A.text: Ignore it, since he has not accepted anything and the prices are fair. But silence reads as permission, and the offer stays until he stops laughing and starts accepting.

B.text: Refuse the arrangement outright and tell the vendor plainly that purchasing decisions are made on price, quality, and service, never on personal perks. Put the policy in writing.

C.text: Tell the manager to accept the gift cards but keep them quiet. But it sells the company's purchasing judgment for $200 a card, and secret perks always grow.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: it kills the kickback cleanly, sets a written standard for all buyers, and keeps purchasing decisions on merit. Discuss: why 'prices are fair anyway' does not make it okay, and how small perks scale. Wrong answers: A permits by silence until the laugh stops (150); C rents out purchasing judgment ($0).

cards.title: The Owner's Personal Expenses
