cards.scenario: At year end, the owner drops a folder of personal receipts on accounting's desk: family vacations, a home theater, dinners with friends. He asks that they run through the business to lower the tax bill. He says his last accountant 'took care of it.' The total is about $14,000.

A.text: Book the receipts as business expenses exactly as asked. It keeps the boss happy, but it puts false numbers in the books and exposes everyone if the return is ever questioned.

B.text: Book half the receipts, the ones that could plausibly relate to business, and return the rest. But 'plausibly related' is not a standard that survives an audit.

C.text: Decline respectfully: the books must reflect reality, and personal spending booked as business expense is misrepresentation. Offer to review legitimate deductions instead.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: it refuses to falsify records, explains the business cost (corrupted management numbers), and offers a legitimate alternative. Discuss: how to say no to the owner with respect, and why clean books are a business asset. Wrong answers: A falsifies records to keep the boss happy (150); B falsifies politely and calls it compromise (150).

cards.title: Make the Report Look Better
cards.scenario: The night before the quarterly owner meeting, the GM asks accounting to move $18,000 of expenses into next quarter 'just on paper' so profit looks stronger. He says the owner is stressed, the business is fine, and the expenses will still be recorded, just later.

A.text: Refuse, and present the real numbers with a clear explanation of what drove the quarter. A tough quarter with a plan reads as leadership.

B.text: Move half the expenses so the quarter looks somewhat better. But half a misstatement is still a misstatement, and the line will move further next quarter.

C.text: Agree to move the expenses, but document the GM's request in an email. The trail protects accounting later, but it turns a refusal into quiet complicity with evidence.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why A wins: it protects the integrity of the numbers the owner manages by, and gives the GM a better alternative: framing the honest story. Discuss: how to refuse a superior's request with respect, and the difference between framing and falsifying. Wrong answers: B invents 'half honest' as a category (150); C documents complicity instead of preventing it (0).

cards.title: The Firing Conversation
cards.scenario: You have decided to let go of a dispatcher after months of documented performance issues. The meeting is tomorrow, and you keep rehearsing ways to soften the blow. How do you handle it?

A.text: Be direct and brief: state the decision in the first minute, give the documented reasons plainly, and explain final pay. Then listen. Bring the paperwork and a witness.

B.text: Open with his strengths, then ease gently into the decision. Softening shows respect and keeps the conversation calm. Offer to serve as a reference for roles that fit him better.

C.text: Offer him the choice to resign instead of being fired. It preserves his dignity and his resume. The outcome is the same for you with far less pain. Put the choice in writing.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why A (+500) wins: clarity is kindness; a direct, prepared, humane conversation respects his dignity far more than softening or dressing the exit as his choice. Discussion: what does 'direct and brief' sound like in real words; how do you handle tears or anger; why does the witness matter? Wrong: B (+150)'s softening confuses him about whether it is really happening; C (+150)'s fake choice insults his intelligence and muddies the record.

cards.title: The Empty Interview Room
cards.scenario: Half of your scheduled candidates no-showed for interviews this month. Managers are frustrated and want to stop chasing people who clearly do not want jobs. The pipeline is thinning fast. What do you change?

A.text: Require a $50 deposit to book an interview, returned when the candidate shows up. It filters for serious applicants and compensates manager time. Fifty dollars proves intent.

B.text: Schedule fewer interviews and only invite the strongest resumes. Fewer interviews means fewer no-shows by simple math, and managers spend their time on qualified candidates.

C.text: Fix your side first: confirm by text the day before, offer flexible times, and make the location and parking clear. Then track no-shows by source and drop bad channels.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why C (+500) wins: no-shows are usually a process failure, not a character failure; fixing confirmation, flexibility, and clarity is a system that works for every candidate, every week. Discussion: what should your confirmation text say; which sources actually produce reliable candidates; how do you measure show-rate improvement? Wrong: A ($0)'s deposit insults good candidates and shrinks the pool; B (+150)'s tighter funnel mistakes fewer interviews for better hiring.

cards.title: The Wrong Mentor
cards.scenario: New hires shadow your most senior tech, who is brilliant but openly cynical: customers lie, management does not care. Two recent hires have picked up his attitude, and he is your best teacher technically. What do you do?

A.text: Stop assigning new hires to him, and tell him why: his skill is respected and his cynicism is contagious. Choose mentors for attitude first, skill second, with a mentoring role.

B.text: Keep the shadowing but add a culture day at the end of onboarding to undo the damage. His technical training is too valuable to lose, and one day can balance weeks of grumbling.

C.text: Talk to him privately about toning it down around new hires. He has earned his opinions over many years, and a conversation should be enough to get him to filter himself.

cards.host_note: Principle: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves. Why A (+500) wins: mentors are culture transmitters, and a cynic in that seat reproduces cynics; selecting mentors for attitude and telling the senior tech the truth protects both the new hires and the standard. Discussion: how do you tell a veteran his attitude disqualifies him without losing his skill; what makes a great mentor beyond tenure; how do you recognize mentors so the role is coveted? Wrong: C (+150)'s quiet word has been tried everywhere and changes nothing; B ($0)'s culture day cannot un-teach six weeks of modeled contempt.

cards.title: The Poaching Call
cards.scenario: A competitor is calling your technicians offering three dollars more per hour. Two good people mentioned it this week, morale is wobbling, and the calls will keep coming. How do you respond?

A.text: Tell the crew that anyone who entertains the competitor's calls will be let go. Loyalty is a two-way street, and a hard clear line now stops the bleeding fast.

B.text: Talk to your people: what works, what does not, what would make leaving unthinkable? Fix the gaps you can afford, keep pay at market, and make staying better than three dollars.

C.text: Call the competitor's owner directly and tell him to back off your people. Poaching is dirty pool in a small market, and a frank owner-to-owner conversation usually stops it cold.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why B (+500) wins: the calls are a symptom, and the cure is making your company the obviously better choice across pay, respect, schedule, and future; threats and bidding wars both lose. Discussion: what questions reveal the real retention risks; which gaps are actually fixable on your budget; how do you talk about the competitor without sounding scared? Wrong: C (+150)'s owner-to-owner call changes nothing about why your people listen; A ($0)'s loyalty threat accelerates exactly the exits it aims to prevent.

cards.title: The Blame Speech
cards.scenario: You fired a manager for repeated missed targets. At the next team meeting, people are anxious and whispering about what happened. You need to address the departure head-on. What do you say?

A.text: Address it and own it: the decision was yours, the standards are the company's. Do not detail his failures to the room. Then talk about what comes next and what you need from them.

B.text: Tell the team why he failed: missed numbers quarter after quarter, excuses in reviews, warnings ignored. Full transparency shows what happens when targets are missed.

C.text: Say nothing about the departure and move to business as usual. Addressing it gives the exit more weight than it deserves, and the team will settle down on its own within a week.

cards.host_note: Principle: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame. Why A (+500) wins: owning the decision and the standard, without dissecting the person, shows the team that accountability flows upward and dignity flows downward; that is what steady teams are built on. Discussion: what does 'brief' mean in actual sentences; how do you answer direct questions without lying or oversharing; what do you say about the transition plan? Wrong: B ($0)'s full story humiliates the departed and terrifies the room; C (+150)'s silence lets anxiety write its own darker story.

cards.title: The Chaotic First Week
cards.scenario: A promising new hire tells you privately that his first week was chaos: no workstation, no login, nobody knew he was starting. He is reconsidering his decision to join you, and his manager looks embarrassed. What do you do?

A.text: Apologize and promise the next hire gets better, then focus forward: equipment, access, introductions. The damage for him is done; make sure the next person never experiences this.

B.text: Ask his manager to smooth it over. Onboarding belongs to the supervisor, and stepping in undermines that manager's authority. Check back in two weeks to confirm it resolved.

C.text: Own it: tell him he deserved better and the failure was yours, not his. Repair his week with a full walkthrough, proper introductions, and a real first project with an early win.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why C (+500) wins: a workstation, a login, and someone expecting you are the basics, and basics done right retain people; owning the failure personally rebuilds trust while the checklist prevents the repeat. Discussion: what belongs on a first-week checklist; who owns each item; how does a leader apologize without groveling? Wrong: A (+150) writes him off as a sunk cost while he is still deciding; B (+0) delegates the repair to the person who caused it.

cards.title: The Counter-Offer
cards.scenario: Your best install lead says a competitor offered him four dollars more per hour. He likes it here but the money gap is real. He has not accepted yet, and he told you first. What do you do?

A.text: Match the four dollars today and add a $2,000 retention bonus at six months. Losing him costs far more than the raise. Every day you wait, the competitor's offer looks better.

B.text: Ask what matters beyond the hourly number: schedule, crew, growth, respect. Close the gap partway if the budget allows, and fix the frustrations he names with a growth plan.

C.text: Let him go and wish him well. Matching counter-offers trains people to job-hunt for raises. Invest the money in his replacement instead of renting loyalty at a premium.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why B (+500) wins: the offer is usually the trigger, not the cause; diagnosing the real drivers lets you fix retention instead of renting it, and a growth plan gives him a future the competitor did not offer. Discussion: which questions reveal the real reason; how far do you close a pay gap without breaking equity; when is the counter-offer conversation already too late? Wrong: A (+150) buys months, not loyalty, and teaches the tactic; C (+150) surrenders a known star to save face.

cards.title: The Off-Limits Question
cards.scenario: You overhear a hiring manager ask a candidate, 'Do you have kids? This job needs someone flexible.' The candidate laughs it off, but you know the question crosses a legal line, and he interviews candidates regularly. What do you do?

A.text: Correct him privately today: explain why the question is off-limits, and give three lawful reliability questions. Then put a do's-and-don'ts sheet in every hiring packet.

B.text: Pull him aside, tell him to stick to the script next time, and move on. He meant no harm and the candidate laughed it off. A quiet word corrects it without embarrassing a manager.

C.text: Send a company-wide email with interview guidelines, no names. Attach approved lawful questions and ask every manager to confirm they read it.

cards.host_note: Principle: Handle It While It's Small. Why A (+500) wins: a small private correction plus a systemic sheet stops the next ten violations; a quiet word alone leaves every other manager still guessing. Discussion: which lawful questions actually assess reliability; how do you correct without shaming; who owns the hiring packet? Wrong: B (+150) fixes nothing beyond one person; C (+150)'s vague email teaches nobody and signals you will not confront directly.

cards.title: Above the Range
cards.scenario: Your top candidate asks for $8,000 above your posted salary range. She is worth it on paper, and the budget is tight but not frozen. Your current staff would hear about any exception. How do you respond?

A.text: Hold the range firmly and do not budge. Ranges exist for fairness: one exception starts a chain you will never contain. Thank her for her time and move on if she will not meet it.

B.text: Check two things: can the budget stretch without breaking equity with current staff, and does her value exceed the range? If both check out, stretch the range and document why.

C.text: Offer the top of the range plus a one-time bonus to bridge the gap. It respects the band structure while getting close to her number. Most candidates accept a creative package.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B (+500) wins: the decision is arithmetic, not ego; checking budget impact and true value before answering produces a yes you can defend or a no she can respect. Discussion: how do you judge 'truly exceeds the range'; what does documenting the exception prevent; how do you present a twelve-month path credibly? Wrong: A (+150) loses a proven difference-maker to protect a spreadsheet; C (+0)'s bonus bridge delays the same fight by one year.

cards.title: The Career Fair Booth
cards.scenario: A regional career fair expects two thousand young job seekers next month. Your biggest competitor will run a large flashy booth. Your budget is small, and the whole local market will be walking past. What is your play?

A.text: Skip the booth and post the roles on three major job boards instead. Boards reach more people for less money. Measurable applications beat expensive theater.

B.text: Send two recruiters with a table, a banner, and a QR code to your application page. Collect names, follow up within 48 hours, and measure cost per applicant. Lean beats absent.

C.text: Put two of your best team members in the booth, not recruiters, for honest talk about the work, good and bad. Bring a one-page handout on where a hire can be in three years.

cards.host_note: Principle: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You. Why C (+500) wins: in a tight labor market the scarcest resource is candidate attention, and authenticity from real employees beats polish; the career-path handout sells a future, not just a job. Discussion: who are your two best ambassadors; what does honest mean (do you admit the hard parts); how do you measure booth ROI? Wrong: A (+150) surrenders the face-to-face channel entirely; B (+150) shows up forgettably.

cards.title: The Sixty-Day Slump
cards.scenario: A new hire you were excited about is struggling at day 60: slow work, repeated errors, quiet in meetings. Her formal 90-day review is coming up, and you need to act before then. What do you do now?

A.text: Sit down with her this week: name what you see and ask what is in her way. Then build a 30-day plan with clear targets and weekly check-ins. Coach her, do not just warn her.

B.text: Extend probation 60 more days and tell her to step it up now. Some people are slow starters, and cutting her wastes your whole hiring investment. More time plus a warning is fair.

C.text: Wait for the 90-day review and decide then with a record. Acting feels premature, and the review gives documentation and a natural moment. Keep notes, but do not intervene early.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why A (+500) wins: she cannot be accountable to a bar she has not been clearly shown; a specific plan with coaching makes day 90 a fair verdict instead of an ambush. Discussion: what do two or three targets look like for this role; how do you ask 'what's in your way' without it becoming an excuse session; what if she meets half the plan? Wrong: B (+150) extends the fog without clearing it; C (+0)'s silence until day 90 turns the review into a trial she did not know she was in.

cards.title: The Signing Bonus
cards.scenario: You are competing for a licensed technician in a tight market. Your advisor suggests a $5,000 signing bonus to win him, but you worry about paying for a signature instead of a career. How do you structure it?

A.text: Skip the bonus and offer $5,000 more in base salary instead. Salary compounds in loyalty while a bonus is forgotten by month two. Permanent money beats temporary money.

B.text: Tie it to staying: $1,500 at 90 days and $3,500 at one year, in writing, with a repayment clause if he leaves early. A signing bonus should buy retention, not just a signature.

C.text: Split it evenly: $2,500 at hire and $2,500 at six months. It balances the immediate win with a reason to stay past the honeymoon.

cards.host_note: Principle: Pay for What You Want Repeated. Why B (+500) wins: the bonus is a tool, and tools should be aimed at the outcome you want; back-loading with a clawback pays for retention while day-one cash pays only for a signature. Discussion: what split actually retains versus what just feels generous; how do you explain a clawback without souring the hire; when is a bonus the wrong tool entirely? Wrong: A (+150) permanently raises fixed cost for a one-time recruiting problem; C (+150)'s even split still pays half for showing up.

cards.title: The Waiting Clearance
cards.scenario: Your top candidate accepted, contingent on a background check now delayed three weeks. He wants to start Monday. The role enters customer homes and handles payments, and he has another offer waiting. What do you do?

A.text: Hold the start date until the clearance completes, and tell him why: the role enters customer homes and handles payments. Stay in touch and send onboarding materials to review.

B.text: Start him Monday on office-only duties: no customer contact, no payment access. He stays engaged, you get work from the wait, and restrictions lift when the clearance arrives.

C.text: Start him Monday with full duties and quietly expedite the check behind the scenes. The delay is probably just backlog, and holding a great hire over paperwork punishes everyone.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A (+500) wins: the check exists to protect customers who open their doors to strangers; holding the line when it costs you a fast start is what makes the promise to customers real. Discussion: how do you keep a candidate warm for three weeks without overpromising; what do you say if he gets another offer; where does the real risk sit? Wrong: B (+150)'s limited duties still put an uncleared person inside the operation; C ($0) gambles customer trust on the assumption that backlog equals clean.

cards.title: The Referral Reward
cards.scenario: Your best hires always came from employee referrals, but that pipeline has dried up over the last year. You want a formal program that actually restarts it, and the budget is flexible if the design is right. What do you roll out?

A.text: Offer a $250 gift card for any referral hired, paid on day one. Keep the rules verbal so you can adjust later. Mention it at the next huddle and watch what happens.

B.text: Run a 60-day contest: the employee with the most hired referrals wins a weekend trip. Post a weekly leaderboard for energy. Competition creates urgency a flat bonus never will.

C.text: Launch a written program: $500 when the hire clears 90 days, $500 more at one year. Post the rules, pay bonuses publicly and on time, and thank referrers by name.

cards.host_note: Principle: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You. Why C (+500) wins: recruiting is a system, not a wish; a trusted, written, reliably paid program compounds while gimmicks spike and die. Discussion cues: why did referrals dry up (distrust? no ask?), does payout timing shape behavior, how does public payment build credibility? Wrong answers: A (+150) trains people the program is casual and changeable; B (+150) creates a burst then a dead pipeline and rewards volume over fit.

cards.title: The Gap Years
cards.scenario: A candidate's resume shows a two-year gap with no explanation. Her skills test is the best you have seen for this role. Your policy says nothing about gaps, and she is waiting on your decision. What do you do?

A.text: Pass and move to the next candidate. An unexplained two-year gap is a risk you do not need when other applicants have clean histories. Choose the one without questions attached.

B.text: Ask about it respectfully, then judge the answer like any other: honestly, without assumptions. Her skills test is real evidence; the gap is just an unanswered question.

C.text: Call her employer about the gap instead of asking her directly. A third party gives you the unfiltered story without a rehearsed answer, and you verify the timeline independently.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Pre-Judge. Why B (+500) wins: the gap is a question, not a verdict, and a direct respectful conversation gets the answer while honoring her dignity; judging the person beats judging the timeline. Discussion: how do you ask about a gap without it feeling like an interrogation; which answers are genuine versus evasive; what should your policy say going forward? Wrong: A (+150) discards your best skills test over an unasked question; C ($0) investigates behind her back and poisons trust before day one.

cards.title: The Exit Interview Truth
cards.scenario: Exit interviews keep surfacing the same theme for a year: new hires feel blindsided by on-call expectations. Nothing has changed, and the pattern is now undeniable. What do you do about it?

A.text: Add a bold paragraph about on-call duties to every offer letter. If it is in writing before day one, nobody can claim they were blindsided. One signed paragraph ends the surprise.

B.text: Add an on-call bonus bump to make the burden worth it, with a published schedule so people can plan their lives. Money softens the surprise, and it shows the team you heard them.

C.text: Treat it as a management failure. Rewrite postings and the interview script so on-call is described honestly, and build a fair rotation that genuinely shares the burden.

cards.host_note: Principle: Problems Are Tests. Why C (+500) wins: a repeated exit theme is data about the system; only honest pitching plus a fair rotation removes the cause. Discussion: what do honest on-call numbers look like in a posting; how do you build a rotation people trust; what should the 30-day check-in ask? Wrong: A (+150) documents the surprise without removing it; B (+150) pays people to endure a problem you could solve.

cards.title: Everyone's Favorite
cards.scenario: A long-tenured warehouse coordinator is beloved: funny, helpful, always early. He cannot learn the new inventory system after six months of training, and his errors are piling up. What do you do?

A.text: Have the honest talk: show the error pattern and give one final 30-day plan with daily support. If he cannot clear it, move him to a role without the system or part ways kindly.

B.text: Keep him where he is and have others double-check his work daily. His attitude lifts the whole shop, and a buddy check works around the errors. Losing him hurts morale more.

C.text: Move him now to deliveries or shop support, where the system is not required. You keep a culture carrier, remove the errors, and he gets a fresh start somewhere he can succeed.

cards.host_note: Principle: Right Person, Right Seat. Why A (+500) wins: it pairs honesty with a genuine final chance, and names the truth that carrying him punishes everyone including him; the outcome, whichever way it goes, is fair and clear. Discussion: what does daily support actually look like; how do you show error patterns without shaming; what alternative roles truly fit? Wrong: B ($0)'s buddy-check taxes the whole team to protect one person's feelings; C (+150) avoids the conversation by moving the problem sideways.

cards.title: The Old Posts
cards.scenario: A strong candidate's public social media shows crude jokes and complaints about former bosses from three years ago. His work history since then is excellent, and he interviewed well. How do you handle the old posts?

A.text: Disqualify him quietly and move on. Public posts are a real window into character, and crude jokes plus boss-bashing predict the employee you do not want in customer homes.

B.text: Bring it up: ask what he would want a future employer to see online today, and listen to how he owns it. Judge the work record and whether he takes responsibility without excuses.

C.text: Have someone else on the team review the posts and decide whether it matters. You are too close to be objective about character, and a second opinion keeps the process fair.

cards.host_note: Principle: Character Over Skill. Why B (+500) wins: it tests character directly instead of guessing from old posts; how he handles the question reveals the maturity the posts cannot, and you keep a strong work record in play. Discussion: what does owning it sound like versus excuses; where is the line between growth and pattern; should you look at social media at all? Wrong: A (+150) discards proven skill over ancient posts; C (+0) outsources a leadership call to avoid discomfort.

cards.title: The One-Interview Hire
cards.scenario: A manager is pushing to hire a candidate after a single great conversation. 'I just know,' he says. 'We will lose her if we slow down.' Two interview steps remain in your process. What do you do?

A.text: Finish the process. One conversation is when discipline matters most, because charm is not competence. Run the steps, check references, and score her on the requirements.

B.text: Compromise: run one reference call, then decide this afternoon. It honors his urgency with a safety check. A positive reference gives speed and diligence; a flag saves you.

C.text: Let the manager decide: it is his team and his vacancy, and he will live with the hire daily. Support his call, help with onboarding, and hold him accountable for the outcome.

cards.host_note: Principle: Hell Yeah, or No. Why A (+500) wins: a fast yes is as dangerous as a slow no; completing the process tests whether the enthusiasm survives evidence. Discussion: what are the remaining steps designed to catch; how do you move fast without skipping; what do you tell the candidate while the process runs? Wrong: B (+150)'s single call is theater that will not catch a real problem; C (+0) abdicates the hiring standard to whoever feels strongest.

cards.title: The Promise
cards.scenario: A candidate you desperately want is hesitating on your offer. Your manager suggests promising him a supervisor promotion within six months to close the deal. No such opening is planned or budgeted. What do you do?

A.text: Make the promise verbally and worry about the opening later. Landing him now solves the vacancy, and six months is a long time. You can explain any delay when the time comes.

B.text: Offer a title bump: senior technician with higher pay. It gives him the status he wants without committing to an opening that does not exist. Titles are cheap.

C.text: Refuse the promise and sell the job honestly: real pay, real work, real timeline. Hires built on honesty stay; hires built on promises quit and warn others.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C (+500) wins: a hire secured by fiction becomes a resignation secured by betrayal, and the story he tells afterward poisons your reputation with every candidate he knows. Discussion: how do you sell a real opportunity hard without inventing one; what do you say when the candidate presses for a timeline; how do you handle the manager who suggested the lie? Wrong: A ($0) trades one vacancy now for a bitter exit and a reputation hit later; B (+150)'s inflated title creates an expectations mess with the existing team.

cards.title: The Growth Question
cards.scenario: A strong coordinator asks you directly, 'Where can I go from here?' You have no formal career path for the role, and she is clearly ambitious. Two competitors are hiring right now. What do you tell her?

A.text: Be honest that the role has no ladder and offer a raise instead. Not every seat leads somewhere. Fair pay for good work is an honest deal, and clarity prevents resentment later.

B.text: Build the path with her: map the skills the next level requires, agree on three milestones, and tie each to new responsibility and pay. Review progress every quarter.

C.text: Promise a promotion track and work out details over the next few months. Keeping a star matters more than having every detail ready today; design the path while she stays.

cards.host_note: Principle: Be a Learning Machine. Why B (+500) wins: it turns a vague anxiety about the future into a concrete, co-owned growth plan with milestones and reviews; ambition answered with structure becomes loyalty. Discussion: what do three milestones look like for a coordinator; how do you tie pay to milestones fairly; what do you do if she outruns the plan? Wrong: A (+150)'s honesty without a path still loses her; C ($0)'s promised track is a lie that explodes on first review.

cards.title: The Empty Chair
cards.scenario: You are down two installers in peak season. The crew is working heavy overtime and fraying at the edges. A mediocre candidate is available to start Monday, and the dispatcher is begging for relief. What do you do?

A.text: Hire him Monday. A warm body relieves the overtime pressure, and you can coach him up or replace him after the season. Doing nothing while the team breaks down is the real failure.

B.text: Lower the bar: hire for attitude and train skills in a two-week crash course. Peak season forbids a six-week search, and a willing learner with coaching beats an empty truck.

C.text: Do not fill the seat with the wrong person. Redistribute the workload, authorize targeted overtime with a firm end date, and tell the crew exactly how long the push lasts.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C (+500) wins: the short-term pain of overtime is cheaper than the compounding cost of a bad hire made under pressure; holding the standard when it hurts is what makes it a standard. Discussion: how do you ask a tired crew for three more weeks honestly; what does targeted overtime look like versus open-ended grinding; how do you keep the search fast without lowering the bar? Wrong: A (+150) trades crew burnout for crew resentment when the weak hire drags everyone down; B (+0)'s crash course produces confident incompetence at the worst moment.

cards.title: The Untouchable
cards.scenario: Your highest-producing salesperson is caught padding expense reports. Small amounts, first offense, clearly against written policy. He personally brings in 30 percent of revenue, and the team will find out whatever you do. What do you do?

A.text: Apply the policy's consequence for anyone else, up to termination. Tell him the standard does not bend for production. If revenue buys exemptions, every policy becomes negotiable.

B.text: Warn him privately and move on with no paper trail. The amounts are small, first offense; losing a third of revenue over it would be reckless management.

C.text: Make him repay double the padded amount and put him on a final warning. The sting teaches the lesson, the paper trail protects the company, and you keep your top producer.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A (+500) wins: selective enforcement destroys every standard at once; the cost of losing him is real, but teaching the team that integrity is for sale is terminal. Discussion: what does the policy prescribe, and would you enforce it on a rookie; how do you have the conversation without flinching; what do the honest producers conclude from each option? Wrong: B (+0) invents a custom penalty that still says rules bend for rainmakers; C (+150) prices integrity at a few hundred dollars.

cards.title: The Phantom Opening
cards.scenario: Applications have slowed to a trickle. Someone on your team suggests posting a job ad for a role you are not actually hiring for, just to build a bench of resumes. The posting would look completely real. What do you do?

A.text: Post the fake ad and mine the interviews for intelligence on competitors' pay and practices. Candidates will tell you everything if you ask right. It is free market research.

B.text: Post it but label it as future opportunities so it stays honest. Growing companies plan ahead, and resumes on file speed up real hiring later. Careful wording keeps you clear.

C.text: Do not post jobs you are not filling. Fake postings burn people's time, and word travels fast locally. Build the bench honestly: keep a file of candidates and stay in touch.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C (+500) wins: fake postings spend other people's hope for your convenience, and in a local market the story of being ghosted outlives any bench you built; honest bench-building works without the lie. Discussion: what do quarterly touchpoints with past candidates look like; how do you ask employees for future-hire names; how do you measure bench strength honestly? Wrong: B (+150)'s 'future opportunities' label still wastes applicants' time on a mirage; A ($0) turns recruiting into deception and calls it research.

cards.title: The Holiday Cut
cards.scenario: A struggling hire will not make it past probation; the decision is final. It is December 18. Terminating now saves three weeks of payroll; waiting until January spares his holidays but costs the company. What do you do?

A.text: Terminate him this week. The decision is made, and delaying wastes three weeks of payroll. Sentiment is not strategy; acting gives him more time in the January hiring market.

B.text: Tell him kindly, and pay him through the first week of January. The money is small and the message is everything: this company treats people as humans, even on the way out.

C.text: Terminate him and tell the team his seat was eliminated to save holiday money. It is efficient: one conversation, payroll saved. Leaders do not let the calendar run the business.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B (+500) wins: it refuses the false choice between honesty and humanity; telling the truth now plus a small bridge costs little and tells every remaining employee exactly what kind of company this is. Discussion: how do you have the conversation before the holidays without ruining them; what does the team actually conclude from watching; where is the line between generosity and policy? Wrong: A (+150)'s efficiency-first cut teaches the team they are line items; C ($0)'s framing adds deception to the damage.

cards.title: The Return
cards.scenario: A solid technician quit eight months ago for a competitor's bigger paycheck. Now he wants to come back, saying the grass was not greener. Your crew remembers him fondly, and his old seat is open. What do you do?

A.text: Talk honestly first: what was missing here, what disappointed him there, what would make this time different. If the answers are real, bring him back at fair market pay.

B.text: Say no and keep the door closed. Rehiring quitters teaches the team that leaving has no consequences. You filled his spot with someone who chose to be here. Protect who stayed.

C.text: Welcome him back at his old pay with open arms. He left for money and learned his lesson; the same rate keeps equity with the crew. A warm welcome costs nothing and buys loyalty.

cards.host_note: Principle: Safe to Speak. Why A (+500) wins: the honest conversation surfaces whether anything actually changed, and a returning employee who chose you twice, heard fully and welcomed clearly, outperforms one who slinks back under penalty. Discussion: what questions reveal whether the competitor stint taught him anything; how do you tell the crew without inviting debate; what does fair market pay mean here? Wrong: B (+150) sacrifices a known quantity to defend a principle nobody asked for; C (+0) skips the conversation that prevents a repeat exit.

cards.title: The Stay Interview
cards.scenario: Turnover is creeping up, but exit interviews always come too late to help. You are considering stay interviews with your best people before anyone else resigns. How do you run them?

A.text: Have each manager run stay interviews with their own team this month. Managers know their people best and can act fastest, and the conversation itself strengthens the relationship.

B.text: Wait until turnover spikes before adding another meeting to everyone's calendar. Right now it is a mild trend, not a crisis. Monitor the numbers and revisit if it gets worse.

C.text: Start with your ten most valuable people: ask what keeps them here, what might tempt them away, and what one change would help. Act within 30 days and tell them what changed.

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why C (+500) wins: the highest-leverage retention conversations are personal, targeted at the people you can least afford to lose, and backed by visible action within weeks. Discussion: who are the ten, and do they know it; which 'one change' requests are actually grantable; how do you report back without overpromising? Wrong: A (+150) delegates the most sensitive conversation to managers of uneven skill; B (+0) waits for the resignations the interviews were meant to prevent.

cards.title: The Star's Hours
cards.scenario: Your top service coordinator, a single parent and your most reliable performer, asks to switch to four ten-hour days to cut childcare costs. Friday coverage is already tight, and the whole team will notice what you decide. How do you respond?

A.text: Map the Friday coverage with her: which hours matter, which tasks can move, who can flex. Approve the four-day schedule with a plan she helps build, then review in 60 days.

B.text: Say no, but offer a raise instead. Friday is your busiest call day and coverage is not negotiable. One exception becomes policy; money helps without breaking the schedule.

C.text: Approve it as a 90-day trial, but leave her Friday workload on the team. If wait times stay flat, make it permanent. A trial limits your risk and the data settles the debate.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why A (+500) wins: she is asking for a life that works, not money; solving the real problem keeps a star who would otherwise quietly job-hunt. Discussion: separate the actual coverage need from the assumed one; who else might want flexibility; how to review without it feeling like probation. Wrong: B (+150) answers a scheduling question with money and loses her anyway; C (+150) dumps her work on the team and breeds resentment.

cards.title: The Lukewarm Reference
cards.scenario: A finalist for a crew lead role interviews brilliantly. Her former supervisor, when you call, says only 'She did her job. I wish her well' in a flat tone. Nothing more. Two other references are available. What do you do?

A.text: Trust the interview and hire her. Flat references often come from policy or bitterness at losing her. Her interview was outstanding and is the freshest evidence you have.

B.text: Call two more references with behavior-based questions: how she handled conflict, what brings out her best. One guarded call is a data point, not a verdict.

C.text: Pass and move to the next candidate. A former boss who cannot manage one warm sentence is telling you something. Hiring is too expensive to gamble; other strong candidates exist.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why B (+500) wins: one flat reference is one side of one story; two more targeted conversations either confirm a pattern or reveal the first call as noise. Discussion: which specific questions reveal truth; how do you read 'would you rehire her'; when is a reference check just theater? Wrong: A (+150) bets the whole hire on interview charm; C (+150) discards a possible star on one ambiguous call.

cards.title: The Gut Feeling
cards.scenario: Two finalists for a dispatcher role. One manager loves Candidate X's energy. The structured scorecards slightly favor Candidate Y. The team is split down the middle, and the hire starts soon. How do you decide?

A.text: Go with X. Energy matters enormously in dispatch, and no scorecard measures how someone handles a stressed customer at 5 p.m. Friday. Trust the human read over the spreadsheet.

B.text: Hire X for dispatch and find another opening for Y in the company. You keep both strong candidates and avoid the conflict entirely. Good people are hard to find.

C.text: Dig into what energy means: ask the manager for specific behaviors he observed, then test both candidates on the role's hardest moments with a job preview, scored on the same card.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why C (+500) wins: 'energy' is a vague impression until converted into observable behavior; a realistic preview tests the actual claim instead of arguing about adjectives. Discussion: what does a dispatcher job preview look like in thirty minutes; how do you score it fairly; what do you do when the preview contradicts both camps? Wrong: A (+150) hires charisma and hopes it equals competence; B (+0) doubles payroll to avoid a decision.

cards.title: The Overqualified Applicant
cards.scenario: A candidate with ten years of management experience applies for your entry-level coordinator role, saying she wants less stress. She could clearly do the work well, and your team is stretched thin. What do you do?

A.text: Interview her normally, but ask why this role and what happens when a bigger offer appears. Name the risk: agree on a minimum commitment and a pay band with no surprises.

B.text: Hire her immediately. Talent rarely applies for entry-level roles, and she will raise the bar from day one. Worry about retention later; hesitation loses rare candidates.

C.text: Pass on her. Overqualified hires get bored, resent the pay, and leave when something better appears. You will spend months training someone who was going to outgrow the seat.

cards.host_note: Principle: Right Person, Right Seat. Why A (+500) wins: it treats the flight risk as a discussable fact instead of a fear, and a candid agreement turns a gamble into a managed bet with huge upside. Discussion: what do honest answers to 'why this role' sound like; how do you set a pay band that will not breed resentment; what minimum commitment is fair to ask? Wrong: B (+150) hires the resume and inherits the surprise exit; C (+150) discards rare talent on a generalization.

cards.title: The Buddy System
cards.scenario: New hires keep quitting in the first month, saying they felt lost and invisible. You want to pair each newcomer with a veteran buddy so someone clearly owns their first weeks. How do you set it up?

A.text: Pay buddies a $100 stipend for the extra responsibility. Money makes people take it seriously, and it is cheaper than another early quit. Let the supervisor pick the buddy.

B.text: Have the buddy take the new hire to lunch in week one and check in weekly. A friendly face early solves most of the feeling-lost problem. Keep it informal.

C.text: Hand-pick buddies for attitude and patience, not tenure, with a job description: a first-day walkthrough, a 30-day checklist, and a weekly 15-minute check-in with the supervisor.

cards.host_note: Principle: Train or Remove. Why C (+500) wins: vague buddy assignments produce vague results; selecting for attitude, defining the work, and recognizing it turns a nice idea into a training system that retains people. Discussion: what makes a good buddy versus just senior; what belongs on the 30-day checklist; how does recognition beat stipends? Wrong: A (+150) pays for a title without defining the work; B (+150)'s lunch-and-hope evaporates by week two.

cards.title: The Silence
cards.scenario: You interviewed twelve candidates for a coordinator role and hired one. The other eleven have heard nothing in three weeks, and two sent polite follow-ups. Your inbox is overflowing. What do you do?

A.text: Send one mass email to all eleven with a rejection. It closes the loop in ten minutes. Personal notes are nice in theory, but a clean form rejection beats silence every time.

B.text: Reply to every candidate this week: thank them, tell them the role is filled, and mean it. For the two or three you would hire in a heartbeat, say so and ask to keep in touch.

C.text: Ignore them. They did not get the job and the position is filled. Candidates understand that no news means no offer; this is how hiring works everywhere, and nobody expects more.

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why B (+500) wins: every candidate is a future applicant, referrer, or customer, and personal closes convert rejected candidates into goodwill; silence converts them into warnings. Discussion: what does the personal note to a strong runner-up say; how do you keep a warm bench without stringing people along; who owns candidate communication? Wrong: A (+150)'s mass email closes the loop but wastes the relationship; C ($0)'s silence actively manufactures detractors.

cards.title: The Example
cards.scenario: A technician was caught stealing materials from the shop. You have decided to terminate him today. A supervisor suggests doing it in front of the crew to send a message about theft. What do you do?

A.text: Terminate him today: state what happened and the consequence, and handle logistics with dignity. Then tell the crew the standard that was violated, without parading the person.

B.text: Do it in front of the crew as the supervisor suggests. Public consequences create deterrence: everyone sees what happens to thieves, and the lesson lands harder than any memo.

C.text: Suspend him for two weeks without pay instead of firing him. Theft is serious, but everyone deserves a second chance, and two weeks of lost wages is a lesson he will not forget.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why A (+500) wins: it separates the person from the principle, protecting his dignity while making the standard unmistakable; public shaming teaches the crew to fear you, not to respect the standard. Discussion: what does the private conversation sound like word for word; what do you tell the crew without violating his privacy; how do you handle the supervisor who wanted theater? Wrong: B ($0)'s spectacle breeds fear and quiet contempt; C (+150)'s second chance for theft tells the crew integrity is negotiable.

cards.title: The Nephew Interview
cards.scenario: The owner's nephew, nineteen, applies for your entry-level dispatcher role. He has no relevant experience. The owner has mentioned his application to you twice this week, and the role is customer-facing and high pressure. What do you do?

A.text: Fast-track him to a final interview as a courtesy to the owner, then hire him if he interviews decently. A dispatcher role is low-risk enough to learn on the job.

B.text: Run him through the same process as everyone else: application, interview, references, same scorecard. Tell the owner up front the process decides, and report the result honestly.

C.text: Steer him toward shop help or warehouse support and interview him for that instead. The family gets a win, and the dispatcher seat stays protected for a qualified hire.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why B (+500) wins: one visible exception teaches the whole company the standard is negotiable. Discussion: how do you say no to an owner without career damage; could the nephew earn credibility after a fast-track; what does the team conclude from watching? Wrong: A (+150) buys short-term favor and spends long-term credibility; C (+150) still bends the process for family and mis-seats him.

cards.title: The Quiet Season
cards.scenario: It is your slow season and cash is comfortable. You know you will need four new installers when demand spikes in spring, and every competitor hires at the same time. When do you hire?

A.text: Wait until spring when you need them. Hiring now pays people to sit idle, and you cannot predict the exact skill mix the spike needs. Hire fast when the need is concrete.

B.text: Cover the spring spike with temporary labor instead of permanent hires. Temps flex with demand and you avoid year-round payroll. Convert the best ones if volume holds.

C.text: Hire two now and train them fully before the rush. Winter hires get real mentoring, not chaos, and are productive by spring. You choose from a calm pool instead of a panic.

cards.host_note: Principle: Created Twice. Why C (+500) wins: the future spike is certain, so building the team before it arrives is planning, not guessing; trained hires in spring outperform panicked hires every time. Discussion: what does 'fully trained' mean by March; how do you keep winter hires busy and billable; is two the right number? Wrong: A (+150) guarantees a desperate spring search at peak wages; B (+0)'s temps learn your systems just in time to leave.

cards.title: The Inside Candidate
cards.scenario: A supervisor role opens. Your best technician wants it but has never led people. An outside candidate has five years of management experience. The whole crew is watching the decision. Who gets the role?

A.text: Give it to your technician. Promoting from within rewards loyalty and shows the crew that growth is real. Leadership can be learned; the trust he already earned cannot be hired.

B.text: Run both through the process, scored on the role's demands: scheduling, accountability, developing people. If the technician wins on potential plus a development plan, promote him.

C.text: Split the difference: make him a lead tech and hire the outsider as supervisor. Everyone gets something, nobody feels passed over. It costs more, but it avoids a morale hit.

cards.host_note: Principle: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You. Why B (+500) wins: the decision serves the role, not sentiment or fear; a fair contest plus honest feedback either produces the best leader or a technician with a real growth target. Discussion: how do you assess leadership potential versus a track record; what does a credible development plan contain; how do you deliver 'not yet' without losing him? Wrong: A (+150) promotes on loyalty into a skill gap; C (+0) invents a consolation prize that muddies accountability.

cards.title: The Bad Reference
cards.scenario: A former employee you fired for cause listed you as a reference. You are still angry about how he left. His prospective new employer calls you today and asks how he performed. What do you say?

A.text: Stick to facts: role, dates, and whether he is eligible for rehire, delivered calmly with no editorial comment. If pressed, say you keep references factual as a matter of policy.

B.text: Give a strictly factual reference: dates and title only, nothing more. Facts cannot be disputed, and you stay out of the judgment business. The thinness says enough on its own.

C.text: Tell the caller the unfiltered truth about why he was fired. He earned the consequences, and warning the next employer is honest. If it costs him the job, that is on him.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Elongated Shadow. Why A (+500) wins: how you speak about former employees, especially ones you fired, is your company's character made audible; factual calm protects the business and your reputation at once. Discussion: what does 'eligible for rehire' communicate without saying more; how do you handle a caller who pushes hard; where should company policy be written down? Wrong: B (+150)'s pointed thinness is punishment wearing a factual mask; C ($0)'s unfiltered truth invites legal exposure and reveals vindictiveness.

cards.title: The Bait Pay
cards.scenario: A candidate accepted your offer at $28 per hour. Before his start date, finance says the budget only supports $25. He has already given notice at his old job, and he starts Monday. What do you do?

A.text: Honor the $28 and absorb the difference. You made an offer and he acted on it in good faith; going back destroys trust before day one. A deal is a deal, and your word is your word.

B.text: Start him at $25 and say nothing, hoping he does not notice. Most new hires never scrutinize their first paychecks, and by the time it comes up he will be settled in.

C.text: Tell him the truth: the budget shifted, the number is $25, and you understand if he walks away. Give him the weekend to decide, then fix approvals so finance signs every offer.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why C (+500) wins: the situation is already damaged, and only immediate honesty plus his free choice can rebuild it; anything else compounds the original error with a second deception. Discussion: what does the call sound like in real words; what does a credible 90-day raise path contain; how do you fix the offer-approval process this week? Wrong: A (+150)'s honor-the-offer is noble but may be impossible and hides the process failure; B ($0)'s silence is wage deception that detonates the moment he reads a pay stub.

cards.title: The Frozen Requisition
cards.scenario: Finance froze all hiring to cut costs. Your appointment center is drowning: hold times tripled and two coordinators quit last month. You need one hire badly, and the phones keep ringing. What do you do?

A.text: Hire anyway and ask forgiveness later. The freeze is blunt and your department is suffering. By the time finance notices, the hire is productive and the results justify it.

B.text: Build a one-page business case: the loaded cost of the hire versus missed calls, overtime, and the next resignation. Show finance the weekly revenue lost to abandoned calls.

C.text: Redistribute the work and push the team harder for one quarter. The freeze exists for a reason and every department feels it. Shared sacrifice now protects everyone's jobs later.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B (+500) wins: finance speaks arithmetic, so you translate the pain into their language and de-risk the ask with a measurable trial; it respects the freeze while challenging it legitimately. Discussion: how do you quantify abandoned-call revenue credibly; what does a fair 90-day target look like; how do you present it without sounding adversarial? Wrong: A ($0)'s end-run destroys your credibility with finance permanently; C (+150) burns out the survivors and guarantees the next resignation.

cards.title: The Tax Surprise
cards.scenario: Your accountant delivers the news: you owe $38,000 more in taxes than expected. Then he offers a way out, a deduction he calls aggressive but defensible, in a gray area he admits. It would wipe out most of the bill. Payment is due in three weeks.

A.text: Take the deduction. It is aggressive but defensible, the audit risk is low, and the savings are real money. Every business pushes the line somewhere. Sign the return and move on.

B.text: Fire the accountant and find one who will take the deduction without the lecture. You pay professionals to solve problems. Loyalty to a cautious accountant is costing you $38,000.

C.text: Decline the gray-area deduction and pay what you owe. Then fix the real problem: set up quarterly estimates so a surprise bill never blindsides you again.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: Pay what's owed, fix the real problem with quarterly estimates, find legitimate deductions. What good discussion sounds like: the true cost of gray-area tax play. What the wrong answers cost: A borrows trouble; B shops for a yes-man.

cards.title: The Software Pitch
cards.scenario: A software rep demos a platform promising to transform your business: dispatch, CRM, marketing automation, all in one. The price is $2,000 a month plus setup. Three competitors use it and swear by it. The rep wants a three-year contract this quarter.

A.text: Buy it because every serious company runs it. Falling behind on technology is how good contractors become irrelevant. The monthly cost is the price of staying competitive.

B.text: Pilot it with one team for ninety days against a written success metric: what specific number has to move, and by how much. If it moves, roll it out. If not, walk away.

C.text: Buy the full rollout now. Your systems are spreadsheets and the team wastes hours on manual work. Rip the bandage off and train everyone at once.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: Ninety-day pilot against a written metric; owners buy results, not demos. What good discussion sounds like: what the success number should be. What the wrong answers cost: A buys the pitch; C follows the herd onto a three-year contract.

cards.title: The Overheard Layoff List
cards.scenario: You sketched a draft list of possible layoffs while thinking through a bad quarter, and left it on the printer. This morning three techs found it. By lunch the whole shop has seen the names, including two people on the list. Your GM is waiting in your office.

A.text: Face the team today. Admit the list is real, explain why cuts were even considered, and apologize for them learning it from a printer. Commit to a straight answer by Friday.

B.text: Say nothing and accelerate your decision quietly. Addressing it now feeds the rumor mill. Most names on the list will never be cut, so a public reckoning wounds people.

C.text: Deny it completely. Tell anyone who asks it was a budgeting exercise with made-up names. A clean lie now keeps the team steady while you decide.

cards.host_note: Principle: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame. Why A wins: Own the mistake the same day, tell the truth, and give a date for the real answer. What good discussion sounds like: how leaders repair trust after an unforced error. What the wrong answers cost: B lets rumors write the story; C destroys credibility when the lie breaks.

cards.title: The Charity Ask
cards.scenario: The town's biggest charity gala wants you as a headline sponsor: $10,000, your logo everywhere, photos with the mayor. Half the business owners in town already said yes. Your marketing lead says the exposure alone is worth it. It was never in any plan.

A.text: Write the big check. The sponsorship puts your name in front of the whole town, the photos go on social media, and goodwill brings customers for years.

B.text: Give from a planned annual giving budget, not from guilt or pressure. Decide once a year what the company gives and to whom. Generosity needs a plan.

C.text: Decline politely. The company's job is to serve customers and pay its people well. Every sponsorship dollar is one that does not go to raises, trucks, or reserves.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why B wins: Planned giving expresses values; reactive giving expresses whoever pressured you last. What good discussion sounds like: what the company actually stands for, and what the annual number should be. What the wrong answers cost: A buys a photo, not a value; C starves generosity.

cards.title: The Widow's Furnace
cards.scenario: Your tech calls from a job: an elderly widow's furnace died overnight, it is January, and she quietly told him she cannot afford the full replacement. She has been a customer for fifteen years and always paid on time. The job costs you $2,800.

A.text: Charge full price. It is a sad story, but the business cannot be a charity on every hard case. The tech can offer her the standard financing options like anyone else. Fair is fair.

B.text: Do it completely free and keep it quiet. Publicizing charity cheapens it, and you do not want a line of people expecting free work. Some things are done quietly or not at all.

C.text: Tell the tech to take care of her at your cost, today. Then build a simple policy so your techs can make this call without phoning the owner. That is who you are.

cards.host_note: Principle: Serve the Human, Not the House. Why C wins: Take care of her at cost today, then give techs a policy so they don't need permission to be human. What good discussion sounds like: where the line sits between compassion and sustainability. What the wrong answers cost: A is fair but cold; B hides the kindness.

cards.title: The Insurance Cut
cards.scenario: Cash is tight after a slow winter, and your broker suggests dropping your umbrella policy and raising deductibles to save $22,000 a year. Nothing bad has happened in years, the crews are careful, and that savings would cover a month of payroll.

A.text: Drop the umbrella for a year until cash recovers. Nothing bad has happened in years and the crews are careful. Reinstate it when the busy season fills the account.

B.text: Keep the coverage and cut somewhere else. One uninsured bad day can erase everything you built. Insurance is the price of surviving it. Do not gamble the company.

C.text: Keep every policy as is. Your broker set this coverage up for a reason, and second-guessing it under pressure is how owners make their worst decisions. Cut marketing instead.

cards.host_note: Principle: Handle It While It's Small. Why B wins: Keep coverage and cut elsewhere; one uninsured bad day erases everything. What good discussion sounds like: what to cut instead, and what the real odds are. What the wrong answers cost: A refuses to manage money; C gambles the company on a quiet year.

cards.title: The Price War
cards.scenario: A competitor slashed his service rates by thirty percent and is advertising it everywhere. Your phones slowed this week, and two techs heard customers mention his prices. Your margins are decent but cannot absorb a deep cut for long.

A.text: Hold your prices and refuse the race to the bottom. A competitor selling thirty percent below market is bleeding, not winning. Win on response time, clean work, and reviews.

B.text: Match his prices until he backs off. You have deeper reserves and better techs, so you can survive a price war longer than he can. Once he folds, you raise yours back.

C.text: Hold your prices and double down on what makes you different. Strengthen the guarantee and call every customer after the job. Some price shoppers will leave, and that is fine.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why A wins: Competing on value instead of price protects margin and trains the market to buy quality. What good discussion sounds like: when to hold price versus when the market has truly moved, and how techs talk price with confidence. What the wrong answers cost: B starts a war you fund; C is honest but passive.

cards.title: The Vanishing Cash
cards.scenario: Your P and L shows a solid profit for the year, but the bank account is nearly empty and payroll is next week. Your bookkeeper says everything is entered correctly, and your accountant is on vacation. You cannot make the two agree.

A.text: Fire the bookkeeper. Profit on paper, empty account: she is stealing or incompetent. Make it clear this never happens again. Accountability starts with the ledger.

B.text: Sit down with your accountant and learn where the cash actually goes. Then read a simple weekly cash report: money in, money out, what you are owed, what you owe.

C.text: Take a short-term credit line to bridge the gap. The business is profitable on paper, so this is just timing. Borrowed cash turns a timing gap into a non-event.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: Learn where the cash goes and read a weekly cash report; profit and cash are different things. What good discussion sounds like: receivables, payables, and why profitable companies go broke. What the wrong answers cost: A borrows over ignorance; C fires the messenger.

cards.title: The Family Hire
cards.scenario: Your nephew just finished a general business degree and wants to join the company. He is a good kid but has no trade experience, no management experience, and a thin work history. Your sister is asking. Your GM warns against inventing a role for him.

A.text: Hire him. Family takes care of family, and you can find useful work while he learns. Giving a young man his start in the family business is a quiet privilege of ownership.

B.text: Tell him you love him, and that love is why he goes through the same hiring process as everyone else. No invented titles. Handing family an unearned job poisons the team.

C.text: Make him a manager over one of the crews. The title will motivate him to grow into it fast. Sink or swim is how leaders are made. A big title forces growth.

cards.host_note: Principle: Right Person, Right Seat. Why B wins: Same process for everyone; love is why there are no invented roles. What good discussion sounds like: how to tell family no without breaking the family. What the wrong answers cost: A poisons the culture; C hands a crew to an unproven manager.

cards.title: The Exit Offer
cards.scenario: A regional competitor wants to buy your company. The number is life-changing: enough to retire at fifty-two, pay off everything, and never work again. You built this from two trucks. Forty-three families depend on it. He wants an answer in sixty days.

A.text: Measure the offer against why you built this company, not just the number. What happens to your people and your standard? If it protects them, consider it.

B.text: Sell and take the money. You built this from nothing, the offer is life-changing, and nobody gets this chance twice. The buyer needs good people. Take the win.

C.text: Refuse outright. Selling to a competitor would betray everything you built. Some things are not for sale at any price. Thank them, say no, and get back to building.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Elongated Shadow. Why A wins: The offer is measured against why the company exists and what happens to its people, not just the number. What good discussion sounds like: what the owner's 'why' actually is, and what a good buyer looks like. What the wrong answers cost: B sells the mission; C refuses to ever consider it.

cards.title: The Kickback Offer
cards.scenario: A new parts vendor takes you to lunch and makes it plain: switch your purchasing to him, and he will pay you $500 a month personally, cash, as a thank-you. His prices are market rate, his delivery is fine. He says every owner he works with takes it.

A.text: Take it but disclose it openly to your accountant and your GM. The deal itself is fair, and the payment is documented income. Sunlight keeps it honest. Put it on the books.

B.text: Take it. It is your company and your money. The parts are fine, the price is market, and the monthly thank-you is just the vendor appreciating your business. Owners get perks.

C.text: Refuse it outright and end the lunch there. A kickback is someone paying you to spend company money without asking hard questions. The owner sets the standard for clean money.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: Refuse and remove the vendor; the owner sets the standard for clean money. What good discussion sounds like: how kickbacks distort purchasing and culture. What the wrong answers cost: A documents a bribe; B takes the cut.

cards.title: The Public Correction
cards.scenario: In yesterday's team meeting you corrected your GM's decision in front of everyone, sharply. You were right on the facts, but her face said humiliated. Today she is polite, distant, and quiet. Two managers asked if she still has your confidence.

A.text: Let it go and move on. Rehashing it only keeps it alive. She knows you respect her. Bringing it up again turns a moment into a saga. Time heals this faster.

B.text: Stand by it. You are the owner, her call was wrong, and the team needed to see standards apply at every level. Softening it now confuses everyone about who is in charge.

C.text: Fix it today. Apologize to her privately first, sincerely, with no excuses. Then in front of the team, publicly back her call and her authority. Authority you break, you rebuild.

cards.host_note: Principle: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame. Why C wins: Apologize privately, then publicly restore her authority the same day. What good discussion sounds like: how owners repair authority they damaged. What the wrong answers cost: A hopes time buries it; B confuses dominance with leadership.

cards.title: The Successor Question
cards.scenario: Your daughter, home from college for the summer, tells you she thinks she wants to run the company someday. She is sharp and grew up around the shop. But she has never held a real job, your GM has given ten years, and the team will read any fast-track as nepotism.

A.text: Start grooming her for the GM role now. She is smart, she absorbed this business growing up, and family succession is the dream. Give her real projects. Blood counts for a lot.

B.text: Steer her somewhere else. The pressure would crush her, and mixing family and ownership ruins both. She should build her own life without your shadow. Keeping her out is kindest.

C.text: Build her a real path, not a coronation. She works outside the company first, learns the business from the ground up, and earns every promotion on merit. Earned, never handed.

cards.host_note: Principle: The Business Serves Its Owner. Why C wins: A real path, outside experience, earned promotions, mentors who aren't Dad; never handed, can be earned. What good discussion sounds like: what 'earned' looks like for a founder's kid. What the wrong answers cost: A crowns her; B wastes her interest.

cards.title: The New Trade
cards.scenario: Your GM wants to launch an electrical division. Customers ask for it constantly, the margins look great on paper, and she found a master electrician who wants to lead it. It would take about $120,000 to launch. Your other sides are solid but not spectacular.

A.text: Launch it now and go big. Customers ask for it, the GM is fired up, and speed beats study. Hire the master electrician and start selling this month.

B.text: Make her build the business case first: real demand data, the true startup cost, who leads it, and how it pays for itself in eighteen months. Then pilot it small.

C.text: Say no and stay in your lane. You are an HVAC and plumbing company, and that focus is why you are good. Every trade you add dilutes your brand. Depth beats breadth.

cards.host_note: Principle: Created Twice. Why B wins: Demand data, true cost, a named leader, and a small pilot before the company bets $120,000. What good discussion sounds like: what the pilot's success metrics should be. What the wrong answers cost: A launches on enthusiasm; C refuses to ever grow.

cards.title: The Bad Quarter
cards.scenario: Revenue dropped eighteen percent last quarter. Two big commercial accounts paused, and the residential side is soft. The team feels it: the phones are quieter, overtime vanished, and the shop talk is nervous. Your recovery plan is not finished.

A.text: Gather the team and tell them the truth before the rumor mill does. Share the real numbers in plain language and the recovery plan as far as it goes. Then ask for help.

B.text: Keep the numbers to yourself and fix it quietly. The team has jobs to do, and worrying them about one bad quarter only hurts morale. They hired you to carry the weight.

C.text: Frame it as a market problem. Rates, competition, and the economy are squeezing every contractor in town, not just you. Nobody panics over a problem the whole industry shares.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why A wins: You cannot fix what you will not name. A tells the truth early and turns the team into problem-solvers instead of rumor-spreaders. What good discussion sounds like: how much financial truth a team can handle, and the difference between transparency and panic. What the wrong answers cost: B breeds distrust when the truth leaks; C insults their intelligence.

cards.title: The Personal Guarantee
cards.scenario: You need six new trucks before the summer rush, and the bank approved the loan, but the paperwork includes an unlimited personal guarantee: your house, your savings, everything, if the business defaults. Your accountant has not seen the documents yet.

A.text: Do not sign anything until you understand every line. Have your accountant and a lawyer review the guarantee and cap your personal exposure. Never sign away your home in a hurry.

B.text: Sign only after the bank agrees in writing to release the guarantee once the loan drops below half. A written release turns a scary signature into a temporary one.

C.text: Sign the guarantee as written so the trucks arrive before summer. You have signed before and nothing bad happened. The business is strong and the risk is theoretical.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why A wins: Unlimited personal liability deserves professional review and negotiated caps, not speed. What good discussion sounds like: what owners actually risk when they sign, and lease-versus-buy math. What the wrong answers cost: B is decent but still rushed; C gambles the house.

cards.title: The Customer's Demand
cards.scenario: Your largest residential customer, a developer with eleven homes under your maintenance plan, demands that you personally attend every service call at his properties. He says he pays for the owner, not the techs. Giving in would eat two days of your week.

A.text: Go yourself. He is a major account, his referrals are worth a fortune, and personal attention is why he stays. Some customers are worth the owner's time. Protect the revenue.

B.text: Fire the customer. No account is worth the owner being treated like a tech on call. Caving invites every big customer to demand the same. No account rents the owner.

C.text: Go to one job yourself, introduce Sam, and tell the customer plainly: this is the person I trust with my own home, and he carries my standard. Then step back and let him prove it.

cards.host_note: Principle: You Are Not the Doer. Why C wins: Transfer trust to Sam in person once, then step back; a business that needs the owner on every job isn't a business. What good discussion sounds like: how to make customers trust the team as much as the owner. What the wrong answers cost: A chains the owner to jobs; B throws away a great account.

cards.title: The Competitor Buyout
cards.scenario: A struggling competitor wants to sell: twelve trucks, a customer list of 4,000 names, and a shop lease, all for a price that looks like a steal. His techs are already calling around for jobs. Your GM says this could double your territory overnight.

A.text: Buy it fast before another contractor grabs it. The price is a steal, and his trucks and customer list alone are worth more than the asking price.

B.text: Slow down and run real due diligence before you fall in love with the price. Audit his books, his list, his reviews, and find out why he is really selling.

C.text: Walk away. Buying a struggling competitor means buying his problems and his unhappy customers. Win them the honest way, one good job at a time. Keep your focus.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: Diligence on books, customers, and motive before price-love; cheap companies are cheap for reasons. What good discussion sounds like: what to check in diligence, and what a fair price looks like. What the wrong answers cost: A buys problems at speed; C may pass a real opportunity.

cards.title: The Data Lie
cards.scenario: Your GM's monthly report looks great: revenue up, callbacks down, everything green. But two big customers complained this month, overtime is through the roof, and the numbers feel too clean. You have never verified a single figure she reports.

A.text: Accept the report and move on. She is your GM, you hired her for judgment, and second-guessing her numbers signals distrust. If something is wrong, it will surface.

B.text: Ask for the raw numbers in a way that makes honesty safe. Tell her: I would rather hear a bad truth Tuesday than a pretty lie at month's end. Owners get the truth they reward.

C.text: Confront her directly and demand to know if she is cooking the books. If she is lying to the owner about money, that is a firing offense. Ask it plainly, then watch her face.

cards.host_note: Principle: Safe to Speak. Why B wins: Ask for raw numbers in a way that makes honesty safe, then prove it by rewarding the next bad truth. What good discussion sounds like: whether the numbers are massaged, and why. What the wrong answers cost: A naps; C accuses before understanding.

cards.title: The GM's Blank Check
cards.scenario: Your GM asks for authority to spend up to $25,000 without your approval. She says waiting on you slows everything: emergency parts, a marketing opportunity, a hire she needs to lock down. You trust her, but you have never given anyone that kind of latitude.

A.text: Give her the full $25,000 and get out of her way. You hired her to run the business, and second-guessing her spending slows everything. If you cannot trust her, you hired wrong.

B.text: Give her real authority with clear guardrails. She spends up to $5,000 on her own, flags $5,000 to $15,000 next day, and gets sign-off above that. She reports weekly.

C.text: Keep every dollar of spending authority yourself. It is your money and your risk. She brings requests, you approve them fast. Nothing gets spent you have not seen.

cards.host_note: Principle: Delegate, Don't Abdicate. Why B wins: Tiered limits plus weekly reporting give real authority with real oversight. What good discussion sounds like: where the dollar thresholds should sit, and what good reporting looks like. What the wrong answers cost: A surrenders the checkbook; C strangles the GM.

cards.title: The Payroll Temptation
cards.scenario: A big receivable is ten days late, payroll hits Friday, and the account will not cover both payroll and the supplier invoices due the same day. Your GM suggests delaying payroll until the check lands, just this once, and being honest with the team.

A.text: Delay payroll until the receivable lands and be upfront with the team. Honesty softens the blow, and a few days is not the end of the world. The check is definitely coming.

B.text: Pay the team on time by holding all vendor payments instead. Your people come first, and suppliers can wait thirty days without real damage. People over paperwork.

C.text: Payroll goes out on time, every time. You cut your own pay first, then every discretionary dollar, then you call the bank before you touch your people's checks.

cards.host_note: Principle: Cash Is Life. Why C wins: Payroll on time, every time; the owner cuts his own pay first. What good discussion sounds like: what to cut before payroll, and how to prevent the next crunch. What the wrong answers cost: A spends trust; B stiffs vendors.

cards.title: The Shiny Investment
