cards.scenario: An old friend is raising money for a real estate development he swears cannot lose. He shows you projections, testimonials, and a deadline: the round closes Friday. The buy-in is $50,000, about what you keep as your operating cushion.

A.text: Pass on it. Your best return is the business you understand, where every extra dollar compounds. Side bets you do not control are expensive distractions with a good story.

B.text: Put in a small amount you can fully afford to lose, and treat it as tuition. Set the number in advance and do not add a dollar more later.

C.text: Go in big. Diversification is smart, and keeping all your wealth tied to one local contracting business is genuinely risky. This deal has real upside. Fortune favors the bold.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why A wins: The business you understand compounds; side bets you don't control are distractions with stories. What good discussion sounds like: the difference between diversification and dilution of focus. What the wrong answers cost: B feeds the itch; C risks the operating cushion.

cards.title: The Boat Money
cards.scenario: You have wanted a boat for years, and this spring the business account is the healthiest it has ever been. A dealer friend found a used one at a steal, but only if you move this week. The boat costs more than three months of your salary.

A.text: Leave the money in the business. You pay yourself a set salary and a planned quarterly distribution. Everything beyond that stays put. The company account is not a personal ATM.

B.text: Take the money as a formal loan from the business with a written repayment schedule and interest. That keeps it clean on the books, gets you the boat now, and the money comes back.

C.text: Take the money outright. The business is profitable, the account is healthy, and you built this company with years of your own sweat. You have earned the right to enjoy it.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why A wins: A fixed pay discipline separates the owner's wallet from the company's, and that standard is what the whole team follows. What good discussion sounds like: what 'enough' looks like for an owner, and how personal draws ripple into culture. What the wrong answers cost: B normalizes raiding the till; C teaches everyone that company money is the owner's pocket money.

cards.title: The Sketchy Supplier
cards.scenario: Your biggest parts supplier offers an exclusive deal: switch all purchasing to him, and he will send you a quarterly rebate check made out to you personally. The parts meet spec on paper, but your lead tech says they fail more often in the field.

A.text: Turn the deal down flat. You will not trade your customers' trust for a rebate, and you will not put parts you doubt into people's homes. Choose suppliers in the open.

B.text: Take the deal and have your lead tech inspect every batch before parts go on the trucks. Inspection catches the quality risk, and the rebate funds the inspection time.

C.text: Accept the rebate but keep it documented with your accountant. The parts meet spec on paper. Track warranty claims closely and switch back if they underperform.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: Parts chosen for a kickback will fail in customers' homes, and no rebate survives that. What good discussion sounds like: where the line sits between a smart deal and a compromised one. What the wrong answers cost: B launders a bribe into process; C documents the bribe instead.

cards.title: The Slow Season
cards.scenario: Every winter your residential work drops forty percent. Your GM proposes keeping the full crew through the slow months to protect morale, which would burn $60,000 of reserve. Last year you laid off six techs in January and spent March rehiring strangers.

A.text: Lay off the bottom third and run lean until spring. Payroll is your biggest cost, and a full crew through a dead winter burns your growth cash. Lean winters make strong summers.

B.text: Keep every job and cut marketing to zero instead. People matter more than ads, and you can restart in the spring. Protecting the team is worth going quiet for one season.

C.text: Keep your core team and flex the edges on purpose. Winter comes every year, so plan for it: cross-train in the fall, bank cash in the summer, use the slow months for training.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why C wins: Winter comes every year, so plan for it: cross-train, bank cash, use slow months for training. What good discussion sounds like: what the seasonal plan should include. What the wrong answers cost: A burns the team to save cash; B goes dark for a season.

cards.title: The Burned-Out GM
cards.scenario: Your GM, Dana, is working seventy-hour weeks and it shows: short temper, missed details, and last week she forgot a payroll deadline for the first time ever. She built your systems and carries the culture. She says she is fine and just needs to get through the season.

A.text: Tell her straight that leadership is hard and the hours come with the chair. She wanted the GM seat. Tough seasons separate real leaders from the rest. Expect more.

B.text: Give her a significant raise and a bonus. The hours are brutal, and money shows you see the sacrifice. A well-paid GM will push through. Compensation is the fastest recognition.

C.text: Sit down with her and redesign the job before you lose her. Map her plate, take real pieces off, and hire the support she needs. A burned-out GM needs a job a human can do.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why C wins: Redesign the job before you lose the person; a burned-out GM needs a doable job, not a pep talk. What good discussion sounds like: what's actually on her plate, and what comes off first. What the wrong answers cost: A confuses cruelty with standards; B buys time with money.

cards.title: The Star Who Berates
cards.scenario: Marcus is your top salesman, bringing in nearly a third of revenue. He is also brutal to the office staff: snapping, name-calling, and last week he made your dispatcher cry. Two office employees have quietly asked about transferring. He laughed off your last mention of it.

A.text: Pull him aside and tell him plainly: the way he speaks to the office staff stops now. His numbers do not buy him a different standard. Draw a clear line with consequences.

B.text: Leave it alone for now because he carries a third of your revenue. Keep an eye on it, and if someone actually quits, deal with it then. Do not break what is working.

C.text: Dock his next commission check as a fine for how he treats people. Money talks, and hitting his wallet beats any lecture. The fines grow until he gets the message.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why A wins: One standard for everyone, stated privately and enforced; production never buys an exemption. What good discussion sounds like: how to confront a top producer without fear, and what the office staff's silence is costing. What the wrong answers cost: B sacrifices the team for one person; C fines dignity instead of fixing behavior.

cards.title: The Second Location
cards.scenario: Your GM wants to open a second shop across town. She has the energy, a couple of techs ready to follow her, and a landlord offering cheap rent. Your current shop is profitable, but margins slipped last quarter and cash covers two months of payroll.

A.text: Tell her not yet: a second shop opens when three gates are met. Steady margin for six months, six months of payroll in reserve, and a trained leader for shop one.

B.text: Let her open it and run it yourself the first year to protect quality. Split your weeks between the two locations and hire fast. Nobody protects your standard like you do.

C.text: Approve it and give her full authority to launch her way. She is hungry and capable, and hovering would kill her drive. Set a monthly revenue target and step back completely.

cards.host_note: Principle: Created Twice. Why A wins: Expansion is a plan, not a mood. A sets measurable gates (margin, reserves, a ready leader) before risking the core. What good discussion sounds like: debating what the three gates should be, and whether the second shop is opportunity or distraction. What the wrong answers cost: B burns the owner out across two shops; C gambles the company on hope.

cards.title: The Vanishing Margin
cards.scenario: Your net margin slipped from fourteen percent to eight in two quarters, and nobody can say exactly why. Revenue is up, the schedule is full, but the money is not landing. Your GM blames pricing, your ops manager blames callbacks, your accountant blames overtime.

A.text: Cut overhead ten percent across the board today. Every department trims: fewer office hours, cheaper supplies, no overtime. When margins shrink, spending shrinks first.

B.text: Raise prices ten percent across the board. Your costs went up, so your prices go up. Customers expect it and your close rate can absorb it.

C.text: Stop guessing and find the leak. Pull job costing on the last ninety days: which jobs, which techs, which neighborhoods make money. Margins bleed in specific places.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: Ninety days of job costing names the leak: underpriced work, callback crews, discount creep. What good discussion sounds like: which jobs actually make money. What the wrong answers cost: A cuts blind; B taxes customers for your confusion.

cards.title: The Grieving Employee
cards.scenario: Your office manager of nine years lost her husband suddenly last week. She came back today because she needed the routine, but she is hollow: invoice mistakes, tears in the break room, gone by noon. The phones are piling up.

A.text: Give her real time and a soft landing. Paid weeks off, no guilt, then a lighter load with flexible hours when she returns. Tell the team to cover her with grace.

B.text: Give her a week off with pay, then expect her back at full speed. Grief is real, but the business has to run. Clear expectations beat vague sympathy.

C.text: Tell her kindly but firmly that grief stays at home. The office depends on her and the team cannot carry her workload forever. Give her three days, then full speed.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why A wins: Real time, a soft landing, and human check-ins; she'll remember this forever, and so will everyone watching. What good discussion sounds like: how to cover the work with grace. What the wrong answers cost: B schedules grief; C tells a grieving woman to perform.

cards.title: The Succession Clock
cards.scenario: You are sixty-two, healthy, and still love the work. But you have no succession plan, no buy-sell agreement, and your kids have their own careers. Your two best managers are quietly wondering what happens if you get hit by a bus.

A.text: Start the conversation this year, not the year you are forced to. Name who could grow into ownership, and give them real development and a real timeline.

B.text: Ignore it. You are healthy, you love the work, and you will figure out the exit when you get there. Succession planning is for corporations. The future will sort itself out.

C.text: Hire a broker and sell within the year while the market is hot. You get maximum value and a clean break. Cash out at the top, and let the next owner solve the people puzzle.

cards.host_note: Principle: Created Twice. Why A wins: Start the conversation now: honest talks, identified candidates, real development, a real timeline. What good discussion sounds like: who could grow into ownership, and what they need. What the wrong answers cost: B hands the team a future crisis; C cashes out the mission.

cards.title: The Lease or Buy
cards.scenario: Your landlord offers to sell you the building: fair price, good location, room to expand. Your lease renews in eight months with a rent hike. The down payment would take half your cash reserve, and your GM worries about tying up capital needed for trucks.

A.text: Buy the building. Owning is what established companies do, and rent just makes the landlord rich. Sign the deal and plant your flag. Rent is paying someone else's mortgage.

B.text: Keep renting. Your capital belongs in trucks, techs, and marketing, not in bricks. A lease keeps you flexible. Real estate is a distraction from the business you run.

C.text: Run it like any investment. Compare the true ten-year cost of buying against renting, factor in what the down payment does to your cash, and get an honest appraisal. Then decide.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: Ten-year math, cash impact, honest appraisal; buildings aren't trophies. What good discussion sounds like: what the down payment could earn inside the business instead. What the wrong answers cost: A buys pride; B refuses to ever own.

cards.title: The Two Candidates
cards.scenario: You need a GM. Two finalists: Tom, your loyal operations manager of eight years who knows every tech by name, and Priya, an outsider with a sharp record turning around bigger shops. Tom would be heartbroken. Priya would change things fast.

A.text: Promote Tom. Eight loyal years, he knows the culture cold, and loyalty has to count for something. Reward the years, keep the culture, and coach him into the seat.

B.text: Hire Priya and move Tom out quickly. Keeping a passed-over insider poisons the new GM's authority from day one. A clean break is kinder. Priya needs a clear runway.

C.text: Interview both against the same clear standard: who can grow the team and the numbers. Tell Tom honestly where he stands either way. Rigor plus care: the winner earns it.

cards.host_note: Principle: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You. Why C wins: Same standard for both, honest conversation with Tom either way; rigor plus care. What good discussion sounds like: what the GM standard actually is. What the wrong answers cost: A hires from guilt; B discards loyalty for speed.

cards.title: The Star's Exit
cards.scenario: Your best tech, Andre, tells you he is leaving to start his own shop across town. He learned everything working for you, and two of your younger techs admire him openly. Your GM wants you to enforce his noncompete. Andre thanks you for everything you taught him.

A.text: Counter with a big raise, a better truck, and a retention bonus. Replacing him will cost triple the raise. Most people threatening to leave just want to feel valued.

B.text: Congratulate him and mean it. Ask what he wished was different here, listen without defending yourself, and fix what you can for the people who stay. Grace keeps your reputation.

C.text: Let him go and make sure the team hears the honest odds. Most new shops fail within two years, and he will likely be back. Honesty now saves three more farewell speeches.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B wins: Congratulate him, ask what could've been better, fix it for those who stay; the team is watching. What good discussion sounds like: what his exit teaches about retention. What the wrong answers cost: A tries to buy back a dream; C poisons the well.

cards.title: The Big Bet
cards.scenario: An agency pitches you a massive brand campaign: radio, billboards, streaming, the works. The creative is the best you have ever seen, and they project it will double your inbound leads. The price is half your cash reserve. Your GM is dazzled.

A.text: Bet the half. The pitch was electric and the creative is the best you have ever seen. If it hits anywhere near their projections, you double the business in a year.

B.text: Skip the campaign and buy two more trucks and crews instead. Capacity you control beats advertising you hope works. Steel and crews compound. Billboards fade by next quarter.

C.text: Test it small before you bet the reserve. Run it in one market with a capped budget, track every dollar to booked revenue, and scale only what the numbers prove.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: Capped pilot, tracked to booked revenue, scale only what the numbers prove; never bet oxygen on a hunch. What good discussion sounds like: what the pilot budget and success line should be. What the wrong answers cost: A gambles the reserve; B buys trucks to avoid a decision.

cards.title: The Longtimer's Slump
cards.scenario: Paul has been with you twelve years, since the two-truck days. Lately his work has slipped: callbacks are up, customers say he seems distracted, and he snapped at a dispatcher last week. Your GM wants him on a formal performance plan. The crew is watching.

A.text: Let him go. The business cannot carry declining performance, and keeping him says tenure protects you from accountability. Do it respectfully, with fair severance.

B.text: Take him to coffee and ask what is going on, then listen. Twelve years earns a real conversation before judgment. Offer concrete help with clear expectations going forward.

C.text: Give him space and say nothing. Twelve years earns him a rough patch without the owner hovering. He will pull out of it on his own. Loyalty means not keeping score.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why B wins: Twelve years earns a real conversation before judgment; listen first, then pair help with clear expectations. What good discussion sounds like: loyalty versus accountability, and how to have the coffee conversation. What the wrong answers cost: A discards a person in a hard season; C avoids leadership.

cards.title: The Equipment Auction
cards.scenario: A retiring contractor's entire fleet and shop equipment goes to auction Saturday: trucks, tools, diagnostic gear, all of it. Prices will be a fraction of new. Your cash is decent but not deep, and your ops manager's wish list is twice your budget.

A.text: Buy aggressively. Quality used equipment at auction prices is the cheapest capacity you will ever add. You can resell what you do not use. Stock up now.

B.text: Walk in with a written list and a hard spending cap, and buy only what is on the list at or below your researched price. Every purchase must pay for itself in twelve months.

C.text: Buy nothing. Auctions are traps for owners with cash burning a hole in their pocket. Discipline means walking past a good deal you do not need.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: Written list, hard cap, researched prices, twelve-month payback test; auctions manufacture urgency. What good discussion sounds like: what's really on the list, and what the cap is. What the wrong answers cost: A buys clutter; C walks past real value.

cards.title: The Under-the-Table Bid
cards.scenario: A property manager with forty rental units offers you all his work if you bill him in cash at a twenty percent discount, no paperwork, no permits pulled. It would fill two crews year-round. He says every contractor he uses works this way.

A.text: Take the deal. Forty units of steady work could carry two crews year-round. Everyone in the trades does some cash work. Do not overthink a gift.

B.text: Decline the off-the-books deal and offer your best legitimate volume pricing in writing. Cash jobs with no paperwork put your license and integrity on the line.

C.text: Report him to the licensing board. Soliciting under-the-table work is illegal, and playing along is why this industry has a trust problem. Someone has to draw the line.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why B wins: Clean paper or no deal; the manager who asks you to cheat with him will cheat you. What good discussion sounds like: how much revenue is too much to walk away from. What the wrong answers cost: A risks license and integrity; C turns a business decision into a crusade.

cards.title: The Fake Review Scheme
cards.scenario: Your marketing lead proposes buying two hundred five-star reviews from a service overseas. Your competitor did it last year and now outranks you everywhere. The service guarantees the reviews look real, and the cost is less than one week's ad spend.

A.text: Shut it down immediately. Fake reviews are lies to your neighbors, and when it comes out, every honest review becomes suspect. Ask every happy customer at the job.

B.text: Skip the fake reviews and build a review engine. Train every tech to ask at the end of every clean job. Slower, but every star is real and permanent.

C.text: Buy the reviews. Everyone in this market does it, and two hundred fresh five-star reviews will fill your schedule for months. The chance of getting caught is tiny.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: Fake reviews are lies to neighbors; exposure poisons every real review too. What good discussion sounds like: building an honest review engine and why trust compounds. What the wrong answers cost: B is slow but honest; C risks the brand's credibility.

cards.title: The Employee's Loan Ask
cards.scenario: Eddie, one of your best techs for four years, asks for a private talk. His car died, he needs $3,000 for the repair, and his credit is shot. He is embarrassed and says he would not ask if he had another option.

A.text: Lend him the money with a written agreement, deducted from his paychecks over three months. The paperwork keeps it professional. Kindness with clear terms protects the friendship.

B.text: Tell him you do not make personal loans, because lending changes the relationship. Then help for real: advance pay he has earned and an intro to your credit union.

C.text: Decline and keep it short. Getting into employees' personal finances is a trap, and once you help one person the whole shop lines up. A clean no keeps the line where it belongs.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B wins: Compassion with boundaries. Real help (earned pay, a day, a credit-union intro) without a loan that warps the relationship. What good discussion sounds like: where helping ends and rescuing begins. What the wrong answers cost: A turns care into collections; C is clean but cold.

cards.title: The Unneeded Part
cards.scenario: A customer says your tech recommended a $1,800 control board, then a second opinion found a $90 sensor was the real problem. The customer feels upsold. Nate is a good producer with no prior complaints and insists the board looked bad. Your service manager is watching.

A.text: Apologize, refund the $1,800 in full, and confirm in writing the same day. Then walk through the job notes with Nate to find the gap, and set the team standard afterward.

B.text: Back Nate. Diagnostics involve judgment calls, and second-guessing techs kills their confidence. Apologize for the confusion but stand by the call. One complaint is not a pattern.

C.text: Call the customer yourself, apologize without excuses, and refund the $1,800 plus cover the sensor. Then review the steps with Nate privately and set the standard.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: the GM apologizes without excuses, refunds fully, and turns the incident into private coaching that distinguishes an honest mistake from a pattern. Discussion: does backing Nate (B) protect the team or teach that upsells go unexamined. Wrong answers: A (+150) skips the one-on-one with Nate where the real fix lives; B (+150) defends the tech at the customer's expense.

cards.title: The Skipped Lockout
cards.scenario: An install crew skipped the electrical lockout procedure on a panel swap to save time. Nothing happened, the job passed inspection, and the crew lead swears it was a one-time shortcut under deadline pressure. Your install manager wants to keep it quiet.

A.text: Report it, document it, and retrain the whole install team this week. A shortcut that could kill someone is not a one-time thing just because nobody got hurt.

B.text: Stop work for a day and retrain every crew on lockout. Find how deadline pressure made the shortcut acceptable, and fix the scheduling behind it. Discipline the lead per policy.

C.text: Keep it quiet inside the company. Give the crew lead a stern private warning and remind crews about lockout next meeting, no details. Discretion protects the company.

cards.host_note: Principle: Handle It While It's Small. Why B wins: the GM treats the near-miss as a system failure, retrains everyone, fixes the deadline pressure that caused it, and verifies compliance. Discussion: is firing the lead strong leadership or fear-based. Wrong answers: A (+150) reports outward before fixing inward; C ($0) covers up a life-safety violation and guarantees the next shortcut.

cards.title: The Blame Game
cards.scenario: A $14,000 job died: wrong equipment on the truck, and the homeowner canceled. Sales lead Dana and Production lead Marcus each blame the other's department, and their teams picked up the fight. The shop is tense. Both are protecting their own crews instead of the company.

A.text: Bring them together today. The miss belongs to the company, not a department. Write the handoff standard, verify it held next week, and rule out blaming other departments.

B.text: Stay out of it. They are proven managers, and a GM who referees fights teaches escalation. Give it a few days and check whether the tension cooled on its own.

C.text: Back the stronger department this month, openly. The numbers tell the story, and winners should know results matter. Quietly tell the weaker side to tighten its handoffs.

cards.host_note: Principle: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame. Why A wins: the GM absorbs the miss at the company level, ends the inter-department war, and replaces blame with a written standard that gets checked. Discussion: does staying out of it (B) build independence or let resentment grow; is picking a side (C) leadership or favoritism. Wrong answers: B (+150) lets the feud harden into culture; C (+150) teaches teams that blame games get rewarded.

cards.title: The Harassment Complaint
cards.scenario: CSR Jen came to you privately: a senior tech has made crude comments to her for weeks. She is scared to name him formally because he is popular and she is new. She asked you to keep it between you two. You believe her, and doing nothing is not an option.

A.text: Thank Jen, explain what happens next, and investigate promptly and privately. Document everything, guard her from retaliation, and act on what you find, up to termination.

B.text: Move Jen to a different shift so she no longer works near the tech. This solves her immediate problem without a confrontation, and she keeps her job.

C.text: Keep it between you two as she asked and handle it informally. Have a quiet word with the tech about professionalism, no names. Most situations resolve with a quiet warning.

cards.host_note: Principle: Safe to Speak. Why A wins: the GM honors Jen's courage with a real process, investigates properly, protects against retaliation, and follows through. Discussion: is the quiet word (C) discretion or cowardice. Wrong answers: B (+150) relocates the victim and leaves the behavior in place; C ($0) buries a harassment complaint and teaches every employee that speaking up changes nothing.

cards.title: The Coasting Star
cards.scenario: Rob was your best salesperson for three years. Lately his numbers slipped 25 percent, he leaves early Fridays, and skipped the last two trainings. He says he is fine, just in a rut. One rep asked why standards seem different for Rob.

A.text: Cut his commission rate until his numbers recover. Money is the language salespeople understand, and the gap between his pay and his output will get his attention fast.

B.text: Give him space. Three years at the top earns a down quarter, and pressuring a proven producer usually backfires. He said he is in a rut, and ruts pass. Check back next quarter.

C.text: Lead with respect for his history. Honor the three great years, then name what you are seeing. Ask what changed and listen. Build a thirty-day plan with targets and training.

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why C wins: the GM honors the history, names the present honestly, listens for the real cause, and builds a plan with accountability. Discussion: does the team's double-standard question set the real urgency. Wrong answers: A ($0) punishes without understanding and may lose him entirely; B (+150) teaches the team that stars play by different rules.

cards.title: The Overbooked Week
cards.scenario: Sales booked 40 percent more jobs than Production can staff. Techs are talking forced overtime, and delay calls start Wednesday. Dana in Sales is celebrating. Marcus in Production is furious. The overbooked customers do not know yet.

A.text: Tell Production to cover it with overtime and weekends. Sales did its job, and the company cannot turn away revenue when the phones are hot. Overtime pay softens the grumbling.

B.text: Cap Sales at capacity and call the overbooked customers now, honestly, with a real date and a named owner. Then build a weekly capacity handshake between Dana and Marcus.

C.text: Hire two temp techs immediately. The demand is real and the fastest fix is more hands. Temps take the simpler installs while your crews handle the complex ones.

cards.host_note: Principle: Selling Is Helping. Why B wins: the GM tells the truth early, protects customers with real dates and ownership, and builds a Sales-Production capacity agreement so it never repeats. Discussion: does capping Sales punish success. Wrong answers: A (+150) burns out the crews and ships sloppy work; C (+150) gambles quality on temp strangers.

cards.title: The Forgotten Win
cards.scenario: Best month ever, and nobody celebrated. The numbers went out in an email, a few thumbs-up replies, everyone back to work. Two long-tenured techs told the office manager the wins just disappear into the next busy week. You can feel the flatness.

A.text: Send a company-wide email with the record numbers by department. Written recognition lasts and shows exactly who contributed what. Copy the owner so leadership sees it.

B.text: Gather everyone for twenty minutes and tell the story of the month out loud, naming the people who stepped up. Thank specific people for specific things, in front of their peers.

C.text: Do nothing special. Record months come from everyone doing their job, and adults do not need parties for meeting expectations. The paycheck already reflects the extra work.

cards.host_note: Principle: Make Me Feel Important. Why B wins: the GM celebrates specifically and publicly, names names, and turns the win into the next goal. Discussion: is the email (A) efficient or forgettable. Wrong answers: A (+150) files the win where nobody feels it; C (0) teaches the team excellence is merely expected.

cards.title: The Chaotic Warehouse
cards.scenario: Your warehouse is a mess. Techs waste forty-five minutes each morning hunting parts, fittings get ordered twice, and two techs argued over the last blower motor. Ben, the warehouse manager, runs it from memory and resists any system. Techs keep personal stashes in their trucks.

A.text: Walk the warehouse with Ben and set the standard: every part gets a labeled home, stock checked weekly. Build the system with him, not over him, and give him thirty days.

B.text: Leave Ben alone. He has run that warehouse for years, and imposing a system on a guy who works from memory will breed resentment. The truck stashes are efficient anyway.

C.text: Hire an assistant for Ben to do the organizing. He knows where everything is and just needs hands. Organized parts pay for themselves in recovered tech hours.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why A wins: the GM sets a clear operational standard, builds the system with Ben instead of around him, and verifies the result in recovered tech time. Discussion: is Ben's resistance pride or a signal the system must fit him. Wrong answers: C (+150) spends payroll to avoid a direct conversation with Ben; B ($0) normalizes forty-five wasted minutes every morning.

cards.title: The Phone-Shy CSR
cards.scenario: Maria, your new CSR, freezes on live calls. Warm and sharp in person, knows the scripts, but stumbles on the phone, holds too long, and yesterday a caller asked for someone else. The lead wants her off the phones. Maria feels sick before every shift.

A.text: Move Maria to back-office work permanently. Some people are not phone people, and forcing calls she dreads hurts her and the customers. Put her strengths where they fit.

B.text: Build her up in stages: scripted outbound confirmations first, then inbound overflow with a buddy, then full calls. Review recordings together weekly and name one thing to improve.

C.text: Give her two more weeks on the phones and see if she settles in. Most new CSRs are shaky at first. Extra attention now may make her more self-conscious. Decide at month's end.

cards.host_note: Principle: Train or Remove. Why B wins: the GM treats phone confidence as a trainable skill and designs a real ramp with stages, coaching, and encouragement. Discussion: is moving her off phones (A) kindness or giving up too early. Wrong answers: A (+150) wastes a good hire the company chose; C ($0) confuses waiting with developing.

cards.title: The Overwhelmed Dispatcher
cards.scenario: Jen, your new dispatcher, is crying in the break room. Third week, the board blew up with emergencies, two techs yelled at her over the radio, and she sent a crew to the wrong address. She told the office manager she is not cut out for this.

A.text: Tell Jen honestly that dispatch might not be for her. The seat needs someone who handles pressure from day one. Offer a graceful exit before a bigger mistake hurts a customer.

B.text: Sit with Jen today and ask what felt hardest. Then build her ramp-up: shadow shifts, a triage playbook, a direct line to you. Speak to the techs privately about radio conduct.

C.text: Give Jen a pep talk. The first month is the hardest, and she needs encouragement more than anything. Tell her to push through. Most dispatchers find their rhythm by month two.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B wins: the GM meets the human moment first, diagnoses the actual gaps, builds a real ramp-up, and corrects the techs' behavior. Discussion: does the company owe Jen real onboarding before judging her on a live board. Wrong answers: C (+150) confuses encouragement with development; A (0) discards a good hire the company never trained.

cards.title: The Vendor Kickback
cards.scenario: A longtime vendor offered you a personal rebate at lunch: two percent of everything the company buys from him, paid to you directly, off the books. About $8,000 a year in your pocket. He laughed and said every GM in town does it.

A.text: Take it but buy his equipment only when it is genuinely the best option. The rebate does not have to corrupt your judgment, and $8,000 is real money for your family.

B.text: Take the rebate and use it to fund team bonuses or the holiday party. The money benefits the people doing the work, and your hands stay clean because you never profited personally.

C.text: Decline it clearly, at the table: your purchasing rests on quality, warranty, and price for the customer, nothing else. Document the offer and tell the owner.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: the GM refuses the bribe outright, protects every future purchasing decision from suspicion, and reports it upward so the pattern cannot continue quietly. Discussion: what does every GM in town does it reveal about the industry. Wrong answers: A (+150) sells the company's judgment for $8,000; B ($0) launders a bribe through the holiday party and teaches the team ethics are flexible.

cards.title: The Rude Dispatcher
cards.scenario: A loyal six-year customer says your dispatcher Tom was short with her and hung up before she finished. She is calling a competitor. Tom says she was rambling and five calls were holding. He is your fastest dispatcher and the board is full.

A.text: Call the customer yourself, take full responsibility, and book a priority visit. Then play the call back with Tom, set the standard, and fix the staffing that set him up to fail.

B.text: Back Tom up. The customer was holding up a busy board, and dispatchers must keep calls moving or the schedule slips. Tell Tom you trust his judgment. Speed matters in that seat.

C.text: Pull the call and review it with Tom privately, focusing on what the customer heard. Coach him on a recovery line for long calls, and fix the board load that made him rush.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why A wins: the GM takes the blame upward, repairs the customer personally, and fixes both the behavior and the system that caused it. Discussion: is the coach-only option (C) almost right but leaves the customer unrepaired; does defending Tom (B) teach the team speed excuses rudeness. Wrong answers: B (+150) trades a six-year customer for a fast board; C (+150) coaches but skips the repair the customer is waiting for.

cards.title: The Mentor Ask
cards.scenario: Rosa is your best installer but has no interest in teaching. Two green techs need mentoring, Rosa told you flatly that training rookies is not her job, and the Production lead wants you to order her to do it. Forced mentoring usually backfires.

A.text: Order Rosa to mentor the new techs as part of her job. Senior people train junior people. Put it in writing, set a schedule, and check weekly. She will step up or reveal herself.

B.text: Ask Rosa what part of mentoring she dislikes, listen, then design a role she can say yes to. Maybe ride-alongs but no classroom sessions. Add a small raise tied to their progress.

C.text: Leave Rosa alone and give the mentoring to a willing mid-level tech. Forcing your best producer into a hated role risks losing her. A willing mentor beats a resentful expert.

cards.host_note: Principle: Train or Remove. Why B wins: the GM finds what is really behind the resistance and builds a mentoring role Rosa can succeed in, with recognition tied to results. Discussion: does ordering her (A) get compliance or quiet sabotage. Wrong answers: A (+150) turns the best tech into a resentful teacher; C (+150) leaves two green techs to figure it out alone.

cards.title: The Revolving Door
cards.scenario: Your appointment center lost four CSRs in five months. Kelly, the lead, says young people do not want to work. Exit interviews mention pay, angry callers, and feeling invisible. Kelly stopped doing them. You are spending a fortune replacing people.

A.text: Raise CSR pay two dollars an hour across the board. The exits mention pay and the market is competitive. Better pay slows the revolving door and attracts stronger candidates.

B.text: Accept the turnover as the nature of the job. Call centers churn, so build a faster hiring pipeline and treat the seat as entry-level by design. Manage the reality.

C.text: Treat it as a leadership problem starting with Kelly. Run real exit interviews yourself to find what would have kept them. Then fix it: scripts, a path upward, recognition.

cards.host_note: Principle: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You. Why C wins: the GM stops blaming the labor market, gathers real data from exits, and makes retention part of Kelly's job with concrete fixes. Discussion: is Kelly the problem or just unequipped. Wrong answers: A ($0) spends payroll without knowing if pay is the real cause; B (+150) normalizes failure as strategy.

cards.title: The Permit Request
cards.scenario: A customer wants you to skip the permit on an $18,000 changeout to save time and the fee. His neighbor did it, he will pay cash today, and he promises not to tell. Your install manager says it is quick money and the crew is free Thursday.

A.text: Do the job without the permit but document everything. The work will be done to code regardless. Refusing just sends him to a competitor who will say yes.

B.text: Decline clearly: permits protect his insurance and resale, and your company does not do unpermitted work, period. Offer prep now, with install booked when the permit clears.

C.text: Agree, but charge the normal price and keep the permit fee as extra margin. The customer asked for the shortcut, so the savings are yours. Few of these jobs get inspected anyway.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why B wins: the GM holds the standard at a cost, explains it in customer terms, and offers a legitimate path forward. Discussion: does the cash temptation reveal what the install manager really values. Wrong answers: A (+150) trades the license and reputation for one Thursday; C (0) adds pocketing the fee to the violation.

cards.title: The Gossiping Dispatcher
cards.scenario: You overheard Angela telling a customer that the tech on their job is slow and they should ask for someone else. The customer laughed. Angela is well-liked and fast on the board. But she told a customer your own tech is not good enough, and he will hear it by Friday.

A.text: Talk to Angela today. Tell her what you heard and how it lands, and set the rule: we never disparage our own people to customers. Ask what frustrated her, then fix the real issue.

B.text: Send a general reminder about professional phone conduct, without naming Angela. A team-wide note covers it, Angela will recognize herself, and you avoid the hard talk.

C.text: Let it slide this time. Angela is one of your best, she was just making conversation, and the customer laughed it off. If it becomes a pattern you will address it then.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why A wins: the GM protects the tech's dignity, sets a clear standard privately, and still gets curious about the underlying frustration. Discussion: is letting it slide (C) trust or neglect. Wrong answers: B (+150) lets Angela learn the standard does not apply to her by name; C ($0) teaches the office that trash-talking techs is tolerated.

cards.title: The Quiet Shop
cards.scenario: Slow season and the shop feels flat. Phones are quiet, two techs were sent home early last week, and the energy is gone. Nobody quit, but people are doing the minimum, waiting for busy season. A flat team in February becomes a sloppy team in May.

A.text: Gather the team, tell the truth about where the company stands, and give the slow season a purpose. Ask each person to own one improvement, check weekly, and celebrate small wins.

B.text: Leave it alone. Adults do not need pep talks, and pushing energy with no work feels fake. Save your leadership capital for busy season. The crew will ramp up when the phones ring.

C.text: Offer a small bonus for every referral that turns into a job. A referral push fills the board and gives the team something to chase. Post a leaderboard and update it daily.

cards.host_note: Principle: Why Power. Why A wins: the GM gives the slow season meaning with honest communication, personal ownership, and visible follow-through. Discussion: is the referral bonus (C) energy bought or rented. Wrong answers: B (+150) lets the flat season set the culture; C (+150) teaches the team motivation only comes with cash attached.

cards.title: The Falsified Timecards
cards.scenario: Accounting found tech Dave adding two hours to his timecard most weeks for three months, about $1,800 total. The evidence is solid: GPS logs versus clock times. Dave is good, well-liked, has a family, and has no idea you know.

A.text: Walk him out today. Falsifying timecards is theft, and the amount and pattern prove intent. Keeping him tells every tech that stealing gets a second chance. Act fast and quietly.

B.text: Fire him in front of the whole shop at the Friday meeting and explain exactly what he did. A public example will kill timecard fraud overnight. Humiliation is a powerful deterrent.

C.text: Confront Dave privately with the evidence, calmly, no audience. Let him explain, then decide per the standard: termination for theft, handled with dignity. Pay what he earned.

cards.host_note: Principle: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything. Why C wins: the GM upholds the standard on theft without exception, but does it privately and with dignity, hearing him out first. Discussion: does the team need to know the reason or just the standard. Wrong answers: A (+150) skips hearing him out; B ($0) turns justice into a spectacle that degrades everyone watching.

cards.title: The Slow Season Cash
cards.scenario: Late winter, cash is tight, and the next two months look thin. You can cover payroll and bills, but barely. Marketing wants to keep ad spending to fill the spring pipeline. The service manager wants to cut all marketing and ride it out.

A.text: Protect cash but spend surgically: cut brand ads to zero, keep only the cheapest cost-per-booked-job channels, and fund a maintenance blitz, bid follow-up, and referral asks.

B.text: Keep marketing spending as planned. Cutting ads now empties the spring pipeline, and companies that advertise through downturns come out stronger. This is what reserves are for.

C.text: Borrow on the business line of credit to keep everything running as normal. The slow season is temporary and the team should not feel it. Pay it down in the spring rush.

cards.host_note: Principle: Cash Is Life. Why A wins: the GM treats cash as the constraint, cuts what does not produce, and funds only pipeline activity with a measurable return, communicated as strategy. Discussion: is cutting deep discipline or fear. Wrong answers: B (+150) spends reserves on hope; C (0) borrows to avoid deciding.

cards.title: The Social Media Rant
cards.scenario: Tech Chris posted publicly that the company overworks everyone and the equipment is junk. Three coworkers liked it, and a customer asked if it is true. Chris is decent with no prior issues. Your office manager wants him fired today. The post is still up.

A.text: Fire Chris today. A public post calling the equipment junk is insubordination, and keeping him tells everyone they can trash the company online. Act fast and the lesson lands.

B.text: Talk to Chris privately today; start by listening. Ask what drove the post. Tell him plainly that public posts hurt the whole team, and complaints stay inside the company.

C.text: Ignore the post and hope it fades. Responding gives it more attention, firing him makes him a martyr, and most storms blow over in a day. The smartest move is no move at all.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why B wins: the GM hears Chris out before judging, addresses the public behavior clearly, and treats the complaint's substance as data worth fixing. Discussion: does firing (A) protect the company or just prove his point. Wrong answers: A (+150) turns a frustrated tech into a public martyr; C ($0) lets a public accusation sit unanswered while the team watches.

cards.title: The Payroll Question
cards.scenario: Every lead is lobbying you on payroll. The standard is $3,000 per department per round, but Sales wants $4,500, Production wants $4,000, and Accounting says the margin cannot take it. Each has a real argument. You must anchor the number, and everyone is watching.

A.text: Split it: $3,750 for every department. Equal treatment keeps the peace, and nobody can say they were singled out. Revisit the numbers next round if workloads change.

B.text: Hold the $3,000 standard and show the margin math in plain numbers. Tell Sales and Production exactly what output would earn more next round, so the raise follows results.

C.text: Give Sales and Production what they asked, and hold the rest at standard. Payroll should follow opportunity. Rebalance next round if the numbers prove you wrong.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why B wins: payroll tied to the margin target with transparent math, and the ask becomes an earned standard. Discussion: does holding the line risk losing good people, or does caving teach leads that lobbying beats arithmetic. Wrong answers: A (+150) spends margin on politics; C (+150) rewards the loudest departments.

cards.title: The Discount Debate
cards.scenario: A competitor is running 20 percent off installs and Sales wants to match it. At 20 percent off you need nearly a third more jobs for the same gross dollars, and crews are near capacity. Dana says they are losing bids on price. The team waits.

A.text: Match the discount on smaller jobs only, where the margin hit is easier to absorb. Give Sales a price weapon without giving away the store. Limit it to two weeks and measure daily.

B.text: Discount maintenance agreements instead of installs. The lower ticket makes the math work, it fills slow weeks, and every agreement is a future replacement customer.

C.text: Say no, and show the team the math: how many extra jobs a 20 percent cut requires at current capacity. Then arm Sales with a clear value story and follow-up on every lost bid.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Price Before Value. Why C wins: the GM refuses to buy revenue with margin, teaches the real math, and arms Sales with value and follow-up instead of a discount crutch. Discussion: is matching on small jobs (A) a clever compromise or the same trap in miniature. Wrong answers: A (+150) trains customers to wait for sales; B (+150) dodges the real question of whether the team can sell value at full price.

cards.title: The Paperwork War
cards.scenario: Lisa in Accounting and Rob in Sales are barely speaking. His job files arrive incomplete, delaying invoicing by weeks; he says her paperwork demands cost him sales. Each blames the other. The invoicing delays are now hurting cash flow.

A.text: Tell Rob paperwork is part of selling: no complete file, no commission paid. Money gets attention faster than lectures. Announce it as company policy so it is not personal.

B.text: Hear each out separately, then bring them together with one question: what does a complete job file look like, exactly. Build a checklist both agree on with a 24-hour turnaround.

C.text: Assign a part-time admin to chase Rob's paperwork after the fact. A detail-loving person keeps invoicing moving while Lisa and Rob focus on what they do best.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why B wins: the GM hears both sides before acting, then replaces the personal conflict with a jointly built standard and a weekly check. Discussion: is withholding commission (A) accountability or a new weapon in the war. Wrong answers: A (+150) turns paperwork into a pay dispute; C (0) spends payroll to avoid the conversation the GM should have had.

cards.title: The Fading Veteran
cards.scenario: Tom has been with you eleven years. His work is slipping: callbacks up, new procedures skipped, and younger techs notice he gets away with it. He is fifty-eight, proud, and you suspect he knows he is fading but cannot admit it.

A.text: Quietly reduce his hours and give the tougher jobs to younger techs, hoping he takes the hint. He will figure it out when the paycheck shrinks.

B.text: Have the honest conversation you owe him after eleven years. Tell him what you see, with specifics, and ask why. Build a plan together: standard, support, timeline.

C.text: Put him on a formal performance plan immediately, same as anyone else. Eleven years does not buy exemption, and the younger techs are watching. Document the gaps and set targets.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why B wins: the GM has the hard conversation with specifics, listens for the real cause, and builds a plan with him, honoring eleven years without exempting him from standards. Discussion: is the formal plan (C) fair or just cold. Wrong answers: A ($0) manages him out through the paycheck, which is cowardly and transparent; C (+150) treats a loyal veteran like a stranger.

cards.title: The Schedule Fight
cards.scenario: Two install crews both need the same lift truck Thursday, and both jobs are sold. Angela booked it first, but Chris says his job is bigger and his customer more important. They are arguing in the shop, techs are watching, and the dispatcher is frozen.

A.text: Decide it yourself, on the spot, and make it final. Assign the truck to one crew and move the other job with a clear explanation. End the arguing in front of the techs.

B.text: Let Angela and Chris settle it like adults. Leadership means working out resource conflicts without running to the GM. Give them thirty minutes and hold them to an answer.

C.text: Give the truck to Chris. His job is bigger and the revenue matters more this week. Reschedule Angela's job with an apology call. Revenue should drive these calls.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why A wins: the GM hears both sides, makes a clear final call, owns the schedule, and ends the public argument without rewarding whoever yelled loudest. Discussion: does letting them settle it (B) build leadership or abdicate the decision. Wrong answers: B (+150) lets a shop-floor fight set the schedule; C (+150) teaches crews that revenue excuses process.

cards.title: The Struggling Coordinator
cards.scenario: Priya, your new project coordinator, is three weeks in and drowning. Jobs get booked without permits pulled, techs cannot find paperwork, and the Production lead wants her moved off the desk. She got a binder and a password on day one. Her confidence is fading.

A.text: Move Priya into a simpler support role. The job needs someone who can already do it, and three weeks of mistakes is enough evidence. Hire for experience this time.

B.text: Tell the Production lead to back off and give Priya another month. Learning curves are normal, and pressure only makes mistakes more likely. Most people figure it out with space.

C.text: Define exactly what good looks like, then pair her with your best coordinator for two weeks shadowing. Give her a daily checklist and review it each morning until she owns it.

cards.host_note: Principle: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool. Why C wins: the GM builds the person instead of discarding her, with a real training plan, daily structure, and a communicated timeline. Discussion: did the company fail Priya first with no training system; is the Production lead's frustration valid but aimed at the wrong target. Wrong answers: A (+150) wastes a good hire and restarts the cycle; B (+150) confuses patience with development.

cards.title: The Open War
cards.scenario: Sales manager Dana and Production lead Marcus had a shouting match in front of the whole shop over a botched handoff. Techs watched, CSRs heard it, and both camps are gossiping. Each told you privately the other is impossible.

A.text: Meet each privately today, then bring them together. Leaders shouting in front of the team is unacceptable. Full stop. Work the handoff problem until there is a written agreement.

B.text: Reorganize so they rarely interact: reroute handoffs through the office manager and separate their schedules. Design around the friction and both keep their authority.

C.text: Call a full team meeting and let Dana and Marcus each present their side, then let the team vote on the handoff process. A democratic process gives the new standard legitimacy.

cards.host_note: Principle: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves. Why A wins: the GM addresses the behavior standard privately with each leader, then fixes the real process problem with both at the table, modeling the culture the shop should copy. Discussion: is restructuring around them (B) smart design or avoidance. Wrong answers: B (+150) builds the company around two egos; C ($0) turns a leadership failure into a popularity contest that humiliates the loser.

cards.title: The Skipped Safety Check
cards.scenario: On a ride-along you watched Dave skip the combustion safety check on a furnace tune-up. It adds ten minutes, the customer was hovering, and Dave says he has done hundreds and could tell it was fine. Nobody got hurt. The service manager says a write-up will kill morale.

A.text: Sit Dave down privately: the safety check happens every time, period. It is about what the company does on every call. Put it in writing, then spot-check his calls for a month.

B.text: Let it go with a quiet word. Dave was right that the furnace was fine, and a formal write-up over a non-incident will make the crew paranoid. Mention it casually and trust him.

C.text: Shorten the safety checklist so techs actually complete it. A short list done every time beats a long list skipped half the time. Have the service manager redesign it with Dave.

cards.host_note: Principle: Brilliant on the Basics. Why A wins: the GM treats the skipped safety check as a standards issue, not a luck issue, addresses it directly, and verifies it stuck. Discussion: does the quiet word (B) show judgment or just leniency for a favorite. Wrong answers: B (+150) teaches the crew standards are optional when you are good; C (0) negotiates the safety standard down to whatever the busiest tech will tolerate.

cards.title: The Damaged Drywall
cards.scenario: Your crew cracked a large section of finished basement drywall running a line set. The homeowner is upset, the crew lead admits they rushed, and repair costs about $900 plus a day of delay. The install manager suggests patching it quietly and not mentioning it.

A.text: Patch it quietly with crew time and say nothing. The customer may never notice the full extent, and the company avoids an awkward talk and a $900 bill. Handle it internally.

B.text: Tell the customer yourself today, before they discover it. Apologize plainly and hire a proper finisher at the company's expense, then review the cutting procedure with the crew.

C.text: Blame the home's construction: the drywall was already weak. Offer to patch it as a courtesy but make clear it was not the crew's fault. This protects the team and keeps the $900.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why B wins: the GM tells the truth before being caught, pays for a professional repair, and fixes the procedure, which is what earns the lifetime customer. Discussion: what does the install manager's quiet-patch suggestion reveal about the culture. Wrong answers: A (+150) bets the reputation that the customer will not look closely; C (0) lies to a customer standing in their own basement.

cards.title: The Viral Complaint
cards.scenario: A customer posted a furious one-star review: your tech tracked mud over her white carpet, broke a vase, and laughed. It is getting shared locally. Your records show boot covers were worn and no vase is in the notes. She demands a refund plus $2,000.

A.text: Respond publicly with the facts: post the job notes, note the boot covers, and note no vase was mentioned during the visit. A firm rebuttal shows you do not get pushed around.

B.text: Ignore the review completely. Responding feeds the algorithm, and most readers discount angry rants on their own. Generate honest positive reviews to bury it, and let silence work.

C.text: Respond publicly once, briefly and warmly, and invite her to call you. Then call her yourself, listen fully, and inspect the carpet in person if allowed. Fix what is real, kindly.

cards.host_note: Principle: Do Right When It Costs You. Why C wins: the GM responds with composure, takes the conversation private, verifies the facts in person, and lets future customers see character instead of combat. Discussion: what do the boot-cover records actually prove. Wrong answers: A ($0) turns a complaint into a public war the company cannot win; B (+150) lets an unanswered story become the truth.

cards.title: The Rogue Purchaser
cards.scenario: Office manager Tina has been ordering supplies and tools without approval: a $600 label printer, $400 in organizers, specialty tools the techs requested. Each is reasonable, but there is no budget or approval step, and accounting found $2,300 in unapproved spending this quarter.

A.text: Reprimand Tina formally and require your personal approval for every purchase over $50. Unapproved spending is a control failure, and a tight line restores discipline fast.

B.text: Do nothing formal. Every purchase was reasonable, and punishing initiative teaches her to let problems sit. Thank her and move on.

C.text: Sit with Tina and build the system together: a monthly budget she manages, a per-item approval limit, and a simple log. Thank her, and be direct that unapproved spending stops now.

cards.host_note: Principle: Systems, Not Heroes. Why C wins: the GM replaces missing controls with a clear, jointly built system, respects Tina's initiative, and draws a firm line without turning it into punishment. Discussion: is the $50 approval line (A) control or distrust. Wrong answers: A (+150) punishes initiative and buries the GM in trivia; B ($0) guarantees the next quarter looks the same.

cards.title: Two Big Jobs, One Crew
cards.scenario: Friday morning. One crew is free and two jobs were promised for today: a $22,000 replacement for a customer who waited three weeks, and a $9,000 emergency repair for a nursing home with no heat in two wings. Other crews are maxed.

A.text: Send the crew to the nursing home first, then the replacement. Call that customer yourself, explain honestly, and set a firm Saturday start.

B.text: Send the crew to the $22,000 replacement. It is far more revenue, the customer waited three weeks, and that margin funds payroll. Promise the nursing home first thing Saturday.

C.text: Split the crew, two techs to each job. Both customers were promised Friday, and keeping both promises halfway beats breaking one. The nursing home gets partial heat back today.

cards.host_note: Principle: One Department: Customer Service. Why A wins: the GM sets a clear priority rule, human need before scheduled revenue, communicates honestly to the delayed customer, and makes the standard visible. Discussion: is the revenue logic of B defensible or short-term. Wrong answers: B (+150) teaches the team dollars outrank people in a crisis; C (+150) delivers two half-done jobs.

cards.title: The Slipping Numbers
cards.scenario: Revenue is down 15 percent over two months and the owner is asking questions. Each lead blames something different: Marketing blames the season, Sales blames lead quality, Production blames the schedule. You meet the owner next week.

A.text: Tell the owner the truth: the numbers are down, you are still diagnosing, and a plan follows by month's end. Then pull the funnel stage by stage and build the fix with your leads.

B.text: Give the owner the leads' explanations, packaged cleanly: seasonal softness plus lead quality, with a plan to spend more on marketing. Present a united front and buy time.

C.text: Diagnose before you explain. Pull the numbers yourself and find the actual break point, not theories. Fix that thing, then walk in with the cause and the fix in motion.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why C wins: the GM finds the real break point in the funnel before theorizing, fixes that specific thing, and walks in with answers already in motion. Discussion: is telling the owner you are still diagnosing (A) honesty or unpreparedness. Wrong answers: A (+150) brings honesty without homework; B ($0) launders excuses upward and the owner will find the truth anyway.

cards.title: The Callback Spike
cards.scenario: Callbacks are up 30 percent this quarter. Techs are returning to fix their own work, which kills the schedule and tells customers the first visit was not good enough. The service manager blames new hires, senior techs blame rushed scheduling. Nobody has data.

A.text: Slow the schedule across the board so techs have more time per job. Rushed techs make mistakes, and the spike matches the busier board. Give every job an extra thirty minutes.

B.text: Buy the new diagnostic tablets the senior techs want. Better tools mean fewer missed problems, and it shows you take quality seriously. Sometimes equipment is the fix.

C.text: Stop guessing and get the data first. Pull ninety days of callbacks, sort by tech, job type, and reason, and find the real pattern before acting. Then fix what the data shows.

cards.host_note: Principle: Define Reality First. Why C wins: the GM refuses to act on theories, finds the real pattern in the data, and fixes that, which is fair as well as pragmatic. Discussion: is slowing the schedule (A) a reasonable precaution or an expensive guess. Wrong answers: A (+150) spends schedule and payroll on a hunch; B ($0) buys tablets to solve what might be a people problem.

cards.title: The Poaching Threat
cards.scenario: A competitor is offering your techs $4 an hour more. Two mid-level installers are already interviewing, and the rumor is spreading. Your service manager wants you to match it across the board: over $150,000 a year, which the margin cannot absorb without price increases.

A.text: Match the raise for everyone, immediately. Losing trained techs costs far more than $150,000. Announce it this week, and raise prices next quarter to cover it.

B.text: Do not match blindly. Learn what keeps your best people beyond pay, fix what you can fix fast, and give targeted raises where the market moved. Say plainly what you did.

C.text: Let the market decide and wish the leavers well. If a rival wants to overpay, that is their problem. Hire strong replacements at current rates and hold your cost structure.

cards.host_note: Principle: Pay for What You Want Repeated. Why B wins: the GM refuses the panic raise, learns what actually retains each person, pays where market and merit both say so, and communicates it openly. Discussion: is holding your nerve discipline or denial about the rumor's power. Wrong answers: A (+150) permanently raises costs on a rumor; C (0) pretends trained techs are interchangeable.

cards.title: The Feuding Techs
cards.scenario: Kyle and Sam, two of your best techs, have not spoken in a week. It started over a borrowed tool, escalated through the group chat, and the shop split into two camps. Jobs get done, but newer techs are walking on eggshells. Each says the other started it.

A.text: Separate them permanently on different crews and shifts. Distance ends the daily friction, both keep producing, and the shop camps dissolve. Frame it as scheduling, not punishment.

B.text: Stay out of it and let the crew sort its own dynamics. As long as jobs get done and customers are happy, the personal stuff is their business. That is not the GM's job.

C.text: Meet each privately first, then sit them down together: the feud ends today. Give each a role in the next team training so they must collaborate, and check in weekly for a month.

cards.host_note: Principle: Never Act on One Side of a Story. Why C wins: the GM hears each side privately, sets a clear behavioral standard face to face, and engineers a reason for them to work together, with follow-up. Discussion: is separation (A) practical or just conflict avoidance. Wrong answers: A (+150) teaches the shop that feuds get rewarded with custom schedules; B (0) lets a tool dispute set the shop's culture.

cards.title: The Price Increase
cards.scenario: Costs are up 12 percent and service rates must rise. The office dreads telling customers, techs fear pushback, and your service manager wants to quietly update the price book and hope nobody notices. The team needs to hear it from you first.

A.text: Lay out the cost reality in plain numbers before customers hear a word. Explain what is rising, what the new rates are, and exactly what to say when asked why. Set a clear date.

B.text: Quietly update the price book and let the team discover the new rates. Announcing it just creates anxiety, and customers accept inflation as normal. Less drama is better.

C.text: Raise prices for new customers only and shield the existing base. New business carries the higher margin, and this rewards loyalty while avoiding hard conversations.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why A wins: the GM tells the team the truth first, arms them with numbers and language, and sets a clear date, so accountability for the new prices is possible. Discussion: is the quiet rollout (B) low-drama or cowardly. Wrong answers: B (+150) lets the team learn it from angry customers; C (+150) trains customers that loyalty means never paying more.

cards.title: The Marketing Overspend
cards.scenario: Marketing spent 40 percent over budget on digital ads. Tina shows click reports and says awareness is up, but booked jobs are flat and cost per booked job nearly doubled. Other leads ask why Marketing can overspend while they hold their budgets.

A.text: Give Tina one more quarter at the same spend. Cutting mid-flight wastes the investment, and brand building takes time. Tell the other leads marketing runs on a longer cycle.

B.text: Approve a 15 percent increase as a compromise. Tina keeps the campaign alive, the other leads see overspending has limits, and you avoid a demoralizing fight. Check in monthly.

C.text: Freeze the overspend and rebuild the budget around cost per booked job. Agree on a target the company can afford, fund only channels that hit it, and review with Tina biweekly.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: the GM replaces click reports with cost per booked job, funds only what hits it, and applies the rule fairly across departments. Discussion: is brand awareness worth any weight at all. Wrong answers: A (+150) funds hope for another quarter; B (0) negotiates the budget instead of managing it.

cards.title: The Staffing Call
cards.scenario: Three jobs are ready and you have crew capacity for two this week: a $25,000 replacement at 35 percent margin, a $12,000 replacement at 28 percent, and a $6,000 repair at 45 percent. All three customers want this week. Production wants the two replacements.

A.text: Schedule the two replacements and push the repair to next week. The two big tickets total $37,000 against $6,000. Revenue pays the bills, and big jobs drive the business.

B.text: Ask the customers who can wait and schedule around their answers. Whoever volunteers to move gets a small discount. That keeps every customer feeling heard.

C.text: Run the profit dollars: $8,750 vs $3,360 vs $2,700. Book the two replacements for $12,110 in profit, and schedule the repair first thing next week with a personal call.

cards.host_note: Principle: Know Your Numbers. Why C wins: the GM decides on gross profit dollars rather than revenue or margin rate alone, then handles the delayed customer honestly with a firm date. Discussion: is letting customers self-sort (B) respectful or an abdication. Wrong answers: A (+150) chases revenue while leaving profit on the table; B (0) lets the schedule be set by whoever complains least.

cards.title: The Late Crew
cards.scenario: Omar's install crew has been late to the first job three times in two weeks. His work quality is good, but the office is fielding apology calls. When it was mentioned, he shrugged about traffic. The other crews are noticing that nothing happened.

A.text: Talk to Omar privately, today. State what you have seen and ask what is going on. Set the standard in writing, then follow up every morning for two weeks.

B.text: Start the whole company ten minutes earlier to absorb the lateness. If one crew cannot hit the start time, the start time may be the problem. Announce it as schedule optimization.

C.text: Ignore it since the work quality is good. Great installers are hard to find, and risking a producer over fifteen minutes is foolish. Omar will probably self-correct.

cards.host_note: Principle: Expectations Before Accountability. Why A wins: the GM states the expectation clearly, asks what is behind it, documents the standard, and follows up, which is how accountability gets built. Discussion: does the shrug about traffic deserve curiosity before consequences. Wrong answers: B (+150) moves the goalposts for everyone to avoid one talk; C (0) teaches every crew that standards are suggestions.
